Out of every automotive segment on the market, the mid-size division is easily the most competitive. It’s where automakers pack the maximum utility buyers crave, and in some cases, pairing some models with spacious three-row seating. When I pitted the Honda Pilot against the Toyota Grand Highlander earlier this year, the Pilot earned my vote thanks to its athletic stance, engaging driving dynamics, and thoughtful tech suite.

For my next mid-size matchup, I’m putting it head-to-head with the redesigned GMC Acadia Denali. The Pilot faces a much tougher challenge here: GMC didn't just update its family cruiser — it gave it a massive footprint, an aggressive exterior presence, upscale cabin appointments, and serious tech.

Even though the 2026 GMC Acadia Denali Ultimate AWD I tested for a week comes with a significantly steeper $67,590 as-tested sticker, you might be surprised by how well it justifies that premium over the $54,990 as-tested price of the 2026 Honda Pilot Elite AWD.

3.5L 4-Cyl. V6 Variable Cylinder Management Engine

21 mpg city / 20 mpg highway / 23 mpg combined

19 mpg city / 25 mpg highway / 21 mpg combined

Both automakers stick to tried-and-true styling approaches, favoring an upright silhouette that prioritizes cabin utility over the radical design cues seen in rivals like the Kia Telluride and Volkswagen Atlas. But while they share a conventional profile, their personalities couldn't be more distinct.

For starters, the Acadia Denali Ultimate takes heavy inspiration from the larger Yukon Denali with its bold, big-truck presence. Between its extended length, squared-off rear, imposing Vader Chrome front grille, and massive 22-inch wheels, GMC built a family hauler that commands attention and looks genuinely intimidating on the road.

The Honda Pilot Elite takes a much cleaner, more disciplined approach. It features chiseled body lines, an elongated hood, and an attractive honeycomb front grille that adds real character without shouting for attention. It avoids unnecessary exterior drama while still projecting an athletic, confident stance.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Neither of these gas-powered mid-size SUVs is going to match the thriftiness of a hybrid like the Toyota Grand Highlander, but I was surprised by the solid numbers I recorded with both. Under the hood, the 2026 GMC Acadia Denali Ultimate AWD is powered by a 2.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine, while the 2026 Honda Pilot Elite AWD sticks with a naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6.

In my week of driving each, the Pilot emerged with slightly better overall fuel economy, averaging 22.3 mpg across 206.4 miles. That’s actually a notch higher than its EPA-estimated combined rating of 21 mpg. Meanwhile, I recorded an average of 21.7 mpg across 191.5 miles behind the wheel of the Acadia Denali.

Diving deeper into the other metrics I track, the short-distance trip breakdowns show that the Acadia’s turbo setup proved slightly more frugal with a peak of 23.6 mpg, though the Pilot wasn’t far behind at 22.4 mpg. On longer highway hauls, the Acadia widened the gap even further, delivering an impressive peak of 26.2 mpg compared to the Pilot’s 24.2 mpg.

While several variables impact real-world efficiency, the bottom-line averages I recorded are the ultimate deciding factor here. With that in mind, the Honda Pilot takes this round.

Buyers often prioritize paper specs, but numbers on a sheet rarely tell the whole story about real-world performance. Looking strictly at the figures, there’s a clear mismatch: the 2026 Acadia Denali Ultimate’s 2.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine cranks out 328 horsepower and 326 lb-ft of torque, easily making the 2026 Honda Pilot Elite’s 3.5-liter V6 look underpowered with its 285 hp and 262 lb-ft.

Getting behind the wheel of both, however, reveals the opposite. The Honda Pilot feels significantly more responsive right off the line. Step on the accelerator, and the Pilot delivers an immediate pull in first gear, launching cleanly with zero hesitation. To my surprise, the Acadia feels noticeably strained when trying to get its hefty frame moving from a dead stop.

Beyond straight-line acceleration, the Pilot proves to be the more agile of the two — composed, predictable, and engaging to maneuver through daily traffic. Even with its larger footprint, I never felt intimidated driving the Acadia Denali, but I feel there noticeably more body roll on winding highway off-ramps. While you’ll adapt to both after a few days behind the wheel, the Pilot’s immediate low-end punch and sharper agility win me over.

Step inside both cabins and the disparity between them is immediate. The 2026 Honda Pilot Elite offers a clean layout trimmed in perforated leather that’s durable and purpose-built for active families shuttling kids to practice and loading up on weekly Costco runs. However, the 2026 GMC Acadia Denali Ultimate takes a very different approach, delivering a near-Cadillac level of luxury. Between its soft leather, contrast stitching, and wood accents, the Acadia’s cabin has an upscale look that makes the Pilot feel a bit plain by comparison.

That edge carries directly into passenger comfort. While the Pilot accommodates up to eight passengers thanks to its versatile second- and third-row bench seating, the Acadia Denali Ultimate comes standard with plush second-row captain's chairs that are noticeably more supportive and comfortable for adults.

As for legroom, both deliver expansive second-row space for taller passengers. The Acadia’s slightly longer footprint also affords a smidge more breathing room in the third row. That larger frame makes a huge different in the back, yielding a generous 23 cubic feet of cargo space behind the third row compared to the Pilot’s 18.6 cubic feet.

Where the Acadia truly widens the gap in overall driving comfort and road-trip ease is GM’s Super Cruise. While Honda Sensing provides reliable adaptive cruise control and lane centering, it still requires your hands on the wheel. Super Cruise, on the other hand, remains one of my absolute favorite hands-free driver-assist systems on the market, elevated by effortless, automated hands-free lane changes on compatible highways.

There’s a significant $12,600 spread between these two mid-size SUV haulers. In the competitive division, this kind of price gap puts them in nearly different price brackets, raising the obvious question: does the Acadia actually pack enough features and amenities to justify its higher cost?

First and foremost, I can’t overlook how the Acadia has a more luxurious look and feel on the inside — highlighted by the enormous 15-inch portrait touchscreen smacked on the dashboard. Throw in front-row power massaging seats, bright head-up display, power-folding third-row seats, power liftgate, rear camera mirror panoramic roof, and crisp 360-degree cameras that are effective at night.

Interestingly, the Pilot Elite makes a strong argument by packing near-identical luxuries: a panoramic moonroof, perforated leather upholstery, heated and ventilated front seats, head-up display, 12-speaker Bose audio system, 360-degree surround-view camera, and a power tailgate. Throw in its 8-passenger versatility with its stowable middle seat, and the Pilot covers almost everything that families actually need without forcing you into luxury-car monthly payments.

After tallying up the scores, the 2026 Honda Pilot Elite AWD emerges as the clear winner in this mid-size face-off. It managed to fend off a much mightier challenger in the redesigned GMC Acadia Denali Ultimate AWD, reaffirming why it remains my favorite mid-size three-row hauler on the market.

That’s not to say the Acadia Denali Ultimate isn’t worth consideration — far from it. GMC has engineered a legitimate near-Cadillac experience here without the Cadillac badge. It delivers undeniable road presence, massive cargo room, plush second-row captain's chairs, and GM’s superior hands-free Super Cruise. If your household budget can comfortably stomach its steep $67,590 as-tested sticker price, the Acadia serves up a noticeably more premium package.

However, for everyday shoppers who don’t want to cross deep into luxury-level pricing, the Honda Pilot is the smarter buy. At $54,990 as-tested, it delivers dramatically better bang for the buck without skimping on core family luxuries. Factor in its punchier, more responsive low-end acceleration and composed road manners, and the Pilot provides the superior everyday driving performance.

#3369. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3368. macOS 27.3 Golden Gate public beta 1 now available, here’s everything new

Following the release of macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, Apple is now rolling out the first test build for users enrolled in the public beta. Here’s what’s coming

Contrary to macOS 27.2, it looks like Apple had quite a bit in store for macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

In addition to expanding Siri AI to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also introduces several new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode for websites, and the ability to organize and manage tabs using Siri AI.

macOS 27.3 also adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look, allowing users to preview .md files with proper formatting instead of raw Markdown syntax.

The update also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

Users who enjoyed the wallpaper introduced with the new touchscreen MacBook Pro will also find a new screensaver called Pro Lighteensaver, which features light moving along the metallic-looking lines that form the word “PRO.”

Earlier this week, Apple also confirmed that macOS 27.3 will introduce new checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links. Starting with the update, files and photos shared using the “Anyone with the link” option will be checked by Apple, which may remove flagged content or take action against accounts that violate its policies.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 1 is 26C5035r, which is the same as the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

Did you spot anything new in today’s beta? Let us know in the comments.

#3367. Portillo's (PTLO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlined a smaller 2028 prototype and a shift toward debt reduction

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Portillo's Inc. (PTLO -5.41%) reported third-quarter results that exceeded internal expectations, driven by positive same-restaurant sales and improved restaurant-level margins. Management introduced a strategic plan built on three pillars to address operational execution and marketing efforts while pursuing disciplined development. The company announced a portfolio strategy that includes closing several underperforming restaurants outside of the Chicago market. This action targets improved portfolio quality and increased long-term returns on invested capital.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to Portillo's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Chris Brandon, Vice President of Investor Relations. Thank you, Chris. You may begin.

Chris Brandon: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Portillo's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. With me today are Brett Patterson, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Kevin Kalicak joining for his first call with Portillo's as Chief Financial Officer. You can find our 10-Q and earnings press release at investors.portillos.com. Any commentary made here about our future results and business conditions are forward-looking statements, which are based on management's current expectations and are not guarantees of future performance. We do not update these forward-looking statements unless required by law. Our 10-Q identifies risk factors that may cause our actual results to vary materially from these forward-looking statements.

Today's earnings call will make reference to non-GAAP financial measures, which are not an alternative to GAAP measures. Reconciliations of these non-GAAP measures to their most comparable GAAP counterparts are included in this morning's posted materials. After we deliver our prepared remarks, we will be happy to take questions from our covering sell-side analysts. And lastly, we will be attending the upcoming Stephens Conference on Tuesday, November 17. as well as the Morgan Stanley Conference on Tuesday, December 1. We look forward to seeing many of you there. And with that, I will turn the call over to Brett.

Brett Patterson: Thanks, Chris. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Before I begin, I want to welcome Kevin to his first earnings call with Portillo's. Kevin is an excellent leader, and I'm glad to have him on the team as we guide Portillo's into its next chapter. Our third quarter results came in ahead of expectations. Same-restaurant sales increased 1.4%, a 260-basis point improvement from the second quarter. Adjusted EBITDA grew 23.7% to $20.65 million versus the prior year quarter. Kevin will walk through the details and our full-year outlook shortly. I'm encouraged by the early progress, but let me be clear, 1 quarter is not a trend.

We have significant work ahead, and our focus is simple: run great restaurants, and run this company with a discipline to deliver durable sales and profitable growth. As a leadership team, we have taken an honest look at our business over the past several months and confronted a hard reality. Portillo's has not delivered the returns our investors expected. Those lessons are already shaping our actions. We have strengthened key parts of our leadership team, rightsized our corporate structure, deepened our understanding of our guests through formalized research, identified meaningful operational and supply chain savings and implemented a more rigorous site selection process, which we have already used to exit several future real estate agreements that lack sufficient return potential.

I also want to update you on 2 commitments that I made to you in August. First, we remain on track to deliver $10 million to $15 million in annualized run rate efficiencies. We will share more specifics on these savings when we provide 2027 guidance in January. Second, as part of our ongoing portfolio assessment, we expect to close a mid- to high single-digit number of underperforming restaurants outside of Chicagoland, most of them in the fiscal fourth quarter. These are very difficult decisions, but they're the right ones for the long-term health of the business. Together, these actions are shaping our focus, improving our cost structure and building the foundation for a much stronger company.

Now let me turn to the growth strategy we introduced this morning, which lays out how we will strengthen Portillo's and build a more sustainable, profitable path forward. The full detail is in our earnings release, so I'll focus on the key elements. Kevin, Chris and I will also use this strategy to frame our conversations with investors in the weeks ahead across several forums, including a webcast conference appearance in mid-November. At its core, this strategy is grounded in one belief: the right to grow must be earned. It builds on the lessons I just described while protecting the distinctive food, hospitality and experience that make Portillo's special.

The strategy rests on the 3 pillars I've shared with you before: operational excellence, integrated marketing and disciplined development, all underpinned by a renewed commitment to financial rigor. Together, they are designed to strengthen our business fundamentals and create sustainable long-term shareholder value. Our brand research gives us a strong place to start. It confirmed that Portillo's strength goes well beyond the food. Our guests have a powerful emotional connection to this brand, both in Chicagoland and beyond. That connection is the foundation we will build on as we bring more discipline to the decisions that shape our future. Let me walk through each pillar. First, operational excellence. Running great restaurants is the foundation of everything we do.

We have refined our regional leadership structure so field leaders oversee fewer restaurants and can give our teams more focused hands-on support. We are raising standards, strengthening accountability and improving tools so our teams consistently deliver great food, accurate orders, faster service and genuine hospitality. We are also updating hourly and management training supported by certified trainers and evaluating restaurant technology and equipment to improve reliability, product quality and consistency. Second, integrated marketing. Our recent brand perception, customer segmentation and menu satisfaction studies are now guiding our brand positioning and the guests we target and our menu priorities. The brand study highlighted a clear opportunity: use the strength of the Portillo's brand to drive profitable transactions and more frequent visits.

We are acting on that with refined brand positioning and an integrated creative and media strategy. Our segmentation work identified 2 distinct millennial audiences where Portillo's is uniquely positioned to win. Focusing on these guests creates meaningful growth potential and allows us to invest marketing dollars more effectively. We're also building digital capabilities that match the strength of our brand. A new technology road map will guide our decisions on building out a modern marketing technology platform to improve the experience and drive conversion and sales. As part of that work, we are fully assessing our Perks loyalty program. To simplify it, increase engagement and drive frequency. We are also putting culinary excellence back at the center of the business.

Our menu satisfaction study reinforced a clear priority: protect and improve the food our guests already love, then use thoughtful innovation to create new reasons to visit as you recently saw with our Char'diniera Dog, Dr Pepper Shake and our recent OREO dessert launch. Our new executive chef is now leading menu strategy, core menu quality and a more strategic innovation pipeline. And third, disciplined development. This may be the most significant change in how we approach growth. We are implementing stricter, data-driven standards for site selection and underwriting. A new restaurant will move forward only if we believe it will generate cash-on-cash returns, consistent with our new restaurant targets and passes rigorous market and site reviews.

A site will not advance simply because we want another restaurant. The economics have to work. We will balance infill opportunities in existing markets with expansion into strategically adjacent new markets. This will enable us to leverage our regional leadership, operating infrastructure and brand awareness as we pursue the significant white space opportunity ahead of us. We are also introducing a more efficient prototype. Our 2028 prototype is approximately 4,600 square feet, more than 40% smaller than our previous average restaurant and requires approximately 1.5 acres compared with 3 acres historically. Smaller does not mean less Portillo's. The new design preserves the character and experience our guests expect along with the potential for high volumes.

Today, nearly 15% of the restaurants in our system generate over $1,500 in sales per square foot with a few surpassing $2,000. We believe the optimized kitchen, more standardized design and greater site flexibility can improve throughput and productivity while targeting a lower capital investment. Across all 3 pillars, financial rigor will shape how we operate and allocate capital. We are reinforcing restaurant-level accountability for sales and profit and aligning incentives with those outcomes. Kevin will cover our capital allocation priorities in more detail. Looking to 2027, we plan to open 4 to 6 new restaurants.

Guests will begin to see this strategy come to life through more consistent execution, refined brand positioning and new creative, a better digital experience and more food news from our culinary team. We will be clear about our priorities: more rigorous in how we operate and allocate capital and more accountable for the results we deliver. That is how we will protect what makes Portillo's special, build a stronger business, create long-term shareholder value and earn the right to grow. I also want to thank the entire Portillo's team, most importantly, our restaurant managers and team members for the hard work and dedication behind our strong third quarter performance.

With that, I'll turn it over to Kevin to discuss the quarter in more detail.

Kevin Kalicak: Thank you, Brett, and good morning, everyone. I'm excited to be here with you today on my first earnings call at Portillo's. Since joining in September, I spent time in our restaurants, with the team at the restaurant support center and with our Board listening and learning. What drew me to Portillo's is simple. It's an exceptional brand with a strong foundation. It has a differentiated and craveable menu, passionate guest base and high-volume operating model. What also excited me about this opportunity was a chance to work with Brett and the rest of the leadership team on the work underway to sharpen the company's direction.

That work culminated in the strategy we shared today, which builds on Portillo's strengths and positions us well with commitment to responsible growth and a clear focus on shareholder returns. After 3 decades in the restaurant industry, I know firsthand how the 3 pillars of our strategy, operational excellence, integrated marketing and disciplined development matter to creating value for both guests and shareholders. Going forward, you can expect me to be disciplined on capital allocation with a focus on creating long-term shareholder value. I look forward to partnering with the team to execute our plan. Now to the third quarter. Our overall results were stronger than anticipated with positive same-restaurant sales.

We achieved this while facing over 200 basis points of traffic headwinds from last year's breakfast test and heavy promotional discounting while also continuing to experience cannibalization from new restaurant growth. Partially offsetting these headwinds was a strong performance of 2 new limited time offers, the Char'diniera Dog and Dr Pepper Shake. These limited time offers brought news and innovation, supporting transactions without the need for deep discounting. Revenues increased 7% in the third quarter to $194.1 million. This was driven by $10.3 million from the addition of noncomp restaurants and by positive same-restaurant sales of 1.4%, consisting of a 2.1% increase in average check and a 0.7% decrease in transactions.

Higher average check was driven by a 2.1% increase in menu price, while transactions improved 270 basis points sequentially from last quarter. Turning to our margin analysis compared to last year. Food, beverage and packaging costs decreased 10 basis points to 34.4% of revenues. This improvement was driven by an increase in average check and improved food waste and was partially offset by a 2.2% increase in commodity inflation led by continued elevated beef costs. Labor expense of 26% improved 60 basis points, primarily due to hourly labor efficiencies and an increase in average check. This favorability was partially offset by higher incentive compensation expense, and sales deleverage from lower transactions and lower average weekly sales for noncomp restaurants.

Other operating expenses remained flat year-over-year at 12.9% for the quarter. Occupancy expense of 6% increased 20 basis points versus last year. This was primarily driven by sales deleverage from noncomp restaurants. Our restaurant-level adjusted EBITDA increased to $40.1 million with margins increasing 50 basis points to 20.7%. Our G&A expense decreased to $19.8 million or 10.2% of revenue in the quarter compared to 11% in the prior year. This decrease was primarily driven by $3.3 million of lower dead site costs, resulting from our 2025 strategic reset as well as salary and benefit savings from our workforce reduction at the restaurant support center.

This was partially offset by a $1.4 million restructuring charge associated with the workforce reduction and the absence of a $1.1 million net benefit recognized in connection with the CEO transition last year. Our preopening expenses were $2.6 million lower, driven by fewer restaurant openings in the third quarter versus last year, and adjusted EBITDA increased $5.1 million to $26.5 million or 13.6% of revenue compared to 11.8% last year. Income tax expense was $1.8 million, and our effective tax rate for the quarter was 27.4%. Cash provided by operating activities increased 26.8% to $61.8 million year-to-date.

We reduced our revolver by $12 million in the quarter, resulting in $85 million outstanding and $24.8 million in cash to end the quarter. We now have approximately $61 (sic) [ $61 million ] of remaining revolver capacity and net debt of $300 million. We will continue to utilize our cash available to pay down debt. In the fourth quarter, we plan to open one additional restaurant on North Michigan Avenue in downtown Chicago. This will be our second in-line restaurant and will bring our total openings to 8 in 2026. As announced this morning, we plan to close a number of underperforming restaurants outside of Chicagoland, with most of these closures occurring in the fourth quarter of this year.

We are not able to share the exact timing, locations or cost with you today as we continue to evaluate lease options for these restaurants. We expect the closures to result in material cash and noncash charges, mostly in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Now turning to our expectations for fiscal '26, which factored in the expected closures in the fourth quarter, we anticipate total revenue of $768 million to $773 million.

Based on our outperformance this quarter and estimates for the remainder of the year, we are raising our full year adjusted EBITDA outlook to between $98 million and $101 million, including mid-single-digit commodity inflation, low single-digit labor inflation, restaurant-level EBITDA margin of 20% to 20.5% and G&A expense between $80 million to $82 million. And finally, Brett shared with you the highlights of our growth strategy. Building on this, I'd like to highlight our capital allocation priorities. We plan to first, reinvest in improved technology and maintenance of our existing restaurant portfolio; second, invest in qualified new restaurant growth; and finally, use excess cash to reduce debt and leverage, strengthening our long-term financial stability.

Based on the collective actions of this strategy, we expect to deliver annual same-restaurant sales of 2% to 3% and in the next 3 years ramp new restaurant growth to a high single-digit percentage while expanding margins by leveraging sales growth and efficiencies. New restaurants are expected to deliver cash-on-cash returns greater than 20%. Thank you for your time today. Now let's open it up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first questions come from the line of Margaret-May Binshtok with Wolfe Research.

Margaret-May Binshtok: It's encouraging to hear the sequential improvement in same-restaurant sales on this quarter. So I just wanted to ask first, how same-restaurant sales are trending so far in the fourth quarter? And then on another note, I know your plan now calls for that 2% to 3% same-store sales growth. How long do you think it takes to get to that range? And as you think about the parts of the plan, which are you most excited about and you think is the strongest lever to drive traffic in the near term?

Brett Patterson: Margaret-May, this is Brett, and thank you for the question. I'll take the second part first and then turn it over to Kevin, and he can talk to you about the sequential improvement. We're -- we believe what needs to happen really is as we laid out the strategy and these 3 pillars, right, is there's got to be synergies between all 3. It's not going to be one of those pillars getting better, the other 2 not getting better that will drive traffic.

But I believe what we'll see and kind of what we saw through quarter 3 is innovation is -- it's really important to Portillo's because as we've learned more about our customer, the fanaticism of this brand is pretty remarkable. And so when you give them good news and you give them news that resonates with the brand, they'll come visit. It doesn't have to be at a discount. Actually, it shouldn't be at a discount.

So I would say, as we continue to ramp up our innovation pipeline, put really quality food out there and our operations gets more consistent across the board, we'll start to see that kind of natural transition to transaction growth and then on top of that, leverage our price increase, which we anticipate kind of keeping at inflation or better to make sure that we focus on our value proposition.

Kevin Kalicak: Yes. And as it relates to the fourth quarter, I think you talked a little bit about the sequential improvement that we saw in the third quarter. Certainly, we're excited about that. As it relates to the fourth quarter, the guidance for our same-restaurant sales is embedded in the total sales guidance of $768 million to $773 million. But I'll tell you that quarter 4 to date, we're running ahead of third quarter same-restaurant sales. And that is in part is driven by strong performance from the OREO desserts, which has been running for period 10 and continues to run the rest of this week and into next week.

Although similar to the third quarter, we continue to face headwinds from last year, most of which were deeply discounted. For instance, like this week, we're wrapping on a free beef sandwich offer, which is a big headwind for the fourth quarter.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Gregory Francfort with Guggenheim.

Gregory Francfort: I had 2 questions. The first is maybe just what the margin implications might be for slowing growth, exiting some of the stores. And just as I look out into next year, what sort of comp maybe would you need to have margins flat or up, just a rough framing there?

Kevin Kalicak: Greg, this is Kevin. I think with the closures, you'll likely see an improvement in margins given that these are underperforming restaurants. And so those will lift the base naturally. And then I think as we continue to look at what's ahead in '27 and beyond, if we're targeting that 2% to 3% sales growth -- same-store sales growth, margins should be flat to slightly improve as we talked about, leveraging same-restaurant sales, leveraging G&A, those factors, particularly as we begin to ramp up new unit growth in the next 3 years.

Gregory Francfort: Okay. Great. And my second question is, Brett, I mean, you've now had a couple of quarters here. Like as you keep getting -- digging into the business and kind of increasing your learnings, what has shifted in your thinking, kind of any major opportunities that maybe presented yourself from the last time we spoke? I'm just curious how you're thinking about it.

Brett Patterson: Yes. Thanks, Greg. I don't know how much has really shifted since the last call. I think my first call, it was obviously, I was just still drinking from a fire hose and learning the brand. But if I had to tell you, probably the most surprising thing that really occurred last quarter is when we got our research back, Greg, honestly, the research kind of confirmed what we believe, but I would say it was almost amplified about how much passion there is for this brand and love the brand. And it was really because it was outside of Chicagoland as well.

And so when we do these studies, we went really deep to all of our markets, talk to lapsed users, new users, loyal fans. And I would say that the brand love stands out. It's a towering strength for us. We learned a lot about our food. And so I'd say those kind of crystallize maybe some thoughts and -- but how we approach the strategy going forward is when you get the type of fanaticism, our job is to shepherd the brand a little bit differently than if we're trying to convince people why to love us. And so I said, really continuing on, you hear us use like rigor and discipline a lot as we speak.

I would say that's what we really need to focus on this organization is really commitment to really good processes that will manufacture better outcomes for the business. And I think you're starting to see that in quarter 3, and you should see that continue on in quarter 4 and 2027.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Sara Senatore with Bank of America.

Ashley Wallace: This is Ashley on for Sara. Just congrats on a really nice quarter. Restaurant margins, they were up 40 bps on the 1.4% comp, and beef was still inflationary. So overall, very impressive. Could you just help us unpack what drove that between the labor model changes in the lower volume units and the early supply chain savings? And just how much do you think carries into next year as the savings program builds?

Kevin Kalicak: Yes. Thanks for the question, Ashley. So as it relates to the margins in the quarter specifically, clearly, our improvement in labor was the big driver being 60 basis points favorable year-over-year. And a lot of that was labor model improvements, particularly in some of our lower volume restaurants and adjusting to accommodate the demand that is more the expectation there now. So I think that's the biggest one in terms of the commodities. Commodities were relatively benign in total at 2.2%, which was in line with our pricing, despite elevated beef costs. So pretty straightforward there. As far as the cost savings, none of the cost savings initiatives have materialized in the food cost line.

They're more on the G&A savings line at this point. So yet to come on some of those savings, and we'll probably talk more about that in the fourth quarter as we tee up the '27 outlook.

Ashley Wallace: Just on catering, it's always been a nice differentiator for Portillo's, and 4Q is the biggest season for it. Can you just give us some color on how catering is trending into the holiday season? And how big a piece of the business come in the newer markets where the brand is still building awareness?

Brett Patterson: Yes. Thank you for the question. One of the things that I think Kevin and I as being new to the brand are realizing how -- like your comment on how powerful catering is for us, particularly in the fourth quarter. But right now, we're feeling good. We're on track, if not a little ahead of where we were last year in catering. And we've amplified our plans this year with our operations teams being ready for it. And so we've got a really strong playbook that existed from our prior teams, and they do a really good job.

So we see that as not necessarily a headwind or tailwind, but if we can hold serve in quarter 4, that's kind of baked into our assumptions for guidance.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris O'Cull with Baird.

Christopher O'Cull: Congrats, Kevin, on the new role. I had a follow-up question, Brett, about the consumer research that you guys have conducted and you were talking about earlier. I'm just curious why -- what the research tells you about why people try Portillo's but don't become regular customers, particularly outside of Chicago?

Brett Patterson: Yes. So that's a really good question. I don't know how you're stating it is fact. And so what we really learned is we do generate the same type of loyalty and regulars. What you find outside of Chicago, it becomes more of a -- it's a longer destination. So if you look at -- for instance, you look at some of our sites in Texas, for people to travel to us, it's a long way, right? You look at Chicagoland, your frequency is going to be higher because you have one every couple of miles. And so what we learned was, yes, we love Portillo's just as much as somebody in Chicago, but destination, it's much harder.

They're not as readily available for us to dine. And so you're not going to have the same frequency with somebody that's having to drive 10 or 15 miles to a Portillo's as you would a couple of miles. So we continue to see our Perks penetration increase. We see our membership increase, and that's -- a lot of that's driven by outside the Chicagoland market.

So I think as part of that is as we look at our future real estate, and that's what we talked about as adjacent growth markets and the right infills that don't really cannibalize, we'll start to build more of that awareness and more of that kind of the access to the brand more so than we have now.

Christopher O'Cull: Is there -- since the repeat visits aren't as frequent as they are in Chicago, is there an opportunity? Or is there a plan to maybe expand the customer base or try to reach more people in these markets outside of Chicago?

Brett Patterson: Yes. I think -- so when we talk about -- we did that guest segmentation work, Chris, and that is -- that was specifically designed to do exactly what you said, is to understand who uses us, why they use us and then where those white space opportunities so we can be much more effective in communicating with them. And that is Denise and her team on the marketing side are working through that now to kind of create the personas. We'll create -- we'll leverage a different type of communication based on those 2 audiences. So we do believe that's going to drive trial and more frequency once we can tap into those audience.

Because prior to that, our communication has been kind of just very broad, right, and not specific to certain targets. And this will really help us refine exactly who we go after and bring into the brand.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Andy Barish with Jefferies.

Andrew Barish: And yes, maybe one for Kevin, just as you get settled in, having come from an organization with vast resources and insights and support. I mean, as you look at '27 for Portillo's in terms of like technology infrastructure, things, is it an investment year? Or are there just ways to kind of implement processes to make what's there more efficient, again, after kind of the G&A saves from the workforce reductions this year?

Kevin Kalicak: Andy, thanks for the question. Yes, I mean, I think it's twofold, right? I think when we think about some of the things that happen here in the Restaurant Support Center, I think certainly, there's not quite the investment. Certainly, there's a little bit in the marketing stack and what Brett talked about in terms of the highlights and the strategy. As we think about going out into the restaurants, there's a decent amount of tech out there that we need to look at and see are there ways to improve operations, make it smoother for our teams. I know the iPad, the tablets for our drive-thru operators is a little bit of a pain point.

And so it's looking at all of those. I don't know that I would call it necessarily an investment year. But as I mentioned, as we look at our fourth quarter and talking about our guide into '27, I think that will -- we'll have a little bit more content for you going into that.

Brett Patterson: Andy, this is Brett. I was going to -- Kevin made some really good points. I think one of the things Kevin and I really began to line on, and we mentioned in the script, is kind of the rigor behind how and where we spend money. And so we're really committed to anything we spend money is going to have to have a return on it, right? And so if we say operational investments in training and food quality, some of those will take a little bit longer to see the return on that.

But there are some like we're talking about with technology and marketing that, to Chris' earlier question, that will have a much quicker return because we're going to target a specific group of people. So we're balancing that of how much do we need and the strength in operations will have a little bit of a lag time on the return versus what are some of those immediate returns. But Kevin nailed the priorities for how and where we're going to invest.

Andrew Barish: Okay. Very helpful. And then I'm happy to hear about the good start to the 4Q. I think there's like a half a dozen units maybe entering the comp base in the 4Q. I want to say a bunch of those are Texas. Are there any just thoughts on how that's -- we should take that into account in terms of the 4Q?

Kevin Kalicak: Yes. I think as it relates to the fourth quarter, certainly, as it relates to the closures, there's the level of total sales guide that is in reduction, that is embedded in the guidance related to those closures. And then as you look at some of those new restaurants that are entering the comp base, I think they're generally going to be on the lower end of volumes and seeing some continued slide in comp performance as they continue to lap their or roll off their honeymoon.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Jim Salera with Stephens.

James Salera: I wanted to start by just walking through the decision to close some of the underperforming restaurants outside Chicagoland. Is there anything you can take away from what specifically about the locations that made them underperform kind of initial expectations and as you've continued to densify outside of Chicagoland, why there wasn't maybe the pickup that you initially expected?

Brett Patterson: Yes, Jim, this is Brett. Thank you for the question. I would -- I'll tell you there's a few factors. And I mentioned my first -- the first call I was on and I had before I joined, had an opportunity to fully drive a lot of those markets and visit the restaurants. And my comments then were a lot of the sites were very, a, very green; b, very casual dining like. And so what I would say we've really learned about Portillo's and the model -- the new model we've created is we have a much deeper understanding now of really what drives the volumes to our restaurants.

And there -- again, there's this fanaticism where people are willing to drive a long way. But at some point, they're not going to come once or twice a week when they live 15, 20 miles away. So I would say one is sites played a huge role into what we're seeing there. Number two is that infill cannibalization. I mean we ramped up so quickly in those markets and plugged in a lot of infills as all we did is redistributed sales from those geographic areas. And so that put a lot of pressure on the business models. And then third is when you're going to new markets is how do you really create awareness.

And we did a little bit of damage to ourselves with how we branded the restaurants. We took -- in some of them, we just have the name Portillo's. We took off what we do, what we serve. And for new market penetration, they don't -- if they don't know what you do, it's kind of hard for people to figure out. And so I think there are some of those awareness opportunities. And that's why the new strategy is, one, we feel really good about our new sales forecast model because it's rooted in all the data. We have a really clear understanding of what drives volumes in Chicago and outside of Chicago.

And two, being very selective on infills, so we don't have a strong cannibalization. And then third, having those adjacent markets where you start to create awareness. So for example, Florida, where we've got -- we're opening a new one in Lutz next year. We've got one in St. Pete, one in Brand and one in Tampa. Can you potentially look at adjacent markets and kind of Florida and start to build out another core market. So that's how we're thinking about it a little bit differently now.

James Salera: Great. And then how should we think about the long-term unit TAM? I mean I know you guys previously, I think it was 900 plus. It sounds like that's probably too high at this point, but maybe you can just help us kind of size up what that opportunity looks like? And also, could we think about markets that are maybe closer to the core in the upper Midwest or places that have, I'll say, a similar talent to where you guys are most successful in Chicagoland?

Brett Patterson: Yes. Look, it's a really good question. I don't want to give you an answer right now. We haven't done the work to say, okay, across the Continental U.S., what's our total white space? Because to your second point, what we've focused on with our new strategy for real estate right now is those adjacent markets and infills, including the Chicagoland area. So ideally, what we'd like to have a growth model that continues to expand our core market as well as go into markets we know that we have a higher chance of success. And so we do well. We know we've got another one coming in Buford, Georgia.

We'll see how that does because Kennesaw still does very well for us. We performed well in Florida. And so take -- but how many we put there and how many we put in the Chicagoland area is what we're determining now just based on the site selection? Because as we said before, we're at the point now is we'll get to the growth number we mentioned in the -- on the call. But more importantly, we need to make sure that we derisk the capital investment and make sure we go in sites that do the volumes and give us the cash-on-cash returns.

So I know there was this belief that can you still do Chicagoland volumes in the new prototype or can you do Chicago -- I'm not so sure that doing Chicagoland volumes would be something that we put as a goal. If we can drive 21% restaurant-level margins in a $5 million restaurant, that would put us in the top decile of fast casual.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Sharon Zackfia with William Blair.

Sharon Zackfia: Can you talk about the simplification of the loyalty program and kind of what you think works well currently and what you'd like to change?

Brett Patterson: Sharon, this is Brett. Thank you. We are just -- I would say it's premature to comment on where we see the Perks program going. I would say what we do like about it now is it does give us access to data and to our loyal fans that we really hadn't had another opportunity to get at. And we do know that it is a lever that we can pull to engage a group of people to visit us. And so it's really our kind of top form of communication for whether it's launching these LTOs we mentioned.

The second, the surprise and delight is, it's interesting, because there's another brand that recently launched a loyalty program that kind of had the same program with the surprise and delight. So I'm not sure we completely run away from that, but I think it's just too early to say what is -- what's the best use of that loyalty program for us and how do we compare it to others in the marketplace. So for now, I'd say it's something we focus on and continue to grow that base because the frequency is higher than our normal guest.

And so we know if we can continue to drive higher frequency and expand the loyal guests, then we benefit from a transaction standpoint.

Sharon Zackfia: And I'm sorry if I missed this, but for the smaller format locations that you'll begin to open in '28, what are the targeted AUVs for those locations?

Brett Patterson: Yes. the target AUV -- and I would guess I'm a little bit different than maybe how we communicated before. I don't believe in you create a prototype for a targeted AUV. As mentioned, we have roughly 15% of our restaurants that do over $1,500 in sales per square foot. So I don't believe we should put a governor on a 4,600 square foot restaurant, Chick-fil-As, they've got those sized restaurants, and we know the volumes they do. So I don't see it as a governor.

I see the site selection as what will drive our sales volume and believe we can do the volumes we see in our higher-volume restaurants at a smaller prototype, again, because we have a large percentage of drive-thru. We have a large percent of off-premise and dine-in, right? So we have -- and catering. So we have 4 really unique channels that are very strong for us. And so I don't -- as long as you get people in and out of drive-thru, you can get food out quickly and accurately on time, I don't see sales as a governor. I say it's the site selection that will be the governor on sales.

Operator: Our final questions will come from the line of JP Wollam with ROTH Capital Partners.

John-Paul Wollam: Maybe just kind of starting on the restaurant-level margin. I think there was some commentary in the press release about evaluating and investing in additional tech. And I just kind of want to square that with the labor savings that you've already made and kind of some of the COGS improvements that are still yet to come. Brett, as you think about the business, and identifying Chicagoland separately from then kind of your remaining new market or other markets, like where are we, inning-wise, with just how you're seeing in-store operations? And what's still kind of an opportunity there as we look forward?

Brett Patterson: Yes. Thanks, JP. Really good question. I would say we're in the early innings, and I'm not saying that's because our operators don't do a good job. We're in the early innings because we're -- we need to provide better resources and tools for our operators to do their job. Right now, it's at these volumes and more than a 50-year history of executing in the same way. It's important that we understand why that works, how it works, but also understand if I can get a piece of equipment that can make my fries more hot, more crispy and last longer, why wouldn't I do that, right?

And so some of those things are what we're really trying to work through now. If we look at tablet technology and our drive-thru that actually has a screen on it to where the guest can confirm that's the order that they order, then it comes out more accurately. So I think it's a lot of those type of things we're looking through. The other piece on operations is, look, candidly, we didn't have a very strong training culture at all. And we are going to over-index on having well-trained team members and managers leading our restaurants. And so that will be -- I would say that part of it is in the really early innings.

But I can say with confidence is, we execute very well compared to the industry. I'd say we just have more inconsistency across the fleet, and that's what we really need to tighten up.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you so much. That does conclude our question-and-answer session. And with that, we have reached the end of our teleconference. We appreciate your participation. You may disconnect your lines at this time, and enjoy the rest of your day.

#3366. Apollo-backed Brightspeed seeks up to $3B from creditors for fibre

The rural broadband provider has about $10B of debt and has warned it may not survive as a going concern.

Fibre optic cables connected to telecommunications equipment in a network rack.

Brightspeed, a US fibre broadband provider owned by Apollo, is in talks with creditors to raise $2B to $3B of new money, Bloomberg reports. It has about $10B of debt, has warned about its survival, and may file for bankruptcy as soon as December.

Brightspeed, an Apollo-backed US fibre broadband provider, is in talks to raise $2B to $3B of new money from its creditors. That is according to Bloomberg, which cited people familiar with the matter on Friday. The amount, and whether the deal will go through a bankruptcy court, are still being worked out.

Brightspeed and Apollo declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the company could file for bankruptcy as soon as December, Light Reading reported.

Brightspeed has about $10B of debt and warned in September that it may not be able to continue as a going concern. Nearly all its debt trades at distressed levels: one $2.5B loan was quoted at about 17 cents on the dollar on Friday.

Brightspeed was formed in 2022, when Apollo bought Lumen’s local phone and broadband business in 20 states for $7.5B. It is spending heavily to bring fibre to mostly rural and suburban areas there. It passed 3 million fibre-ready locations in April, and fibre sales are up 16% from a year earlier.

It has been through this before. In 2024, Brightspeed cut $1.1B of debt and raised $3.7B of new capital in a deal with its lenders. This month, it named Shawn O’Donnell, a former senior managing director at FTI Consulting, as chief executive.

Apollo is better known in tech circles for its lending to AI, including a $36B debt deal it is arranging with Blackstone to buy chips for Anthropic. Lumen, meanwhile, has turned to AI customers, and this week agreed to sell AI networks with Microsoft.

#3365. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

What was wrong with the headline "Engineering Jobs That AI Can't Replace"?

Different headlines appear in different places for stories. Not seeing it on the article doesn't mean that the headline appeared differently somewhere else.

The screen on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is downright impressive. We measured close to 2,000 nits of brightness using a 10% HDR pattern. As someone who lab-tests every laptop that comes through Tom's Guide for review, I immediately wondered how Apple's latest display would stack up against the competition.

The numbers don't lie. After digging through our benchmark spreadsheets and comparing the results against 80 laptops tested in our lab this year, I can confidently say that Apple's latest MacBook Pro is the brightest laptop we've tested in 2026.

Everyone conducts display testing differently and uses different equipment, so results can vary by equipment and a publication’s testing standards. This is why it is important to understand how we test.

At Tom’s Guide, we test both a display's SDR and HDR performance. For SDR brightness testing, we display a white image on the screen, set the brightness to 100%, and measure it using our Klein K10-A and DisplayCal software.

For HDR testing, which is where we test a laptop’s maximum brightness, we use the same software and colorimeter, paired with copies of HDR test patterns. With the screen at 100% brightness, these patterns play as a movie in the laptop’s native movie player. We use 10%, 40%, and 100% HDR patterns. These patterns fill the screen with the corresponding percentages on a black background while playing.

And a lab tester’s note. The 10% window is a commonly used benchmark for evaluating peak HDR brightness, particularly in television testing. Smaller windows, such as 2% or 5%, can sometimes produce higher peak brightness readings, while larger windows help illustrate how a display handles brighter content across more of the screen.

In two of those HDR patterns (10% and 40%), the 16-inch MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display beat the list of 79 laptops that went through our lab this year. I am talking about both Mini LED and OLED displays. Now that’s impressive!

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The 16-inch MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display is Apple’s current flagship, so it is our primary comparison point. On that unit, we measured 1,949 nits with a 10% pattern and 1,965 nits with a 40% pattern. This sets a new record for us in the lab.

Coming in second is the new Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark. Equipped with a mini-LED display, it reaches 1,444 nits at 10% and 1,311 nits at 40%. In third place is the LG Gram 16, which is also an OLED laptop. It measured 1,067 nits at 10% and 1,033 nits at 40%.

As you can see, Apple's HDR results are nowhere close to what we measured on the Windows-powered OLED laptop. In fact, the new MacBook Pro is nearly twice as bright as LG's laptop.

Even more remarkable, Apple is outdoing itself. In our testing, the miniLED display on the Apple MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Pro reached 1,427 nits on a 10% pattern and 1,444 nits on a 40% pattern. The new PROLED panel takes Apple's performance to an entirely new level.

What's also impressive is how consistently the new MacBook maintains its brightness. At 10%, we measured 1,949 nits, and increasing the illuminated area to 40% pushed that figure to 1,965 nits. That's a difference of just 16 nits. This shows Apple's new display isn't just producing impressive peak brightness in smaller HDR highlights; it's maintaining it across a much larger portion of the screen for a better HDR picture overall.

As someone who occasionally reviews TVs for Tom's Guide, I couldn't resist putting these numbers into another perspective. How does Apple's latest laptop compare with some of the brightest OLED TVs we've tested?

To be clear, this isn't an apples-to-apples comparison (pun intended). We test televisions in one of their most color-accurate picture modes, Filmmaker Mode, which can limit peak brightness. Meanwhile, our laptop brightness testing prioritizes maximum output. Nevertheless, it's an interesting comparison.

Currently, the brightest OLED TV we tested in Filmmaker Mode with a 10% pattern in HDR is the LG G6, which reaches 2,932 nits. Second among OLED TVs is the Samsung 65-inch S95H OLED TV, which reaches 2,721 nits. A budget OLED TV like the Samsung S90H, meanwhile, reaches 1,496 nits.

Samsung 65-inch S95H OLED TV (Filmmaker Mode)

Of course, other TV technologies are on the market. The Hisense UR9 currently holds the brightness record. Using Mini LED technology, it reached 4,370 nits — the brightest TV we tested to date.

Considering flagship OLED TVs cost nearly as much as a fully specced MacBook Pro, seeing Apple push nearly 2,000 nits on a portable laptop display says a lot about what you’re getting. It’s nearly TV-level quality.

Raw brightness is only half the story because image presentation and human perception matter just as much. Apple claims a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio on these new OLED panels, and in person, it truly shows.

When lab testing at home, I had the Lenovo Yoga 9n with an OLED panel on the right, my personal mini LED MacBook Pro M3 Max on the left, and the new MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display in the middle. A 4K HDR nature video was playing as I peeked at the screens, and it was obvious which was the best.

On one screen showing a parrot, the difference was immediately noticeable. The new MacBook delivered particularly striking detail in the parrot’s individual feathers, and the greens looked more vibrant. Compared with the Mini-LED MacBook Pro and the Lenovo Yoga 9i, the image on Apple's new display looked considerably more lifelike.

As a final note, my colleague watched the “Dune: Part Three" trailer on the 16-inch MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display. While standing behind him as he took pictures, I paid close attention to skin tones and color rendition on the MacBook’s screen, as I do when reviewing a TV.

Having personally tested more than two dozen TVs this year, I can say the color reproduction was particularly impressive. In our lab tests, it covered 99.9% of the sRGB color gamut, which is why I came away with the impression of natural-looking skin tones and that exceptionally wide range of colors in the parrot video.

I was impressed by how closely the overall presentation reminded me of some of the best displays I've evaluated. Apple wasn’t playing around this year, and they have set the bar sky-high for the rest of the industry.

#3362. Musk says government work will be under 10% of SpaceX revenue

AI computing, led by Anthropic, has overtaken NASA and the Pentagon as SpaceX's main source of money.

Elon Musk at VivaTech in Paris, 16 June 2023

Elon Musk said government contracts will make up less than 10% of SpaceX’s revenue this quarter, down from 16.6%. SpaceX now earns most from renting AI computing, with Anthropic its biggest customer, though Anthropic can exit from early 2027.

Government contracts will make up less than 10% of SpaceX’s revenue this quarter, Elon Musk said on X, Bloomberg reported on Friday. That is down from 16.6% in the third quarter and roughly a fifth in 2025.

Musk said the share would fall below 5% about a year from now, Reuters reported. NASA and the Pentagon were long SpaceX’s most important customers, paying it to launch astronauts and national security satellites.

The money now comes from AI. In the third quarter, SpaceX’s AI unit brought in $7.56B, more than Starlink, mostly by renting out computing power from its data centres in Memphis. Anthropic alone accounted for 34.5% of revenue, making it SpaceX’s biggest customer.

That brings its own risk. Anthropic can exit its contracts with 90 days’ notice from early 2027, and Wall Street has recently soured on companies that rent out AI computing, Bloomberg said. Musk himself warned last month that few will survive without other sources of revenue.

Musk’s comments came days after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress. He spent more than $445M backing Republicans, most of whom lost, and Bloomberg said that could strain his companies’ ties with the new Congress. SpaceX still holds a NASA contract to land astronauts on the Moon with Starship as early as 2028.
