#3361. Warren Buffett Says This 1 Investing Move Is Key After a Midterm Election. History Says He's Right.

Stocks are tumbling post-election, but Warren Buffett has some reassuring advice.

It's been a rough week for the stock market.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.46%) recently experienced their worst day in over a year. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%) fared even worse, falling nearly 12% from its October high and entering a technical correction.

Much of the volatility stems from AI stocks, as concerns around their sustainability mount. With Democrats sweeping Congress in this week's midterm elections, many investors are concerned that stricter regulations may slow the data center build-out and negatively affect stocks spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

While nobody can say where the market is headed in the coming weeks, Warren Buffett has some timeless advice on how political uncertainty should affect your investment strategy.

In Berkshire Hathaway's 2018 annual shareholder letter, published in early 2019, Buffett offered some words of wisdom on investing during high-tension political periods.

At the time, the U.S. was in a similar political boat as today. The 2018 midterms had occurred just a few months prior, when Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and ended the Republican trifecta during President Trump's first term.

Also similar to today, all three major market indexes sank in the week following the elections.

However, Buffett's advice for investing during politically charged eras is simple: continue buying quality stocks. The market will thrive over time regardless of who is president, and the wisest investors look past volatility and bet on strong businesses.

"Our country's almost unbelievable prosperity has been gained in a bipartisan manner," he noted in the Berkshire letter.

"Since 1942, we have had seven Republican presidents and seven Democrats. In the years they served, the country contended at various times with a long period of viral inflation, a 21% prime rate, several controversial and costly wars, the resignation of a president, a pervasive collapse in home values, a paralyzing financial panic and a host of other problems. All engendered scary headlines; all are now history."

The market's short-term performance will always be volatile to some degree, but what really matters is how it recovers over time.

While the market was shaky in the days following the 2018 elections, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 200% since then -- despite experiencing the COVID-19 crash and 2022 bear market in that time. If you'd invested in an S&P 500 ETF on Election Day 2018, you'd have more than tripled your money by today.

If we're on the cusp of a bear market, stock prices could plunge yet again. Yet the healthiest companies will not only pull through, but go on to experience lucrative returns over the coming years.

In Berkshire's 2018 letter, Buffett outlined his and then-business partner Charlie Munger's investing strategy:

"Charlie and I have no idea as to how stocks will behave next week or next year. Predictions of that sort have never been a part of our activities. Our thinking, rather, is focused on calculating whether a portion of an attractive business is worth more than its market price."

Quality stocks with robust underlying fundamentals are the most likely to thrive over time, and loading up on those stocks now can protect your portfolio against even the most severe volatility.

During the dot-com bubble, for example, the companies that fell apart were those with unsustainable business models, weak competitive advantages, or inexperienced leadership teams. But plenty of stocks survived, even if the short term was rocky.

Amazon sank by nearly 95% between 1999 and 2001, for instance. Nvidia crashed by more than 87% in 2002 alone. And Apple lost more than 51% of its value in a single trading day in 2000. Investors who held on to those stocks back then, however, would have built life-changing wealth by today.

If history proves just one thing, it's that buying quality companies with solid fundamentals and then holding those stocks for years (or, ideally, decades) is the most effective way to hedge against volatility.

The market's short-term performance can be daunting, and if you're feeling rattled by all the recent turbulence, that's normal. But with a solid portfolio full of long-term investments, you'll be well-positioned for whatever may come next.

#3360. Report: Apple’s planned $7 billion bond sale attracts four times as much demand

Apple has filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds. Here are the details.

Over the past week, several Big Tech companies have turned to the bond market to raise billions of dollars amid growing investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta, for instance, just raised $15 billion through a US bond offering, followed by another €9 billion (roughly $10 billion) in European bonds. Earlier this week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (approximately $6.7 billion), while Microsoft completed a $25 billion bond sale last week, its first since 2017.

Apple has also turned to bond sales in the past to raise billions of dollars.

Previous offerings include those in 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Most recently, Apple raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond offering in May 2025, which attracted approximately $10 billion in investor orders.

Earlier today, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

However, while other Big Tech companies have been borrowing heavily amid growing AI infrastructure investments, Apple’s filing makes no specific mention of AI.

Instead, the company says it intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, potentially including stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment, as it has done in previous bond offerings.

And while the prospectus didn’t specify how much Apple intends to raise, Bloomberg reported soon after that the company is targeting approximately $7 billion, with investors already placing orders totaling around $31 billion.

According to Bloomberg, strong investor demand has also helped Apple secure more favorable borrowing terms, with investors willing to accept lower interest rates than those offered by Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle in their recent bond sales.

All of this is happening amid a massive tech sell-off, which saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge more than 6% at one point today, with Nvidia shares falling about 8% and the S&P 500 dropping nearly 4%.

Apple’s own stock is also taking a hit, trading down 1.49% at the time of publication, but it is faring better than those of its Big Tech peers, whose stocks have become more closely tied to the AI spending boom.

Be that as it may, Apple is expected to finalize the size and pricing of its bond offering soon, potentially as early as later today, after which the company will file the definitive terms with the SEC.

#3359. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Apple Intelligence can now turn plans, to-dos, and tracking numbers into one-tap shortcuts inside your chats

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We have all lived the routine: someone texts you a dinner time or a parcel tracking code, and suddenly you are juggling three apps, highlighting tiny strings of text, and manually populating calendar slots like an unpaid personal assistant. In iOS 27.2, Apple eliminates that chore by weaving Apple Intelligence straight into Messages through Suggested Actions.

Instead of leaving you to juggle apps, the system scans incoming texts on-device and places one-tap action buttons directly beneath the chat bubble. Here is what the feature automates, how it cuts out the friction, and how to manage your settings.

Enabled by default, the feature tackles routine admin across five core areas. Mention a time or dinner plan, and an Add to Calendar button pre-fills the invite. Get texted an errand, and Add to Reminders logs the chore without making you open the app.

It clears up reference notes and travel logistics just as quickly. Longer texts trigger an Add to Notes shortcut, while addresses produce an instant Show in Maps link. The system also catches flight numbers and parcel codes, launching live status cards right in the thread.

Just keep in mind it is an Apple-only perk: shortcuts route strictly to native apps and only appear in blue-bubble iMessage chats.

Every category is switched on by default, but you do not have to live with buttons you never plan to tap. To clean up your threads, go to Settings, head into Apps, choose Messages, and select Suggested Actions.

You will find individual switches for Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Maps, and Flights and Packages, making it easy to keep the shortcuts that save you time and shut off the ones that get in the way.

#3357. Microsoft is winding down its deal to rent AI computing from Oracle

The rented servers ran older Nvidia chips, and Microsoft is rethinking billions in outside cloud deals.

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle after declining to renew it, Bloomberg reports. The servers ran older Nvidia chips. Microsoft is reassessing more than $80B in contracts with outside cloud providers.

Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Microsoft has been switching off the rented capacity in recent months after deciding not to renew the contract.

The servers ran older Nvidia chips and no longer matched what Microsoft needed, the people said. Ageing hardware is a growing worry: Gartner has warned that much AI infrastructure spending could face large write-downs as newer chips arrive.

The deal, announced in 2023, gave Microsoft Oracle servers to run its AI-powered Bing search, and Bloomberg could not determine its full size. Separate talks for Microsoft to lease more Oracle capacity collapsed in June, Business Insider reported.

Microsoft declined to comment. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for older chips, and its shares fell about 3%.

Microsoft has committed more than $80B to rent capacity from other cloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. Its leaders have grown frustrated with their costs and delays, Bloomberg said. This week, it reportedly turned down an option to expand a Nscale deal in Texas, weeks after pulling out of a Nscale site in the UK.

The news adds to Oracle’s troubles. Heavy spending on AI data centres has pushed its free cash flow negative and its credit rating to one notch above junk. Its shares have more than halved since a June peak.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. #3353. Castellum (CTM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins narrowed as acquisition spending rose, while the qualified pipeline grew sharply.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Castellum, Inc. (CTM -19.93%) reported that its strategic focus shifted toward a combination of organic growth and inorganic scaling through acquisitions. Management stated that the company completed its transition from integrating prior acquisitions to executing major prime contracts won in 2025. The company prioritized investments in business development and M&A infrastructure, anticipating these costs will yield revenue and earnings benefits within 6 to 12 months. Management indicated that the company is prioritizing acquisitions that offer cultural fit and financial discipline in addition to increased scale.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Castellum Inc.'s Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. An earnings press release was distributed yesterday, November 5, after the close of the market. A copy of that release as well as an earnings presentation is available on the company's website in the Investor Relations section and should be reviewed in conjunction with the Form 10-Q filed yesterday with the SEC. Please note that this call is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] Before we get started, I would like to remind you that today's call may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

Each as amended, these statements represent the company's expectations or beliefs concerning future events, including our expectations for future revenue growth, new customer opportunities, improvements to cost structure and profitability. Forward-looking statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties, which are outside of the company's control that could cause actual results to differ from those expressed or implied on this call. These include, among others, the company's ability to grow and execute on total backlog and qualified pipeline, ability to integrate and grow acquired companies, ability to identify and close additional acquisitions and factors affecting U.S. government spending, including budget delays, continuing resolutions and government shutdowns.

Please also note that on this call, we'll reference non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA, which is a non-GAAP financial measure used by management to measure the company's operating performance as required by SEC rules and regulations. Non-GAAP financial measures are reconciled to their most comparable GAAP financial measures in the earnings release issued yesterday afternoon. All forward-looking statements speak only as of today, and the company undertakes no obligation to update them, except as required by law. I would now like to turn the call over to Glen Ives, President and Chief Executive Officer of Castellum. Glen, please go ahead.

Glen Ives: Well, thank you, and good morning to everyone on our call. Joining me today are David Bell, our Chief Financial Officer; and Drew Merriman, our Chief Operating Officer. And they'll both be available to answer questions as well during the Q&A period at the end of the call. Following my opening remarks on the company's performance during our third quarter and first nine months, David will take you through the financials in more detail, and then I'll provide some commentary on our strategic priorities and also our outlook for the balance of 2026, and then we'll get to the questions during the Q&A period.

For the first nine months of 2026, we generated $42.9 million in revenue, up 6% from last year. And as previously announced, we expect record revenue for the full year period 2026. Much of that growth reflects the large Navy contracts we won in 2025. Our NAVAIR PMA-290 Special Missions Program contract continues to be a very meaningful contributor. And in August, the ceiling on that contract was increased by $32.8 million to a total of $136.2 million. And we're also seeing revenue from the five-year $66.2 million NAWCAD Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division Lakehurst program, which is still early in its ramp-up.

As we've regularly emphasized, we encourage investors to evaluate our performance over the long term rather than focusing too narrowly or too heavily on any single quarter. Given the nature of government contracting, the timing of the awards, program ramp-ups, revenue recognition, they can all fluctuate significantly from quarter-to-quarter and a very common factor in our industry. While those fluctuations are a normal part of our business, our year-over-year growth is what provides a much clearer picture of Castellum's overall trajectory and the steady progress that we're making. Government services revenue does not move in a straight line, particularly for a company our size with annual revenue between $55 million to $60 million.

Contracts do wind-down, new contracts ramp up and the crossover quarters can look very flat even when the underlying trajectory is clearly up. Our focus, our work, our effort, our commitment is always on delivering flawlessly for our existing mission customers and growing and strengthening every opportunity that we can possibly have for sustaining our growth. Turning now to our backlog. We ended the quarter with a total backlog of $254.5 million, including $18.2 million funded and $236.3 million unfunded. This compares to $271.7 million at June 30 of this year in 2026 as part of that backlog has moved to work in progress.

During the quarter, we refined how we report backlog by including priced contract options in our unfunded backlog. This change provides a much clearer view of our contracted business and aligns our reporting with industry standards. We do expect to recognize approximately 25% of our backlog over the next 12 months and about 51% over the next 24. Our qualified pipeline also grew to a record level of approximately $1.66 billion from $953.5 million at June 30 of this year. The pipeline represents potential future awards and reflects the investments we have made in our business development capacity this year, specifically to increase the volume and quality of opportunities we do pursue.

Our team continues to focus on serving our Army, Navy and our federal customers pursuing new awards and expanding our work under existing programs. The August modification to the NAVAIR PMA-290 special missions contract is a very real example of how strong program execution can create additional opportunities. I think our proven CTM team knows how to execute on contracts, and we know how to grow them. Finally, I'd like to briefly discuss our investments in business development and M&A, which I will expand upon following David's discussion of our financial results. During this year, we purposely increased our investments in these areas in accordance with our current strategy.

And the near-term impact on EBITDA because of these strategic investments was planned and anticipated, we view these strategic investments as the upfront work that we need to win, grow and scale Castellum as these are investments that we see new contract awards and associated revenue that we do expect to generate. We're making these investments from a position of financial strength, funded by our own operations using net operating income, and we believe they will support and strengthen our sustained growth over the next several years. Just want to reemphasize that point that we are making these investments from a position of financial strength, a strong balance sheet and funded by our own operations using net operating income.

With that, let me turn the call over to David to take you through the financial results in more detail.

David Bell: Thank you, Glen, and good morning to everyone. I'll go over our financial results for the quarter and the first nine months, then discuss cash flow and our balance sheet. Third quarter revenue came in at $14.7 million compared to $14.6 million a year ago and $13.9 million last quarter. The NAVAIR, PMA-290 special missions and NAWCAD Lakehurst MO&I contracts continue to contribute revenue as work continues to ramp up, although timing of work across our contracts can be affected and can affect individual quarters. Gross profit for the quarter was $5.3 million compared to $5.5 million last year.

Gross margin was 36.1% compared to 37.6% a year ago, but improved from approximately 34% in the second quarter of this year. The main factor driving this fluctuation is contract mix. During the third quarter, we carried a higher mix of subcontractor work on larger programs, and that generally carries a lower margin than our own direct labor. As just stated, sequentially, gross margin has improved from approximately 34% last quarter. Operating expenses were $5.9 million for the quarter versus $5 million a year ago. The increase reflects the business development team we've added, higher employee-related costs, outside support for acquisition activities and stock-based compensation.

These are areas where we made intentional investments as part of our growth plan rather than unexpected expenses, just as Glen stated a second ago. Adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was positive at approximately $600,000 compared to $1.1 million last year. The calculation excludes non-cash expenses such as $800,000 for stock-based compensation and employee stock purchase plan costs as well as $300,000 in depreciation and amortization. The full non-GAAP reconciliation is available in our earnings press release and presentation. As Glen mentioned, the decline in adjusted EBITDA was planned and anticipated as we made a deliberate decision to invest in our business development and acquisition efforts.

We have the capacity to spend more, but we're taking a measured approach, investing where we see the strongest potential return while protecting our financial flexibility. We reported a net loss of about $500,000 for the quarter versus a net income of $400,000 last year. The majority of this net loss was due to noncash items such as stock-based compensation and depreciation and amortization. Of course, the growth initiatives I just discussed had a real cost and impact. Looking at the nine-month period puts those results in context. Revenue increased by 6% to $42.9 million from $40.3 million a year ago, driven primarily by the ramp-up of our Navy contracts. Nine-month gross profit was essentially flat at $15.1 million.

Gross margin was 35.2% compared to 37.5% last year. Operating expenses were $17.4 million compared to $16.5 million a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA remained positive at approximately $1 million versus $1.8 million and a net loss of $1.8 million compared to $1.1 million last year. Those figures reflect the contract mix and the investment decisions that both Glen and I have just discussed. Turning to cash flow, which I think is a highlight of the period. Net cash provided by operating activities was $1.1 million for the period compared to a use of $1.3 million in the nine months of the prior year, a positive swing of $2.4 million.

That improvement was primarily driven by a smaller increase in accounts receivable in 2026 than in 2025. Importantly, we continue to generate positive operating cash flow while investing in business development and M&A. Turning to liquidity. We ended September with $15.7 million in cash and $8.8 million in net accounts receivable or $24.5 million combined. That combined balance was approximately $23.1 million at the end of 2025. That's an increase of roughly $1.5 million or about $500,000 per quarter on average. Receivables are not the same in cash, but together with these balances provide a useful context for our liquidity and working capital. We also ended the quarter with no outstanding debt and approximately $36.3 million of stockholders' equity.

Finally, an additional word on backlog composition. As Glen mentioned, total backlog was $254.5 million at quarter end with $18.2 million funded and $236.3 million unfunded. We expect to recognize approximately 25% of our backlog over the next 12 months and approximately 51% over the next 24. Importantly, these figures reflect only our existing backlog and do not include potential revenue from new contract awards or other business not currently included in our backlog. As with all government contracting, the timing of funding and option exercises rest with our customers. But this backlog provides a multiyear foundation of revenue visibility.

So to summarize the current financial picture, first nine months of revenue is up 6%, adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow are positive, and we have $24.5 million in cash and accounts receivable with no outstanding debt. While our investments in business development and M&A have weighed on near-term earnings as expected, we anticipate to begin seeing the benefits of these investments over the next six to 12 months. Building on this momentum, we remain on pace for record full year revenue for 2026. And with that, I'll turn the call back to Glen to discuss our strategy and our outlook.

Glen Ives: David, thanks very much. Yes, the financial results reflect the choices that we planned for and that we've been making throughout this year. That is continue to serve and grow our existing mission customers while putting more resources behind the next phase of our growth here at Castellum. So let's focus just for a minute here on how we are positioning Castellum for that next very important phase of growth and why we see acquisitions as really our greatest opportunity to achieve the scale that we are driving towards and are absolutely 100% committed to. That is, again, grow organically and scale inorganically. Organic growth does remain important for us.

It is a top priority as we move through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It's disciplined execution that always remains our priority. And I believe our CTM team over the last 1.5 years has really proven that and hammered that home. We expect record revenue for 2026, supported by the work we've already won. We've also strengthened our business development team to pursue larger opportunities and the increase in our qualified pipeline gives us more to compete for. We will also keep delivering flawlessly on our Army and Navy contracts and programs and also our federal civilian contracts that we've already won.

Strong execution supports and fortifies our business today and provides that rock-solid business foundation for the right acquisitions that we're looking to make. However, organic growth alone, as I've said, will not get us to scale. So we are definitely targeting acquisitions to get to the pace that we want to achieve. Again, that is why M&A is at the center of our growth strategy. This year, we've invested additional time and resources in identifying, screening and evaluating potential businesses, including support from outside advisers. We've targeted businesses that complement our current capabilities, strengthen our position with federal customers, add useful contracts and profitable contracts or technologies and contribute meaningful revenue and earnings, but scale alone is not the goal.

The price, the cultural fit, the chemistry and ability to integrate the business all must make sense to us and to our shareholders. We believe the work we put into that process is bringing us much closer to the right acquisition opportunity, and we are fast approaching that next phase. And while no transaction is assured and timing can change, our goal is to begin showing investors tangible results from these efforts over the next six to 12 months. We're actively evaluating several opportunities, and we intend to move quickly as we determine the strategic fit and financial terms are right.

We do see acquisitions as a primary way to accelerate our growth here at Castellum and improve our earnings potential beyond what organic expansion alone can deliver. That is why we have worked hard to position ourselves for this acquisition phase of our strategic plan. We've built a strong business foundation with multiple large prime contracts that take us well over five years. We've got a strong cash position, no debt, a very strong and healthy balance sheet. And so we're ready to move.

As we move through the end of 2026 and 2027, we expect the next six to 12 months to be a very important period for demonstrating our potential to scale and our goal once again to grow Castellum to our shareholders. I'd like to thank once again all our shareholders, our employees, our partners, our mission customers for your ongoing support, trust, confidence and commitment to CTM and our vital national security and defense mission. I feel very blessed to have an incomparable world-class team of the very best professionals in our industry. I truly believe and are wholly committed to our important and purposeful mission as directly supporting our nation's war fighters to help ensure our freedom of security.

That may sound a lot like mom and apple pie, but it's our truth, and it's what drives your CTM team to do our very best to grow and scale and bring real value to our shareholders, our mission customers and our people. That concludes our prepared remarks. Let's go to questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question comes from Derek Greenberg with Maxim Group.

Derek Greenberg: I wanted to start off with -- I think it was important the point you made about how short-term results aren't really as important and as indicative of company performance as the long term and as those contracts get recognized over their long length. I was wondering maybe if you could just talk about how visibility is in your current contracts in terms of those beginning to ramp? And if you could comment maybe on -- I noticed the backlog, the percent you expect to recognize over the next 12 and 24 months, both jumped a decent amount sequentially. So I was wondering if you're expecting acceleration from current contracts.

Glen Ives: Yes. Derek, thanks very much for your question and the point about how to look at government contracting for -- especially for a company our size at $55 million to $60 million in revenue, how those contracts are executed, what those time lines are, our relationship with our mission customers and the government and how all that impacts when we realize revenue on those contracts. I do think it may be helpful for some of our callers or our listeners and our shareholders who don't always hear this part of the business to maybe give a little more detail on the contracts themselves because that's the strength of our company, right?

These are all technology services and solutions contracts in very, very key tech domains that our war fighters and our mission customers need, obviously, to deal with all the different situations across the world. So the fact that they're so relevant and so important gives us great confidence that these contracts and the value of these contracts are going to be realized over their five-year period of performance. But I've got my Chief Operating Officer, Drew Merriman, on the line here. Drew, can you share with our listeners just a little bit about our contracts and how we execute on them?

Andrew Merriman: Sure. So I'll go over the top 3. The first being the 290 special missions contract, which is supporting the PA program with intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance and targeting. And that's one we recently expanded the scope on as we're continuing to perform well. We've got some new requirements, which answers one of the questions on why we see our -- executing our backlog has grown a little bit. And then also on our mission operations and integration contract, I think that's a good example to explain the ramp-up. So that contract was in its base year, and it's a consolidation contract with logistics, engineering and cyber. And so as other contracts come to an end, that work rolls in.

So the ramp-up in the base year is a little bit slower as it is in the out years. And then our other large contract is the software support activity up at Lakehurst, supporting aircraft launch and recovery where we do all of the software development for the systems that involve launching aircraft and landing them on the carriers. That's kind of an overview of our top 3.

Glen Ives: Thanks, Drew. And so Derek, going back to your question, just a lot of factors that influence how we execute on contracts in terms of requirements that change depending upon our mission customers and how they fund them. So going back to your point about why it's important to look at revenue growth and EBITDA for us across more of a year time frame than a quarter-by-quarter is because those requirements change regularly, constantly. And so something that they had planned to do for one quarter, they may push to the next and something else may come up where they want to -- for us to take on. So it's very, very difficult to predict.

And so when we're looked at quarter-to-quarter, you're going to see a lot of ups and downs. And our goal is by the end of the year to achieve our objectives, both in terms of how we support a customer and the revenue and EBITDA that we're able to attain. Does that answer you, Derek?

Derek Greenberg: Yes. That was very helpful. And then maybe turning to the pipeline. Maybe if you could just give some more color that shot up pretty significantly quarter-over-quarter. But I was wondering if you could maybe talk about the composition of that pipeline, how far along those opportunities are and maybe like a rough estimate of when those potential opportunities could potentially be converted upon.

Glen Ives: Sure. Yes. So the strength of our pipeline and the growth of our pipeline is due directly to the investments we've been making in business development over the past year. So we all know that in government contracting, we're basically on five-year cycles. And so it's an imperative for us to have not just a pipeline of good opportunities, but a very realistic one, one that matches up with our sweet spot, the things that we do really, really well. And I think our listeners on this call understand what we do here at CTM, right?

We provide those tech solutions and services in those key tech domains, whether it's C5ISR, a mission domain like that or a tech domain, whether it's AI or cyber or any of those that are very relevant to our mission customers. So the idea behind our pipeline is to ensure that we have the kind of opportunities that work directly to our strengths and to the mission customers that we feel we are very, very familiar with, and can compete on these opportunities for. But we also want to balance the pipeline to get us into new markets.

And the ones I just spoke about with our current market and our current mission customers tend to be more near term because we're ready to jump on those opportunities. The pipeline opportunities that we have that are longer term are really associated with markets that are newer to us, ones that we have not penetrated yet. That's going to take us some time to do the kind of capture and the kind of development that we need to do. So I feel very good about our pipeline. It's a good balance of opportunities that will test us in terms of staying on top of our game from a technology perspective.

But it's also a pipeline that's balanced in terms of opportunities related to customers and markets that we know where I know we can be very, very competitive. But then also opportunities that will stretch us, right, and hopefully get us into new markets. But that ties directly into the message that I was really trying to send today, Derek, and that is it's just not about pipeline. It's just not about organic growth. We've proven that we can win. We've proven we can compete when it comes to organic growth. 2025 was certainly a year that I think should reinforce that. But as importantly, organic growth will just -- it will be steady and take us so far.

It's going to have to be our acquisition strategy and our acquisition efforts and doing that part of the business properly that will help us really scale the company. So that blend of organic and inorganic growth is a vital part of our strategy, and it's what's going to drive CTM to the kind of value that we outlined.

David Bell: Glen, I can add a little more, too. So as far as the composition and time line, so we track our top 10 for 2027, and we prioritize by our core market, which is NAVAIR and then we look at new markets from same capabilities. So we have opportunities in Space Force, Air Force, Army, where the capabilities line up and the pipeline goes out to 2030. So as we start to qualify new opportunities, the pipeline is strong and keeps growing based on -- we know there's a real requirement. We know there's money behind it, and we know we have same capabilities. Does that answer the question.

Derek Greenberg: Yes, that's really helpful. And then I was curious just how you view the investments you've made so far this year in terms of where you're at now with business development and the other areas of investment, do you feel comfortable with the level you've made? Or do you think there'll be more investments to be made going forward? Just your outlook on that.

Glen Ives: Yes. So Derek, that's a question I think I ask myself just about every day because when -- again, when you're a company our size, you really have to be very, very smart and disciplined about your resources. We certainly are not a $1 billion company, and we don't have the kind of resources that some of our large business competitors have. So we have to make the most of what we have. And so we challenge ourselves as a team literally every day to ensure that we're balancing our costs and getting the most out of our -- the most return out of our investments when it comes to business growth.

If I could get two more business developers and two more proposal developers and add another consultant to help in our acquisition strategy, I jump all over it. But no, I can't do that. We need to balance that with what we can really, really do I feel very confident that, that's what we've done. Derek Greenberg: Yes. That makes sense. Last one from me, and then I'll pass the line. I was wondering if you can maybe just comment macro-wise, if you're seeing any impact either from just the elections or if you have any visibility in terms of funding and appropriations and if those will have any impacts on your business over the next couple of years?

Glen Ives: Sure. I think the election piece is probably a little too early to really give you an intelligent comment on. Although there are some things I think we can probably anticipate. For example, there's a very key initiative right now that the Small Business Administration is considering, and that is changing the small business high standards. Depending upon how that plays out, that could be a very significant change in a very positive way for Castellum and companies like ours.

But every administration, every change in Congress does come with some impact. But I think history has proven, especially with our company that we're pretty resilient. The changes that we see with administration changes and changes in Congress, even with some policy changes, we're able to sort of work through and weather.

And there may be some spikes up and down in terms of impact to some of our contracts or some of our opportunities quarter-to-quarter. But over the period of our sales cycle, which basically in government contracting is about five years because of the length of contracts, we're able to mitigate those. Derek Greenberg: Thank you for taking my questions.

Glen Ives: No problem, Derek. I think you actually asked four. So we're trying to keep it to two, but that's okay.

Operator: Your next question comes from Chip Rewey with Rewey Asset Management.

Glen Ives: Chip, thanks for your questions here. So let's break that down a little bit. And to me, just based on my own experience in this business, we need to grow the company, and we need to grow it in a way that makes sense. It's disciplined, it's deliberate, it's thoughtful. But it also needs to be -- there also needs to be a sense of urgency, right? There needs to be a sense of drive. Let's move this company forward as quickly as we can. disciplined, smart, but quickly, expeditiously. Stock buyback, they're all, I think, meet strategies.

But at the end of the day, I've got to grow the company and organic growth is something that is certainly achievable. It's certainly a part of our plan. It's certainly a priority of our plan. But I think anyone who has run a business in our industry will tell you that organic growth is a grind. It's tough. It takes time. It doesn't happen. You don't go from $55 million to $60 million to $120 million in 18 months with just organic growth, unless you're very, very, very fortunate and very, very lucky. And so if you look at various models in our industry, whether it's private or public, there is an acquisition plan.

And so it's a plan -- it's a strategy that just about every successful company, and I mean a successful company in our industry employs. And that is a mix of -- the right mix of organic and inorganic growth. Because if you do not integrate those strategies, you're looking at long-term growth that takes you over an extended period of time. And if you're privately held and you have the patience, that works great. And I've had that experience before. But if you're publicly traded, you don't have that same time line. You don't necessarily have the same patience from your investors and your shareholders. They're expecting more.

And here at CTM, that's what we're trying to do, Chip, is we're trying to move the company forward in a way that makes sense for us. And it's not just -- I don't want you to think that we're just making acquisitions haphazardly. There's a lot of planning and thought that goes behind them. They have to be the right acquisition. And so when we look at our plan, we know that to scale the company to get it to where we want it to go, organic growth is not enough. Stock buybacks are not enough. I want to leverage our cash.

I want to leverage our position to the maximum extent possible and do what's best for the company in terms of how quickly we can grow in a way that is sustainable. And it has to be through M&A. And again, it's not rocket science. It's not an exceptional model. Many companies have performed to it successfully. But it's the execution piece, right? It's not the model itself. It's understanding the model, but it's really the execution piece. Can you take advantage of your pipeline? Can you make it real? We can, and we will. But I don't have the patience to wait five years for that to happen to realize all those opportunities or even longer.

We have to have a smart strategy. And I like it to -- I don't know if you watched the ball game last night with the Jags beat the Ravens. I happen to be a Jags fan, so I got at least half the game. The Jags won because they have a balanced attack. They had a strong ground game and a strong passing game. Our ground game is the organic growth and our passing game is the inorganic growth. And the teams that have the balanced strategy and can execute on them are the ones that are going to succeed. And that's basically what we're trying to do.

Chip Rewey: I hear you, and I think that's a great strategy. I think I've been doing this a very long time. And your balance sheet right now has a lot of cash on it. Charles Bichiro: Great. And I know this is another subject that's brought up already. But ideally, we are a company that we can finance where we can do it intelligently and smartly in terms of any debt, just the number of options for the number of shares that we would use, the amount of equity we would use, the amount of cash we would use. But the kind of companies we're looking for are ones that would take us deeper into our market or into an adjacent market where we can leverage our capabilities even to a greater extent.

Companies that have the kind of contracts that we feel are -- that we can strengthen and grow upon and continue to strengthen the company, those will be very, very important. David Bell: Yes, I'll jump in real quickly. Yes. And thank you very much for that question, Charles. Like Glen said, we're going to be smart about the acquisitions. The previous four years, the first phase of this company from 2020 until 2024, there were a lot of good things done. But while doing it, the company accumulated over $12 million in debt.

And the companies that we had acquired at the time were all very small businesses and three of them had done extremely well, but they certainly weren't postured for continued organic growth. So in mid-2024, we realized that the company really needed to adjust in a big way. And we went from integrating those companies into Phase 2, and that was, hey, we absolutely have to focus and grow this company organically. That is due in large part to the team that we've built here. And that's important to understand because it's one thing to do business in our industry as a large business or a small. But bottom line is we're going to continue to press organically. We're going to continue to press to make the right acquisitions, and that's how we're going to scale. And that's how we're going to get our stock to where it needs to be. We can talk about buybacks. We can talk about reverse splits. We can talk about all those kinds of things.

But what I want to do is make sure that we have a healthy, strong company that's going to endure for our shareholders and bring that value that they're looking for. I can't guarantee that in six months. No. But if you hang in there for a little while here while we execute on our strategy and give us a chance to do that, I think we'll also attract more institutional investors, which has to be a big part of our plan. Follow this ultimate checklist before the frost hits

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

My yard is absolutely covered in leaves and that's always one of the biggest indicators that I need to start seriously thinking about getting it ready for winter. The winter months bring their own set of challenges from thinning grass to damaged roots, so being prepared and protecting your shrubs and lawn will ultimately save you a lot of time, money and hard work.

Over the past few years, I've streamlined the steps I take in order to fit in my winter garden prep before it gets too cold and before the frost starts to wreak havoc on my plants. Here's the 5-step checklist I swear by each year to get my yard winter ready.

As mentioned, the fallen leaves are the first problem I know I need to tackle. They can quickly damage the glass, blocking sunlight and reducing air circulation. Once I've raked up the leaves with my favorite 'tarp burrito' method, I need to focus on removing any more debris and clutter.

Over the summer months, my yard has been lovingly used, but that means there are tools, toys and leftover gardening items lying around. For winter, it's important to clear up and pack away everything that doesn't belong. Not only because leaving them out will damage your yard, but it'll ruin the items too.

It's hard to pick plants for your yard that last all-year round and some in particular are sensitive to the winter weather, especially those which are tropical/exotic. After you identify which plants these are, it's a great idea to wrap them up to protect them. For this, I look to the 5 household items that can protect your plants from frost.

My personal favorites to use are horticultural fleece or bubble wrap as it's something I usually have leftover from the year before (or ready for wrapping presents in the holiday season). As soon as the temperature really drops or there's warning of frost, I like to wrap them up and leave them until spring.

This large fleece is specifically designed to protect outdoor plants from the cold weather. Available in three sizes, it also comes with the pegs needed to pin and secure the fleece into the ground. Importantly, it's also breathable material meaning your plants will still manage to survive underneath.

Working out when to give your lawn one last mow depends on where you're living, but it also shouldn't just be dictated because you know you're heading into the winter months. As the Farmers' Almanac explains: "Keep mowing your lawn as long as the grass is actively growing." And that's a rule I live by.

Adding: "A useful temperature clue is when daytime high temperatures consistently remain near or below 50°F." But you also shouldn't go on temperature alone. Consider the growth, temperature and type of grass you have in your yard as well – and, of course, whether it's still growing.

Another way to protect the plants before the winter hits is to apply some compost or bark mulch around the roots. This works as a great insulator to protect them from frost, as well as protecting the soil in general which can deteriorate during extreme winds and heavy rains.

As a rule, I like to add about a 2 to 3 inch layer as a sort of winter blanket that mimics the one I find myself sitting under. This is also an effective way to stop weeds that are hardy enough to penetrate the soil from growing all winter long.

In the same way I like to clear up any debris or clutter in my yard, I think it's also important to focus on any lawn, yard or patio furniture you've been putting to good use over the summer months.

It's far too easy when it gets cold and dark outside to forget about the furniture and put off clearing it up or covering it over for another day. If you keep forgetting, you're putting your furniture in danger of rust, excessive wear or even rotting. So, get out there and get it wrapped up before it's too late!

#3351. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3350. Google takes over the Wyoming data centre site Crusoe had planned

The AI data centre developer is handing over the site a day after Google pledged $17B there.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, after pledging $17B there. Bloomberg had reported Crusoe was pushed aside after failing to sign customers. Terms were not disclosed.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, Crusoe said on Friday. Neither company disclosed the terms.

The deal comes a day after Google said it would spend $17B on its first Wyoming data centre, in Laramie County. It ends Crusoe’s early work on the site, which included choosing the location, winning government approvals and planning its power supply.

Crusoe announced the project with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass Energy in July 2025, saying it could eventually grow to 10 GW. In June, Crusoe was being pushed aside after failing to sign customers, with Google raising concerns about costs and timing, Bloomberg reported.

Crusoe said it still has more than 6 GW of capacity under contract and over 40 GW in its pipeline. It is also building a data centre campus for Google near Amarillo, Texas, and raised $3.9B at a $30.9B valuation in September. Elsewhere it has landed customers, including deals with Meta in June and a reported $13B contract with Jane Street.

Developers face a tougher climate. Several new governors elected this week have promised to rein in data centres, Bloomberg said, and voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures.

#3348. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3346. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.
