Total revenue grew 24.6% to $79.9 million. Organic revenue growth was 16.6%. Total written premiums grew 18.5% to $554.2 million. Adjusted EBITDA grew 15% to $19.5 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 24.4%.

On profitability, our 24.4% adjusted EBITDA margin was within our full-year guidance range. As we discussed last quarter, we expect the temporary benefit from MGA Florida takeout books to normalize as those policies renew at the full-term premiums with standard commission expenses. And that is what we are seeing. The year-over-year comparison also reflects lower interest income as we deployed cash into share repurchases and acquisitions, as well as planned investments in growth initiatives. Janice will cover the margin bridge in more detail shortly. The market environment continued to soften in the third quarter, with most carriers turning their focus toward growth initiatives.

Carrier demand for new business flow remains strong, and carriers continue to roll out incentives and broaden their underwriting appetite to win new business. This environment rewards distribution platforms with scale, and our results demonstrate the value we bring to our agents, policyholders, and carrier partners across market cycles. Every part of our platform contributed this quarter. In Insurance Services, written premium grew 12.5% to $444.7 million, led by our corporate branches, where written premiums grew 19.9%, and our commission income grew 20.4%. Our agency in-a-box channel grew written premiums 10.1%. Our MGA channel continued to scale, with written premiums up 50.9% to $109.5 million and MGA new business more than doubling.

MGA revenue increased 78.1% to $24.8 million and now represents 31% of total revenue, up from 22% just a year ago. We also continue to diversify our mix, with Commercial Lines written premiums growing 32.2% to $107.1 million or 19% of total written premium. Our strategy remains consistent. We are executing our 4 core priorities, delivering strong double-digit organic growth, executing accretive M&A, investing in technology and platform enhancements to drive agent productivity, and deploying capital with discipline. This quarter, we again made meaningful progress on all 4. On the acquisition front, TWFG Insurance Services completed the branch conversion acquisition of Select Insurance Solutions during the third quarter.

Select joins a 2026 roster of corporate store and MGA acquisitions that include APIA, Lofton Wells, and Fortress Insurance Services. Branch conversions are accretive; margin-expanding opportunities may move established TWFG agency-in-a-box branches onto our corporate store platform, where commission expense is replaced by a lower salary cost, creating a higher-margin corporate store. These branches are led by seasoned agency owners with established books requiring minimal integration. Integration of our first-half acquisitions remains on track, and these teams are positioned to contribute to TWFG's long-term growth strategy. On capital allocation, our balance sheet continues to give us flexibility.

Our Class A share count stood at approximately 12.9 million shares at quarter end, down from approximately 15 million at the end of 2025, reflecting the share repurchase program we executed earlier this year. We also expanded our revolving credit facility to $125 million, which remains fully undrawn. Combined with our cash positions, this gives us approximately $203 million to invest in growth, pursue accretive M&A, and return capital to shareholders. On technology, we continue to invest in AI-enabled capabilities that help make our agents more productive and available to the clients they serve.

TWFG is positioned to benefit from AI's continued evolution because we own our technology stacks, have proprietary policy and client data, and are deploying AI to amplify what our people do best. We look forward to sharing more at our Investor Day on Thursday, November 12, at our home office in the Woodlands, where we will provide more detailed overviews of agencyinabox, corporate stores, M&A opportunities, the MGA platform strategy, geographic expansion plans, and technology roadmap. Our goal for attendees is to leave with a deeper understanding of our diversified distribution platform and to meet the leaders driving our business. Before turning it over to Janice, I want to acknowledge the outstanding execution of our team this quarter.

Our results are the product of thousands of individuals contributing every day from our agents, our carrier partners, and our corporate team. I could not be more proud of the entire TWFG family. With that, I will turn the call over to Janice for a closer look at our financial results.

Janice Zwinggi: Thank you, Gordy. I am pleased to report the following third-quarter results, beginning with our top KPI, written premium. Total written premium grew $86.5 million or 18.5% to $554.2 million, driven by strong renewal and new business performance. Renewal premium grew $48.5 million or 13.4% to $410.7 million, and new business grew $37.9 million or 35.9% to $143.5 million. For the third quarter, consolidated written premium retention was 88% compared to 91% in the prior-year period. Insurance services retention was 90% compared to 92%, and TWFG NTA retention was 78% compared to 80%. On a year-to-date basis, consolidated retention was 91%, up from 89% in the prior-year period. Looking at the components of our written premium.

Insurance services grew $49.5 million or 12.5% to $444.7 million, driven primarily by renewal growth of $40.6 million or 13% and new business growth of $8.9 million or 10.8%, supported by organic and inorganic growth across both agency in the box and corporate stores. Our MGA channel grew $37 million or 50.9% to $109.5 million with new business growth of $29.1 million or 122%, driven by the ramp of our voluntary Florida homeowners program, the continued renewal cycle of our Citizens takeout book, and contributions from APIA, which we acquired in the first quarter of 2026. Total revenues increased $15.8 million or 24.6% to $79.9 million.

Commission income grew $15.1 million or 25.9% to $73.4 million, which was driven by strong MGA performance, with growth of $10.7 million or 92.6% as a result of contributions from the acquisitions of MGA Florida and the APIA programs, which generate higher commission rates. Insurance services grew $4.4 million or 9.4% due to organic growth as well as contributions from acquisitions. Commission income growth outpaced written premium growth by 740 basis points as the MGA programs contribute higher commission rates than the insurance services business. Contingent income was $2.6 million compared to $2.1 million in the prior-year period, and fee income was comparable to the prior-year quarter at $3.6 million.

Organic revenues reached $68.7 million, representing a $9.8 million increase over the $58.9 million reported in the prior-year quarter. This yielded an organic revenue growth rate of 16.6% and was at the top of our full-year guidance range and above industry averages. Importantly, our growth this quarter was volume-led rather than rate-driven. With rates moderating, we grew by adding policies and clients as well as retaining our client base, as indicated in our renewal growth across both offerings. Our Insurance Services business continues to generate sustainable and consistent organic growth independent of acquisition contributions. Turning to operating expenses. Commission expense increased $7.3 million, or 20.9%, to $41.9 million, growing 500 basis points slower than commission income.

This operating leverage was primarily driven by higher commission income rates on MGA program business as well as an increased concentration of corporate store acquisitions carrying minimal commission expense. Salaries and employee benefits increased $1.9 million or 19.3% to $11.8 million due mainly to added headcount from our recent acquisitions. Other administrative expenses increased $4.5 million or 85.8% to $9.7 million, primarily due to professional and legal fees associated with capital markets activity and the expansion of our credit facility, as well as continued investments to support our growth initiatives. Approximately $1.8 million of the costs in the quarter were nonrecurring, primarily those legal and professional fees, as previously mentioned, are excluded from our adjusted results.

Depreciation and amortization increased $2.2 million, or 40.7%, to $7.5 million, primarily from amortization related to our recent acquisitions. Now moving to profitability. Net income for the quarter was $9 million compared to $9.6 million in the prior-year quarter, and net income margin was 11.3% compared to 15%. Diluted earnings per share were $0.09 compared to $0.11. The quarter-over-quarter comparison reflects higher administrative and personnel expenses, lower interest income, and higher noncash amortization related to acquisitions. Adjusted net income increased 16.3% to $15.1 million with an adjusted net income margin of 18.9% compared to 20.2% in the prior year quarter.

Adjusted EBITDA grew 15% to $19.5 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 24.4% compared to 26.5% in the prior-year quarter. The 210 basis points decrease was primarily due to interest income, which we include in adjusted EBITDA, declining to $0.5 million from $1.6 million in the prior-year period as we deployed cash into share repurchases and acquisitions. This accounts for roughly 180 basis points of the decline. The remaining 30 basis point decline was primarily due to corporate overhead costs for business growth, including technology initiatives. Year-to-date, adjusted EBITDA margin was 28%, up 310 basis points from 24.9%, and adjusted diluted earnings per share increased to $0.28, up 21.7% from $0.23 in the prior quarter.

From a cash and capital perspective, cash flow from operating activities for the quarter was $10.6 million compared to $15 million in the prior year period, and adjusted free cash flow was $7.5 million compared to $12.3 million, primarily reflecting working capital impacts, including higher commission receivables and lower commission payables and other liabilities. These impacts were partially offset by amortization. On a year-to-date basis, operating cash flow was $43.1 million, up 7.2% from $40.2 million, and adjusted free cash flow was $31.2 million, up 8.2% from $28.8 million. Our balance sheet remains strong. As of September 30, we had $77.8 million in unrestricted cash and cash equivalents plus $17.8 million in restricted cash.

We have full unused capacity on our expanded $125 million revolving credit facility and only $2.5 million of term notes outstanding, giving us approximately $202.8 million of available liquidity from unrestricted cash and revolver capacity. And with that, I will now turn it back to Gordy for closing remarks.

Richard Bunch: Thank you, Janice. Turning to our outlook. We are updating our 2026 guidance from the second quarter based on our strong year-to-date performance and our line of sight to the balance of the year. We expect total revenues of $300 million to $320 million, organic revenue growth of 15% to 17% and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 24% to 27%. Through the first 9 months, organic growth of 21.5% and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 28% are tracking above the high end of those ranges. And our outlook reflects a prudent view of the fourth quarter, including the continued normalization of the MGA outlook and the softening market conditions.

In closing, I want to thank our employees, agents, carriers, executive team, and shareholders for their continued trust in TWFG. We see significant opportunities ahead, and we look forward to hosting many of you at our Investor Day on Thursday, November 12, at our home office here in the Woodlands, Texas. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question or comment comes from the line of Michael Zaremski from BMO Capital Markets.

Michael Zaremski: A question on the guidance. I recall last quarter, the sticking points in the guidance were contingents, which could be choppy, and M&A-related revenues. Organic growth beat and raised, but total revs guide staying the same. So I guess does that imply -- is it contingents or M&A-related revenues that are falling a bit shy of the upside scenarios into the year-end? It's just a bit of a wide range. So hoping to get some color.

Richard Bunch: Yes, sure. Great question, Mike. So we chose not to up the contingent line coming out of the third quarter. We have locked in most of our major profit-sharing contingencies at the 9-month lock-in. And when you do that, you take a little bit of a haircut on the ultimate payable. So there's still potential upside to the contingent line, but that would be coming from more variable contingencies of which we won't know the outcome until after the calendar year. So we chose not to increase the contingent revenue line at this time. As far as M&A, there's always potential for additional M&A at any time.

We didn't have any significant transactions that altered that potential upside in the quarter. We did announce an internal branch conversion, which also helps support margin expansion going into the fourth quarter.

Michael Zaremski: You mentioned the pricing environment and just the backdrop a number of times. Can you just further elaborate on specifically, maybe quantitatively, what you're seeing with pricing and how it's impacting revenues, maybe MGA versus non-MGA or personal lines versus commercial or whatever you feel would be the best way you guys think about it?

Richard Bunch: Sure. So on personal lines, it's really geographically different, and the more cat-exposed geography, you're seeing high single digits to low teens property decreases in pricing in the personal lines auto; more countrywide, you're seeing less rate coming down than perhaps we saw earlier in the year. So I'd call that more rate moderation. And on commercial lines, we're primarily in small business, lower end of middle market, less volatile areas of commercial lines where we don't have wild swings up or down.

On the commercial property side, I think you have the read through all the other brokers out there; there's still a little pressure on the property side, but not as acute as it was in the prior years. So overall, we see a moderating rate environment, geographical, more significant in cat-prone geography, less so in less cat-exposed, less cat reinsurance-oriented lines.

Operator: Our next question or comment comes from the line of Tommy McJoynt from KBW.

Unknown Analyst: This is Molly on for Tommy. My first question is on written premium retention. I saw it fell 5 points from last quarter and 3 points year-over-year to 88%. Does this primarily reflect normalization given Florida takeout renewals in prior periods? Or are you seeing any underlying changes in retention? And is 88% a reasonable starting point as we think about 2027?

Janice Zwinggi: Yes. I think when you're looking at quarter-over-quarter, the renewals are being taken into account. However, what I noticed in Q3 compared to Q3 of '26 compared to Q3 of '25, in the denominator where you take new business and renewals from the prior year, the new business uptick was due to Florida. So it wasn't always just based on renewals, but it was the new business and renewals, '25 to '26. And then renewals in '26, the numerator did increase.

Richard Bunch: We've previously put out that our long-term average retention is in the 88th- 89th percentile range. Yes. On a consolidated basis, we've been in the 90%, 91% range the last several quarters. If you isolate out, and we're not allowed to tell you specifically, but we would be in that same range without some of the impacts regarding the Florida book.

Janice Zwinggi: And then shifting gears here a little, does the expanded credit facility of $125 million signal a more actionable acquisition pipeline? And how would you weigh M&A against authorizing additional share repurchases?

Richard Bunch: Yes. I think we have had the credit facility in place for multiple years; given our size and growth initiatives and our constructive pipeline, it made sense for us to upsize the facility in advance of all the opportunities that we have that we're looking at. I think in our prepared comments, between the base credit facility and cash on hand, that implies $203 million of capital available for us to invest across M&A, across internal investment for infrastructure improvements, and initial growth initiatives. That's without using equity in transactions. So if we use equity in combination with cash, that significantly raises the size of transactions we can entertain.

Last year, we mentioned we had quite a few larger transactions in the pipe. Most of those cooled off as the spring market volatility took hold. Some of those are coming back out and giving us visibility to additional opportunities. We've been very disciplined in our M&A. We've got a very healthy pipeline going into '27, and we thought it was prudent for us to be in a position to execute without having to go through credit and other workflows in order to get a deal done. I should supplement with the fact that the facility also has a $75 million built-in accordion. So that takes the facility up to $200 million.

So that broadens even further the size of deals we can retain.

Operator: Our next question or comment comes from the line of Brian Meredith from UBS.

Brian Meredith: Gordy, I guess the first question is, obviously, a lot of people have been asking this: these personal agents, AI-enabled. Maybe some thoughts and comments on that one as far as what the potential impact on your business is. And then, as an add-on to that, I'm just curious: has that helped at all with respect to your pipeline for potential acquisitions and lowering valuations? Are you seeing more agencies looking to maybe potentially sell?

Richard Bunch: Good question, Brian. I think on just the whole AI narrative, I think there's going to be really multiple camps on how they interpret the future. So I would say there are probably opportunities for agencies that are a little bit longer in the tooth, closer to retirement that possibly don't want to go through the next inflection point of technology innovation and change for our industry. Those become buying opportunities as they're not going to want to reinvest and/or learn the new way forward. So we are seeing a few tenured agencies raise their hands and start to look for the exit. So that's a buying opportunity.

Those are going to be lower-sized agencies, and that becomes part of our M&A pipeline going forward. I think for the most part, the long-term forward-looking agencies are all adopting AI initiatives within their agencies. It's going to be the haves and havenots. We will be in the camp with ads. If they're not already doing it, they probably should be updating their search results. A year ago today, everybody would be talking about SEO. Today, everybody is talking about GEO. And that's the distinction between how your business is found online. SEO is Google; GEO is your ChatGPTs, your AI-initiated search. And we're seeing flow coming through from both.

I think most agencies are adopting and changing their technology platforms to be where they need to be in the new world going forward. As far as the districtinediation concerns, we've seen what's been rolled out so far. I think even Progressive announced in their call that they're seeing very little traffic coming from that side, but they'll be in a position to be responsive should that ever change. And I think for us, we're going to be similarly forward-thinking and being in a position to attract that traffic should that increase.

Brian Meredith: Makes sense. And then one other just quick numbers question, and I may have missed this, but it looks like that the commission rate on agency and Fox is declining. Is there anything going on there?

Richard Bunch: It should be relatively flat. And I think that's because when we get incentive comp, most of that ends up in our contingency line. Then there is a little differential between new business and renewal commission. And as your portfolio grows, renewal commission becomes a larger portion of your portfolio than new business. So that could be slight shifts, but nothing material that I see.

Operator: Our next question or comment comes from the line of Cameron Bianchi from Piper Sandler.

Unknown Analyst: This is Cameron on for Paul. I was wondering if you could just talk about a little bit what you're seeing in the M&A pipeline. And if you continue to believe the pipeline will be accretive to margins, like the M&A operations that you're seeing from recent acquisitions?

Richard Bunch: Yes. So we did a reflective look back on all the prior acquisitions from the last several years, and we are seeing a consistent margin expansion theme from those operations. We believe that everything we're looking at in our pipeline needs to be accretive in order for it to be considered. And so we're monitoring what's working best in our prior acquisitions so we can make sure we incorporate those structures as we go forward for future acquisitions. But it's our belief, and in our real results, that the things we are acquiring are accretive to margin, accretive to revenue growth, and provide us with talent that's going to be beneficial to us to sustain long-term growth.

Unknown Analyst: And then could you talk a little bit about what you're seeing from a competitive standpoint in Texas and maybe a little on the Florida MGA business as well?

Richard Bunch: Texas is its own country, as most people know. You have multiple geographies with different risk exposures. The areas towards the coastline have rate moderation at a higher level than those that are only hail exposed in Central Texas. So similarly with North Texas, it's more of a hail tornado exposure and their rates are moderating, but not as significant as you would see along the hurricane exposed more cat price around hurricane than inland. When you get to Florida, the whole state is a CAT zone. You had a lot of successful takeout companies started in the last 5 years. You had a lot of combined ratios come down with tort reform.

So when they got rid of the assignment of benefits, that made a significant improvement in average loss costs and frequency of litigation. That market is softening, and everybody is positioning for retention and growth of their programs. Our programs are no different. We have to remain competitive in order to retain the initial takeout portfolios as well as position the new business voluntary programs to be competitive in today's marketplace. The good news for us is we didn't have those voluntary programs in place prior.

So we're not going to have massive decreases in premium over multiple years, given that most of the business we're writing is new business at more current rates, which would have been lower than they would have been 2 or 3 years ago.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question or comment comes from the line of Rowland Mayor from RBC Capital Markets.

Rowland Mayor: I think in the prepared remarks, you mentioned PIF growth as a revenue driver, but I don't know if you gave an actual number. Could you maybe help me understand how the policies in force are growing? And does organic normalize towards that as pricing softens?

Richard Bunch: Yes. So 2 things there. We've never provided discounts. We introduced that in our prepared remarks to explain the difference in our growth going into this softer market. During a hard market, you're getting growth both from PIF count, but more pressure or more growth coming from rate. As the market is softening. Now we're shifting the narrative to say that more of our organic growth is coming from PIF count rather than rate. The rate environment is something that will make it incumbent upon us to add new customers, cross-sell existing customers, and grow our total policies in order to sustain organic growth at the levels that we want to achieve.

Rowland Mayor: Then I guess, during the year, the margin guide has moved up. Part of that, I think, is contingent. And I think if my memory serves, the first half was impacted by some hiring. Could you help me understand what normalized margins might look like and how your business mix towards corporate and MGA impacts that?

Richard Bunch: Yes. We've talked about our margin. So where our margin has been for '26 is elevated. Most of that elevation was due to the MGA takeout business that had income without corresponding commission expense. As that's normalizing, policies are renewing with full-term economics where we're actually paying the commission expenses, that's going to come down. When we went public several years ago, our target long-term margin was in the low 20s, so between 22% and 23%. We've given and reaffirmed our full-year guidance for this calendar year at a higher range. And that's because we've had the benefit of the first 3 quarters with that takeout business and the favorable economics there.

Operator: Our next question or comment comes from the line of Pablo Singzon from JPMorgan.

Pablo Singzon: For organic growth this quarter, I was wondering what it was, excluding the impact of the Florida takeout business?

Richard Bunch: Janice has been waiting for you to ask that question, Pablo. Excluding the takeout business. No, it's 15.6%. But excluding the takeout. We can give that. Well, we're not supposed to give you the excluding stuff because it's smoothing over the results. So what we can say is organic was in the double digits regardless of activities in the state of Florida.

Pablo Singzon: And then I guess just a follow-up to the last question on margins. It's a similar attack here, right? So, to your point, Gordy, the margins benefited from Florida. Is your outlook for margins still in the low 20s ex Florida? Or are we moving closer to the mid-20s here?

Richard Bunch: So for '26 is the only guidance we put out, we put margin. We've given you the range. And if we look at long term, we think that our margins, as we continue to do accretive M&A, as we continue to expand the mix shift to commercial lines and MGA programs that's going to be the lower end of the mid-20s probably is a better range as we normalize the economics. And so right now, our reaffirmed was 24% to 27%, and that's for calendar year '26. And we haven't given guidance for '27. But that's how I would frame it.

Operator: Our next question or comment is a follow-up from Mr. Michael Zaremski from BMO Capital Markets.

Michael Zaremski: Just a quick follow-up. And if you think it's just splitting hairs, feel free to say we could follow up offline. But back to the contingent question earlier. So I think your answer was that you're taking a haircut by locking in certain elements of commission now. And then you also said there could be upside in January, so in 4Q based on -- I'm not sure what, maybe how the loss ratio trends for home and auto. But I know, is it worth teasing out what you mean by potential upside?

Richard Bunch: So we had a higher total contingency revenue in '25. And that was an outstanding combined ratio year across multiple geographies and all lines of business. We have a lower current accrual for contingent income. That's a very solid number based on everything we've already locked in. Many of the contingencies we get from smaller regional or super regional carriers do not provide us with line of sight midyear or at 9 months on where we're at on the performance of those plans.

So we still have some accruals left for those, but there's room for them to come in at higher levels, similar to what happened in '25, which they don't communicate to us, so we don't know what's coming.

Janice Zwinggi: So if you look at quarter-over-quarter, though, our contingent is relatively flat. So Q4 is when we'll get the increase, just like we did in Q4 of '25. We do expect that number to go up in Q4 for sure.

Operator: I'm showing no additional questions in the queue at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to Mr. Bunch for any closing remarks.

Richard Bunch: Thank you, operator, and thank you all for attending today's call. I do want to reiterate, we've had excellent 3 quarters so far through '26. We've given out tightened guidance for the remainder of calendar year '26. We have, throughout the calendar year, mentioned the economic changes of the takeout business normalizing, and that view is included in our updated guidance as well as the current softening market. We see great opportunities for our company going forward, and we look forward to hosting many of you here in our office next week for our very first Investor Day and look forward to seeing those who are able to attend in person on November 12 and those who can participate online.

Without any other questions, I just thank you again for attending today's call.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for participating in today's conference. This concludes the program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a wonderful day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Is there a better time than the weekend to kick back and relax with a nice film? We work all week, and having the chance to kick our feet up and watch a movie is the ultimate way to relax.

This week, I'm locked in on slightly older movies from the Prime Video new releases. We have a late 1980s cartoon that's extremely near and dear to my heart, a Christmas classic and a 2010s goofball movie that'll have you rolling on the floor laughing (assuming you have a tolerance for this sort of oddball humor).

These are the three new-to-Prime Video movies I think you should watch this weekend. There are only so many hours in a weekend, and you don't want to waste a bunch watching a bad film, so we'll guide you to the good ones.

I love "All Dogs Go to Heaven." It's a sad movie — both from a real-world perspective, given the circumstances of young actress Judith Eva Barsi, and from the plot involving the dog Charlie B. Barkin, his best friend Itchy Itchiford, and what happens to dogs when they die. But it's also heartwarming and highly entertaining for people of all ages.

Why is it special to me? As a kid, I went on vacation to Florida, and the day I arrived, I came down with a stomach bug that knocked me out of commission for the entire one-week trip. I literally did nothing but sit around in my grandparents' house for my entire annual vacation. And between trips to the bathroom, I watched "All Dogs Go to Heaven" over and over. You'd think that would make me dislike the movie, since I associate it with a ruined trip, but it brings back happy memories and got me through a difficult week. But it's not nostalgia; I watched it again as an adult with my 9-year-old stepson, and we both loved it.

Watch "All Dogs Go to Heaven" on Prime Video now

This is another throwback to my childhood — I guess I'm in a nostalgic mood today. But instead of associating this with sleeping on the bathroom floor, I remember watching it every winter to get ready for Christmas with the tale of Turbo Man (and sometimes in the middle of summer when I felt like throwing in a funny VHS).

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Starring Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sinbad (yes, unlike the Mandela Effect version of "Shazam," he's really in this one), "Jingle All The Way" follows the hunt for a special toy (the aforementioned Turbo Man) and the chaos of trying to find it on Christmas Eve. Like many kids' movies, it all wraps up with a tidy bow in a completely unrealistic way, but that doesn't make it any less entertaining.

Watch "Jingle All The Way" on Prime Video now

I couldn't put only kid-friendly movies on the list, so the entirely not-child-appropriate "Hot Tub Time Machine" rounds it out. John Cusack, Rob Corddry, Craig Robinson, and Clark Duke contrast each other to create pure hilarity in this raunchy R-rated comedy, where the four go into a hot tub that sends them on a trip through time. It's a goofy premise for a goofy movie.

Keeping today's throwback theme alive, though, is the crew's first destination: 1986, the year I was born. If you remember the 80s fondly and want to see what a group of goofballs from 2010 do in the middle of the decade, you'll love this movie. It even has sci-fi elements that'll scratch fans' itch while keeping them laughing the whole way through.

#3336. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

Bring xcode,terminal and ability to download apps from anywhere on iPad Pro!

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

To read the full report, follow this link.

#3335. How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO

“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.

The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.

On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.

The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”

“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”

A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.

But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

This article was updated on 29 October 2026.

Tom Clynes, an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, is a writer and photojournalist who covers science and the environment.

The problem for this and all electric plane manufacturers is timing. When the Wright Brothers first flew, people were OK with barely safe enough and planes had time to mature and get better. Now, people expect absolute safety from day 1 and that's difficult to achieve and even more difficult to demonstrate without first flying 100,000 hours.

This sounds like a test plane more than a commercial one, but I guess that makes sense while companies are figuring out how to integrate new technologies into our existing safety regulations.The other thing that stands out to me is how the motors have redundant sub-systems. I can see the value, but it sure seems like a steep price to pay in terms of weight and complexity. Looking forward to seeing how that evolves.

#3334. WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

Select WhatsApp users on TestFlight and in the main app are now seeing the option to expand an image in the app’s photo editor. Here are the details.

iPhone users with access to Apple Intelligence have a native AI-powered photo expansion tool called Extend, which lets users pinch or drag to expand an image beyond its original borders.

This feature, which is also present on AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and image-editing platforms like Photoshop, is now also making its way into WhatsApp.

According to WABetaInfo, the platform is rolling out a Meta AI-powered image expansion tool, though it is currently limited to select users, primarily those in WhatsApp’s beta program via TestFlight.

When users select a photo in their chats, WhatsApp opens the drawing editor. Here, they can choose to apply some AI effect to improve it. Among these, users can find a new option to expand their photos. Once users select this option, Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the expanded version. Once the process is complete, WhatsApp shows the expanded photo in the drawing editor, and users can choose to send it. Note that this feature is also compatible with status updates.

The site notes that if the user isn’t happy with the result, they can tap an undo button to revert to the original and then try using the tool again to generate a different result.

As is usually the case with beta features on WhatsApp, there is no telling when it might become widely available.

That said, given that it has also rolled out to users in the Android beta and some users on the public iOS version already have access, a broader rollout might not be too far off.

#3332. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

Since it's actually two, opposite, single line command states;

Why can't it simply be an on/off button, in Settings?

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link. And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro.
