Then here in the middle of the page, we see investment for growth, $63 million, mainly expansion of CapEx and now mainly is catching up, ramping up the investments and cash investments in Era Dorada. And to the right side is more the financial like items, mainly the proceeds -- net proceeds from debt. We received $200 million from the syndicated loan and some debt amortization. So we have net proceeds of $182 million. Dividend and share repurchase $71 million in Q3.

And then Rodrigo highlighted at the beginning, if you take the $158 million recurring free cash flow that we generated for the quarter that paid both for the losses with the hedges, also the dividends and share buybacks and also paid entirely for the expansion CapEx we had in the quarter. So with this, we end the presentation and open to questions. Thank you.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Mr. Marcelo Arazi from BTG Pactual.

Marcelo Arazi: Two questions on my side. So the first one on Era Dorada. It was very nice to see that the project has been evolving on time and within budget and with 13% physical progress. But I would like to understand a little bit more what are the main milestones and potential execution bottlenecks over the next 12 months? And especially regarding the geothermal side of the project, which remains a major concern for a few investors that we normally talk to. And if I could make a second one about the fleet insourcing announcement. So a few questions here as well. So how quickly should this benefit materialize next year?

What are the main risks associated with bringing those operations in-house? And what was actually the final trigger for Aura to decide and make this change?

Rodrigo Barbosa: Thank you, Marcelo. I can start answering here real quick, and then I will ask Kleber that can give you more details about next steps in Era Dorada and also how he sees the insource of the mine fleet upcoming in the next year with the potential also savings. The geothermal plant, I'm not sure if you ask about the geothermal plant is something that will come along the next few years. It is not -- we will not start construction anytime soon. We still need to partner and find the right partner and do the right feasibility study engineering. So that will -- once -- that will probably go into production after 2 or 3 years of operations.

In the meanwhile, we have other alternatives to supply the power. And if you were mentioning about the potential high temperature underground, Kleber can also walk you through. That's not usual conditions to have the fuel other mines in the world that run actually even in the worst conditions. It's a matter of calculating and do the proper underground infrastructure, pumping hot water and also bringing a cool air down. But Kleber can walk you through more in the detail of this situation, plus what he sees coming up in the next 12 months. Glauber?

Glauber Rosa-Luvizotto: Yes, as Rodrigo said, we are -- in terms of construction and preparation of the mining that we call the pre-operation. We are on track for that. So it's a lot of challenge from the hydrothermal water, but we have the support from the specialists and also a very robust plan to offset that point. Right now, everything that we found is as we expected, but we are still -- we are just in the beginning. So we are pumping the water because the key point is we should pump the water in advance.

We should go down with the table water to make sure that the moment that we assess that region, there is no more hot water in that region and the rock have had time to refresh. So it's what we are doing right now. So the pumps are under construction, and we are using some old -- the wells are under preparation. We are using some old ones. We are being able to reduce the table water and doing all the mine development on time. But in parallel, all the infrastructure that we have like the refrigeration plant and all the other stuff, it's already on site, under commissioning.

And I think that the main milestones in the next 12 months from the construction side we have the main equipment to arrive on site, the mill and all the other equipment and also put the mine development in the run rate. So it's -- we are considering -- right now, we have a contractor doing the underground development. We are considering as well to have part of the work made by us. So we already bought some equipment that are on time to be delivered in the end of this month and beginning of the next month.

And we have also some contingent plan to bring to the region some experts because the main point is find people with experience in the underground that there isn't much in Guatemala, but we are considering like -- we are doing like a task force to train and prepare people and have some experts to -- mainly in this beginning to put the mine on track. And the other question from the insourcing the key point is that we are seeing a lot of adjustment in the cost when we went to the market to have -- to make an assessment about the price and cost to do that primarily -- to do that with by contractor.

The costs are being significantly higher than we are practicing. And also, we feel that we are prepared to -- considering the maturity that we have in the operations, we are prepared to assume this another part of the work. But the process right now, we are in the transition to creating the company that will assume all the assets from the contractor. We have the gate to be approved on CADE. Once we have that in the beginning of next year, should be fully ours. Right now, we are in the transition phase. Everything is going well. We expect to be more efficient, mainly doing the property maintenance to make sure that we have the reliability in the fleet.

So I think that we can increase productivity from the equipment, and we can also see the impact in our cost. So for next year, in terms of cost, we have seen some reduction in the 3 mines. But most part of the reimbursement for the equipment that we are paying will be next year once we phase it in accordance with we are advancing in the contract that we did. So it's going on track.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mr. Lawson Winder from Bank of America Securities.

Lawson Winder: If I could ask about MSG, I think that would be a very helpful place to start, particularly in thinking about the growth trajectory into 2026. So what specifically changed underground at MSG during Q3 in development meters, stope availability, mining flexibility? And then what still needs to be completed before you consider the turnaround finished? And then all-in sustaining costs were, well, I mean, very high in the quarter. Like what's your latest thinking on where all-in sustaining costs can go on a run rate basis for MSG?

Rodrigo Barbosa: Well, I'll let Glauber to answer, but I can, we see all-in sustaining cash cost going close to $2,000 per ounce and production at 80,000 ounces per year probably next year, right? But Glauber can go into details how he sees the progress on Q3 and project to you what we can expect in Q4 and most importantly next year.

Glauber Rosa-Luvizotto: Yes. The key point there is the performance in mining development. So we have a combination of 2 things. So when we assume MSG is a backlog in mining development, in mining preparation, and we also decided to do the change in the mining method that require much more development in advance to go to the bottom of the panel and start to mine bottom-up. We still in preparation. So we have some areas in production already, but not fully capacity in the underground mining. It will take -- I think that 4, 5 months more to have the mine fully prepared and the reserve release in the time that is required.

In parallel, a bunch of change has been made. So we are improving the quality in the method that we mine, reducing dilution, increased mining recovery and also review all the contracts with a significant reduction in our costs. We can't see right now the reflect of how those changes will reflect because we are not in the full capacity. So I can say that we are spending more in development proportionately with what we are producing.

So once we increase production, we do not will keep the same level of mine development because once we achieve the stabilization in the mine, we can back for the full -- for the normal profile of mine development, but we are be able to feed the plant with more ore from the underground because right now, almost 50% of the ore came from some lower grade stockpiles from the surface because we are preparing the mine. But once we are putting much more room of mine in the plant with better grade, the production will increase. And also, we will be able to stabilize the mining development in the underground.

And the combination of those can give us the production close to the 80,000 ounces per year and the cash cost or the all-in sustaining cost should reduce significantly.

Rodrigo Barbosa: And again, Aura Day, we will provide a full detail on what has been done in MSG, including all the physical measurements, the speed, how we are -- the savings Glauber mentioned, have important savings can go in POR is 30%, 40%. So that I think it will be important to invite everybody to be there and see. We also bring the manager of MSG so that we can interact directly also with him.

Lawson Winder: Yes. Fantastic. I mean it's nice to see MSG improving substantially in Q3. If I could ask one more question, it would probably be on the reserve and resource update and your expectations around that globally for the entire firm, whether you anticipate replacing reserves this year mine. But then just particularly with respect to Apoena and Minosa, your 2 really short mine lives. Are you starting to see the potential to drive material expansion in mine life there?

Rodrigo Barbosa: We will share what we've been finding during the Aura Day. Apoena, yes, there are several -- now we are opening more. We are focusing a lot on the near mine. We opened a little bit on 20 kilometers, 30 kilometers. So finding very interesting interceptions that we will -- we are now finalizing all the results and be able to publish and then before the Aura Day. Honduras, it is still an unknown. This is where Minosa is where we are less optimistic about extending life of mine. But Apoena, yes, there will be important improvements, we believe.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mr. Rabi Nizami from National Bank of Canada.

Rodrigo Barbosa: Rabi, if you are talking, I think you are on mute. Yes, maybe he has some connection problems. Let us go to the next one, and then we will still reserve a room for him.

So I'm just wondering how should we think of this CapEx for the fourth quarter specifically? Do you still expect to reach your guidance? Or should we see some spill out towards 2027? João Cardoso: Yes. Matheus, we -- the expansion CapEx, we have opportunities to be closer to the low end of the guidance or even below. That's mainly because that's actually good news. It's the negotiation we have been done with providers, so equipments for example, for the project. So we are negotiating lower down payments. So that improves our cash position at the moment. But then in terms of whatever we don't spend this year to your question, yes, that would move to 2027, the CapEx for the project itself wouldn't change. It's just a matter of having more working capital like, let's say, now in 2026 because of the negotiations that we're doing in country.

Matheus Moreira: Great. That's very clear, Kleber. Maybe if I may, a second quick question on MSG is actually a follow-up. I mean, it was encouraging to see the operational performance in the quarter, right, which was much better than we were expecting. Still, I believe, far from the operational conditions Aura wants to achieve, but definitely on track. I noticed that your production improved materially quarter-on-quarter also because of higher throughput rates. Glauber Rosa-Luvizotto: The stockpile is not the most relevant part of the plan to recover the production. So it's just to complement or to keep the plant fully feed once we weren't able to feed with more ore from the underground mine. But the focus is mainly to put the mine in operation, debottleneck the mine, and get some reserves released in advance to make sure that we can feed the plant with room of mine that is the highest grade that we have because the stockpile is a marginal ore that was left in the past for the other company.

We are using that as an opportunity once we have this spare capacity in the plant, but it's not the base of the plan for the growth.

Rodrigo Barbosa: Yes. The stockpile is just a buffer that we are using why we are doing the turnaround. The grades you asked can vary 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.4, but it will be around this.

Rabi Nizami: Apologies for that audio issue earlier. So a couple of my questions have been answered, but I'll move on to a few more. So on the CapEx run rate, you already answered that. Rodrigo Barbosa: And then in the meanwhile, as we do with all our mines, as you see Almas we built then we started generating cash, then we started doing more exploration. Rabi Nizami: Okay. Just in the short term, looking at the strip ratio of Borborema in Q3 at 4.6. Is there any guidance you can give us at this time with respect to how that evolves into Q4 and into next year?

Glauber Rosa-Luvizotto: Yes. We operate in the beginning once the mine was open when we assume. So they have the past work that they did, the strip ratio was lower, but we should run much more closer to what was the Q3, but a little bit higher for next year once we should achieve the average strip rate for the mine. Rodrigo Barbosa: In terms of M&A, we continue to see opportunities. We continue to invest time understanding what are the interesting M&A to do, invest time trying to do transactions. We are also doing what we call a zero-based budget this year, review line by line, each of the areas, and we're already finding some opportunities, but that then we will be able to include in the guidance for next year. Henrique Tavian Marques: Just I wanted to understand, Rodrigo, what is your priorities as we enter 2027? I believe Era Dorada will definitely be the top one for you. So just wanted to understand what really is the priority for you after Era Dorada. And if I may add one more question, just regarding the all-in sustaining cash cost of Apoena. I mean it was really high this quarter, and I think it was mostly related to the Nosde CapEx.

So I just want to understand if this was more of a one-off or is something that we should still see for a while? And if this was already expected to happen at this moment?

Rodrigo Barbosa: Okay. So in terms of priorities, as you mentioned, first priority is construction of Era Dorada on time on budget together with turnaround of MSG, be able to produce 80,000 ounces at $2,000 all-in sustaining cash costs. Then, of course, there's always optimizations on improvements going operations. But I would highlight then it's continue to invest in exploration and expand the life of mine so that we can increase resources and reserves. That's very interesting, significant potential for us to continue to do so. And then M&As, right? We know very much how to get to 600,000 ounces and now we want to -- we want to be able to achieve 1 million ounces.

So I invest a significant part of my time prospecting and talking and understanding what would be the potential M&A to do. We don't have a target. I want to do an M&A next year. But we do want to continue to grow through M&As, right? So in the end, it's the same strategy that we had 5 years ago, investing in Greenfield projects to increase production to increase invest in life of mine, increase resource and reserves and continue to grow through M&A. That's what we've been doing in the last 5 years, and that's what we'll continue to do in the next 3 to 5 years. And then you asked about of Apoena.

Apoena this quarter was much higher than the last quarter, but within what we projected. What happened this quarter that we significantly advanced at the Nosde Pit, while we didn't reach the high grade for the full quarter. And now we are there already. So the strip ratio has mostly been done. So we're going to see higher production and higher grades coming in on the fourth quarter. So we will see a reduction on the all-in sustaining cash cost for the fourth quarter. And for next year, we will put on the guidance as we have probably in January, February.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mr. Graham Tanaka. Please, Mr. Tanaka, from Tanaka Capital.

Rodrigo Barbosa: Mr. Tanaka, if you're talking, you are on mute. I don't think we hear him? Very well. So with that, I will conclude our earnings call. Just a quick wrap-up. Aura is walking the talk. So we are developing Greenfield project at Era Dorada is coming moving according to the plan. We are doing also important investment in exploration that I invite you again to be in Aura Day so that we can walk you through more in the details of what is going on exploration.

We continue to look alternatives for lowering all-in sustaining cash costs, which we are already in the first quartile, but we are not happy. We want to -- we see opportunities to continue to decrease our all-in sustaining cash cost while we continue to see M&A. So again, thank you very much. And I didn't say important thing, right? Doing all of that, paying dividends, significant dividends to our shareholders, 4% dividend yield together with the share buyback, while we are doing all these investments in exploration, expansion and improvements, maintaining the low net debt to EBITDA level. Again, will be important day, Aura Day on November 30, New York, Nasdaq. Please be able to attend there.

So we will be able to guide you in more detail what is going on in Aura. I appreciate. Thank you.

#3330. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Aside from the best foldable phones, I tend to see a lot of innovation around rugged phones built for long-term off-grid living or weekend camping getaways.

I’ve tested my fair share of unconventional ones: from the projector-packing Blackview Xplore 2 all the way to the Sonim XP Pro Thermal with its Predator-like heat vision. Every single one brought something wild to the table, but the Oukitel WP63 packs something I genuinely haven't seen before: a built-in electronic fire igniter.

While most phone manufacturers design their hardware specifically to avoid catching fire (ahem, Note 7), this heavy-duty slab embraces it for emergency survival. Honestly, it’s one of the most interesting rugged phones I’ve come across this year.

If the igniter alone isn’t enough to convince you, it also packs a massive 20,000mAh battery, a built-in reverse-charging cable, an all-in-one camping lantern, and a night vision camera.

Best of all, it’s currently 43% off for a limited time, dropping the price from $599 down to $339.

Built for extreme off-grid adventures, the Oukitel WP63 features an emergency electronic fire igniter, massive 20,000 mAh battery, built-in reverse-charging cable, 6.67-inch 120Hz display, rear camping lantern, and an 8MP night vision camera to see through the darkness.

The integrated lighter on the Oukitel WP63 brings back memories of the push-in cigarette lighters found in old-school cars. The heating element is tucked away on the top edge of the phone, popping open to reveal the recessed coil with a light press. Through the dedicated Lighter app, I can trigger the ignition process, which quickly causes the coil to glow with that familiar cherry-red warmth.

It generates concentrated heat capable of sparking dry materials on direct contact — like scrap paper or dried-up leaves that have been baking under the sun. For safety reasons, the igniter enforces an automatic cooldown period of around 10 seconds to prevent the housing from overheating.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While I was genuinely surprised by how easily it lit the corner of an envelope, keep in mind that nursing that spark into a sustainable fire takes real effort. Because it doesn’t produce an open flame like a Bic lighter or butane torch, having prior campfire-building experience makes a huge difference. After several tries, I managed to get a small bundle of brittle autumn leaves to catch, but it definitely requires patience and bone-dry kindling.

Beyond its standard 64MP main shooter — which delivers respectable shots when lighting conditions cooperate — Oukitel also throws in a dedicated 8MP infrared night vision camera. For a rugged phone built for the backcountry, it’s an invaluable tool the moment true darkness sets in.

While dedicated night vision cameras I’ve tested offer superior performance, especially in how far their IR illuminators can reach, the WP63’s sensor is still ideal for scanning your immediate vicinity for critters rustling in the brush. If you're out camping, it's especially handy when you have to step out of your tent half-asleep in the dead of night and your eyes haven't yet adjusted to the blackness.

Even though the setup is limited to just a single main camera and a night vision lens, the quality from the primary sensor more than suffices for the quick run-and-gun shots I want to share on social media. And the selfie camera up front isn’t too shabby, either.

As much as I rely on the flashlight on my phones, they’re dinky compared to the blinding beam produced by the WP63’s rear-mounted camping light. At its brightest, it effortlessly illuminates an entire pitch-dark area, and it has serious endurance thanks to the massive 20,000 mAh battery packed inside. With hurricane season in full swing, I’m confident it could easily hold up through an extended power outage. On top of that, an emergency strobe function unleashes an intense beacon that can be spotted from long distances.

I also want to highlight the 3W loudspeaker mounted on the back, which completely puts flagship phone audio to shame. While most phones tend to distort heavily at maximum volume, this speaker delivers surprising low-end punch and clarity — making it feel like I’m carrying a dedicated Bluetooth speaker in my pocket.

The Oukitel WP63 is an unlocked phone ready to run on virtually any wireless carrier, and I love that it features one of the easiest SIM card slots to access without hunting down an ejector pin.

This Swiss Army knife approach works because it nails the practical essentials for off the grid excursions — headlined by its halo feature, the built-in igniter. That utility is backed by smart additions like an integrated USB-C cable, allowing it to double as a ready-to-go power bank for other gear.

Tipping the scales at over 1.3 pounds, it’s certainly not a device I’d want as my primary everyday carry. But as a secondary backup? It’s an easy sell, especially while it's 43% off. Whether you toss it into a glove compartment for road trips or pack it along for a weekend in the woods, the Oukitel WP63 delivers rugged peace of mind when facing worst-case scenarios.

#3326. Apple confirms $7.5 billion bond sale following strong investor demand

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

You can read the full filing with the SEC here.

#3325. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3324. Atlanticus (ATLC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Two divestitures and record receivables shape a strong quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Atlanticus Holdings Corporation (ATLC -5.41%) reported third quarter results characterized by record managed receivables of $7.1 billion and a 60% increase in total operating revenue to $776 million. Management completed two significant strategic divestitures during the period, selling the CAR Auto Finance operations for $71.2 million and the Mercury intellectual property for $27.5 million to concentrate capital on core consumer credit opportunities. The company reported adjusted diluted EPS of $3.00 and an adjusted return on equity of 30%, which management attributed to sustained organic growth and the ongoing integration of the Mercury portfolio. CFO Bill McCamey noted that while expenses rose to $162 million, the operating expense ratio improved as revenue growth outpaced the expansion of the platform.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome, everyone, to the Atlanticus Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Today's conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Dan Mauch, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Dan Mauch: Thank you, operator, and good afternoon, everyone. Atlanticus released results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, this afternoon, after market close. If you did not receive a copy of our earnings press release, you may obtain it from the Investor Relations section of our website at investors.atlanticus.com. We have also posted an updated investor presentation. With me on today's call are Jeff Howard, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Bill McCamey, Chief Financial Officer. This call is being webcast and will be archived on the Investor Relations section of our website.

Excluding these one-time items, adjusted diluted EPS was $3 and adjusted return on average equity was 30%, well exceeding our 20% return goals and reaffirming the earnings power of our platform. Our sustained organic growth is being driven by our third consecutive quarter of record new account originations on behalf of our bank partners. While I talk about growth, it's important to reiterate that a tight focus on unit level profitability remains our guide for account origination levels. We lean into growth as we see attractive returns.

We have over 40 models in production at any given time and are continuously updating and refining those models for better outcomes within the subsegments across our business. Growth is a byproduct of that process. Accordingly, the increases in originations are not the result of risk expansion. Our growth stems from ongoing investment in newer marketing channels and model development within those channels along with continued growth with strategic clients in our retail credit business. The Mercury acquisition continues to deliver better-than-modeled performance on both the back book and new origination volumes.

The Mercury acquisition was a significant contributor to both revenue and earnings growth, compounded by the fact that we only own the business for approximately half of September in the prior year period. As for the consumer, we are still mindful of inflation levels being above target, volatile gas prices and ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty. The headlines regarding the state of the consumer are not new, but our data continues to show that the consumers we serve remain resilient and rational, making appropriate changes to spending while exhibiting consistent payment behaviors. Much of the negative headwinds appear to be offset by a very stable employment market.

That being said, we will continue to monitor metrics across numerous acquisitions, portfolio, customer service and third-party data attributes and lean heavily on our dynamic infrastructure to quickly enact empirically derived changes in underwriting when necessary. Now let me briefly cover the onetime items this quarter. First, we completed the sale of our CAR Auto Finance operations to an unaffiliated buyer for approximately $71.2 million in total consideration, which resulted in a gain of approximately $20 million. While CAR had been a contributor to our business for over 20 years, the sale represented an opportunity to concentrate our capital and management resources on the consumer credit products where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term value creation.

Second, we completed the sale of the MERCURY word mark and related intellectual property for $27.5 million in cash. The transaction did not include any credit card receivables associated with the Mercury-branded program. Under the agreement, we have the right to use the brand for marketing purposes for 12 months and for servicing for an additional 5 years, giving us ample time for the necessary rebranding. We view these transactions as a continued refinement of our strategic focus, and the proceeds will be invested in our higher return, higher growth lines of business. We are pleased with another record-breaking quarter for Atlanticus and a period of important strategic progress.

We are making deliberate decisions to direct capital towards opportunities with the greatest growth and return potential. This reflects our long-term focus on building the capabilities and reach to become the preferred financial partner for everyday Americans. We're proud of the progress our team has made and are committed to carrying that work forward. Now I'll turn it over to Bill to walk through our financial results in more detail. Bill?

William McCamey: Fantastic. Thanks, Jeff. It really was a great quarter. Let me start by addressing a few reporting notes. First, on CAR Auto Finance, CAR comprised our entire auto finance segment. Jeffrey Howard: Yes. Thank you all for your participation. In closing, we continue to see really strong performance across our core general purpose and retail credit lines of business. #3322. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3320. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3319. Apple Store now offers extended holiday returns for all products

Apple has rolled out its holiday theming at the online Apple Store, and with it a new, extended return policy has just been put into place. Here are the details.

Every year for the holiday season, like many other retailers, Apple institutes an extended return period for eligible purchases.

Today that extended return window has officially kicked off. Per Apple’s website:

Eligible products at the Apple Store Online that are received between November 6, 2026 and December 25, 2026, may be returned through January 8, 2027. Please note that all other terms and conditions provided in the Apple Store Online Sales and Refunds Policy are still applicable with respect to such products purchased. iPhone purchases that are carrier-financed with T-Mobile or Verizon are not eligible and are subject to standard return policy. iPad purchases that are carrier-financed with Verizon are not eligible and are subject to standard return policy. All purchases made after December 25, 2026 are subject to the Standard Return Policy.

The extended return window applies to all products. However, Apple does state that as always, certain types of products are ineligible for return altogether. They include:

Most of the year, the Apple Store has a 14-day return policy. But unless you’re a last-minute shopper, that wouldn’t work very well for any product you intend to gift.

Thus, Apple’s extended return window means any purchase you make as a holiday gift won’t have its return period end before the holidays even arrive.

Traffic pressure drove a sales drop, but profit beat management's outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Under Armour, Inc. (UAA -5.21%) reported a 7% decline in total revenue for the second quarter as traffic challenges in North America and a promotional global environment weighed on results. Management indicated that the company is currently executing a multiyear transformation focused on reducing product complexity and improving operational speed through calendar compression. The company revised its full-year gross margin expansion target downward to reflect increased supply chain costs and inventory markdowns. Despite these headwinds, management maintained its adjusted operating income guidance for the fiscal year, supported by cost discipline and anticipated performance improvements in the fourth quarter.

Putting our resources behind innovative products aspirational storytelling, and elite execution while maintaining expense discipline. Our cleat of business in American football is a good example of this. It grew double digits in the quarter. With higher average selling prices and market share gains. In fact, Under Armour is now the number 2 brand in football cleats in the US. Peak gear and core vanish also grew double digits.

And France and Shawn continued to grow. These results give us confidence to back proven franchises and bring that same to upcoming launches. This starts with a simpler company, We have deliberately evolved our leadership structure clarified accountability. Reduced competing priorities. We are building a stronger operational foundation, improving the system and processes behind our products and how we bring them to market. Our initial work with AI is focused on supply chain, product merchandising, and marketing.

A priority is calendar compression, shorten the time from an athlete insight to a product in the market supported by a complete launch plan. We see opportunities for AI to speed decisions reduce repetitive work so our teams can spend more time developing products and serving athletes. We are also evaluating where asset light models can bring in expertise and scale. We will judge those opportunities by the earnings and cash we retain, and the complexity and capital requirements we can reduce. An early example of this work is our decision to transition our youth apparel business to an expanded licensing model with Centric Brands, a long standing partner with deep children's product and retail expertise.

Beginning in fall 27, the model should reduce inventory. Working capital, operating complexity while delivering a consistent Under Armour product experience for young athletes. As a key entry point for consumers discovering Under Armour this category plays an important role in building our community. We are confident that this decision will help grow this business over the coming years. This partnership should give our teams more time to concentrate on the products and categories where Under Armour's capabilities can create the greatest value. We are simplifying our product line as well. Targeting a reduction of nearly 50% in SKUs from the level when I returned in 2024.

We have also removed more than 60% of materials while increasing global product commonality. Smaller assortment lets us invest more deeply in our strongest products. Simplify decisions, focus our storytelling, and make the offer clearer for our teams, partners, and consumers. This is about taking weight out of the system so we can amplify the products we make, with volume and demand. That means selling so much more of so much less at full retail price. Within that focus line, we are sharpening our good, better, best offerings across price points and channels to elevate Under Armour. That means strengthening product performance and presentation at every level giving athletes a compelling reason to choose UA at full price.

Our essentials must deliver performance and value Our established franchises must offer differentiated benefits and our most advanced innovation must set a higher standard for performance. All the while, we are communicating a much clearer story to the consumer as to why UA is different and better. We are being more deliberate about design, features, pricing, and distribution. So each level strengthens the brand and earns its place in the athlete's closet. That opportunity reaches into our highest volume programs including Tech Tee, a staple that we sell in the tens of millions. But not often enough at full price. We are building on that work with Tech Helix, an upgrade launching later this month.

With the ambition to become 1 of our top 10 volume drivers over time. See, the Under Armour innovation team developed a completely new fabric by taking 2 separate polyester fibers and wrapping them into a coil construction creates an actual helix shape. This allows the fabric to lift off the skin and provide stretch without spandex. Enhancing airflow and helping the fabric dry at amazing rates. It addresses a need central to Under Armour from the beginning. Helping athletes feel better and perform better in the heat. At $35, that innovation reaches a broad athlete base. And with focused marketing supporting its story, this should be a multimillion unit program for us at full price.

Our focused assortment lets us invest more behind products performance value and potential to become meaningful business contributors. Innovation is there. Our job is to explain the science clearly connect it to what athletes feel and how they perform. Earning pricing power by taking credit for the innovation we build into every UA product. We have seen what that combination could deliver with our $65 bouncy tee. Its launch sell through and growing volumes across geographies are an encouraging example of consumers choosing Under Armour at full price when they understand and value the product difference. That response gives us confidence in the opportunity ahead.

We are applying those lessons to Tech Helix and future launches with the goal of making that success more consistent across our business. Another example comes next month, with the Armor Short. Based on our goal to build the best compression short an athlete can wear. Compression shorts are already 1 of our largest volume programs, but traditionally serve that athlete with only a $35 good level option. Applying our 50% SKU reduction across categories, the discipline good, better, best architecture is not just about cutting, but also about highlighting on brand opportunities and leaving room to create something better. During team sports competition, less than 10% of male athletes wear a hard plastic cup.

Because of the bulk and restriction. We saw an opportunity to address that trade off. Our brand new shield form technology brings targeted growing padding into a compression short without sacrificing mobility. It does not replace the protection of a hard cup, but it gives athletes who otherwise go without 1 an added layer of confidence. The Armor Short's patent-pending design launched in December at $80 for adults and $55 for kids. On UA.com and 500 DICK'S Sporting Goods stores in the US. And, yes, we believe the opportunity is significant over the long term as the addressable market is virtually every male athlete who plays almost any sport.

We are building on the trust athletes already place in us for their first layer. A benefit they understand immediately in 1 single item. Early next spring, we plan to expand the Under Armour collection with a different enhanced solution for female athletes as well. This is where Under Armour plays best. Bringing differentiated innovation to a real athlete need. That is our DNA. All in, the Armor Short made it from concept to market inside of 10 months. With the product, epic storytelling, and full marketing and retail support all developed together. That is the speed and coordination we aim to make repeatable as we compress our calendar.

Earn a place in athletes' everyday routines, and strengthen our position as the official first layer of sports. That focus on athletes needs is guiding our footwear reset as well. We are building on strength in team sports while improving design and value across the portfolio. Running offers an opportunity to expand on the credentials we have established with our Velocity franchise. Our task is to translate that expertise into a broader segmented assortment that meets the needs of more athletes and earns its place at retail. Sharon Lokedi demonstrated those credentials with Shawn Chicago Marathon in October. She finished second in the Velociti Elite 3.

Improving her personal best by over 3 minutes and becoming the 8th fastest female marathoner in history. it is an exceptional achievement for Sharon, another demonstration of Under Armour footwear at the highest level. Her work with our product teams brings elite athlete insight the continued evolution of our running footwear. More commercial based execution of this $250 elite shoe will build on this momentum with upcoming expressions at more accessible price points this coming spring. Across apparel and footwear, each introduction must address a specific athlete need. Have a defined place in the line. With enough depth to become a business we can build over multiple seasons. Building demand is central to this stage of the transformation.

Over the past several months, we have established a more unified marketing model. bringing global creative direction, Content, and campaign priorities together under Simon James Pestridge, Simon became chief marketing officer in June after overseeing our Asia Pacific business. He brings more than 30 years of global brand marketing and leadership experience. Together with a direct understanding of our consumers, and commercial operations. Our investments moving forward will support fewer, bigger campaigns, giving our strongest products and athlete stories more reach a more recognizable Under Armour voice. Visual teams will bring those stories to life through local media, our own DTC channels, and wholesale partners.

We are aligning product inventory and retail plans earlier so athletes can find what they see in our marketing. We will assess that work through product discovery and full price sell through alongside reach and engagement. We are also introducing a globally consistent creative platform built on the concept of This Is Your Armor. It connects an athlete's ambition with product performance giving our stories a recognizable Under Armour identity across sports and markets. Also in marketing, starting with this month's Tech Helix launch, followed by the Armor Short in December, We plan to introduce 1 major product story each month throughout the calendar year. The approach is deliberately simple: 1 global product priority coordinated execution across regions and markets.

Local teams will adopt their story for their consumers while reinforcing the same technical product benefit. Support across social, digital, and retail will continue beyond launch to build recognition and demand. This coordinated execution will come to life with demonstrating the product's benefit through science, of course, but also through personality and, yes, humor. And social content and digital education will further support that connection. Dedicated retail presentations will bring that story to stores with select UK retailers joining our US launch. Our product and athlete stories are generating encouraging social engagement. From July through September, our Instagram brand account generated approximately 43 million impressions, up 55% year-over-year. And 27 million video views, up 126%.

Our TikTok account just crossed 1 million followers, That engagement gives us useful direction for our creative work. Our focus now is converting that attention to product consideration and purchase. Alongside marketing, evolving our retail concepts is a priority. Our stores must strengthen the brand and improve the productivity of our business. We are developing key city showrooms that highlight our strongest products, refining our full price stores around a clearer performance assortment, and reworking our factory house locations with a more deliberate mix of full price product. Each format has a distinct role, with assortments tailored to local athletes and shopping behavior.

Execution means connecting product presentation, launch support, and availability so consumers can understand the benefit, and find what they came to buy. These lessons will help guide investment with an emphasis on conversion. Full price selling, and store profitability. Our regional teams are translating these product and retail priorities into focused commercial plans. In North America, we are concentrating support behind the apparel franchises, including footwear that are performing. While addressing traffic and broader sell through pressure. That means coordinating launches more closely with wholesale partners and our own channels. Aligning inventory with demand, and making our product benefits more visible at retail.

Our priority is to turn strength in these businesses into more consistent performance across our largest market, right here in North America. In EMEA, we are building a momentum in France and Shawn while improving ecommerce execution. We are connecting marketing more closely with locally relevant assortments and product availability. So consumer interest has a clearer path to purchase. In The UK, we are focused on execution with partners and aligning inventory and investment with current demand. Across the region, we are backing the markets and channels where we see opportunity while maintaining discipline where conditions remain dynamic. In Asia Pacific, our priorities are improving productivity product availability. In China and optimizing our licensing business.

We are refining assortments in each channel, so our strongest products are supported by a better shopping experience. Carol Chen, who succeeded Simon as APAC's regional leader, brings more than 30 years of brand and commercial leadership experience across Greater China. Asia, and The United States. Her mandate is to bring those priorities together into stronger marketplace execution. Drawing on our understanding of local consumers and retail partners to improve the performance of the business. Altogether, we are challenging ourselves to improve how we operate every day. From the products we build, how we create demand and serve athletes.

We are setting clear priorities, acting on what we learn, and directing resources to the work that can make the greatest difference. Under Armour has a long track record of solving problems for athletes. Our responsibility is to bring that same discipline to the business. Follow through on the decisions and turn product strength, into stronger results. Our ambition remains high. We will measure progress by the results we deliver. And with that, thank you. Reza, over to you.

Reza Taleghani: Thanks, Kevin, and good morning, everyone. Turning to our second quarter fiscal 27 results. Revenue declined 7% to $1.2 billion By region, North America revenue declined 7%, reflecting traffic pressure in our direct to consumer business and softer wholesale sell through. Growth in select apparel franchises helped but did not fully offset broader demand pressure. EMEA revenue declined 9%, Retail traffic remains challenged in the UK. Partly offset by growth in France and Shawn. Shipment timing also remains a factor in quarterly progression, particularly in our distributor business. APAC revenue declined 9%, reflecting pressure in China in our licensing business, Pockets of improvement in e commerce and areas of wholesale resilience provided some offset.

Latin America revenue increased 3% largely due to favorable foreign exchange as revenue in the region declined 4% on a constant currency basis. Looking at performance by channel, wholesale revenue decreased 6% to $725 million reflecting the impact of softer full price sell through and pressure in parts of the distributor business, partly offset by select accounts and markets. Direct to consumer revenue decreased 8% to $494 million including a 7% decline in owned and operated stores and a 12% decline in e-commerce. Traffic remained the primary challenge, particularly in North America, with better conversion and targeted digital initiatives providing some offset. Licensing revenue decreased 4% to $28 million driven by a decline in North America.

By product category, apparel revenue decreased 6% to $880 million HeatGear and Core Vanish were areas of strength, while fleece and women's bottoms were challenged. Accessories revenue decreased 7% to $105 million differentiated products such as StealthForm provided encouraging signals within a softer overall environment. Gross margin was 47.0%, down 30 basis points.

The year over year decline was due to 40 basis points of unfavorable foreign currency impacts, 35 basis points of combined unfavorable channel and regional mix and 20 basis points of unfavorable pricing, a slightly higher discount than in the prior year more than offset the benefit of our pricing actions. These headwinds were partially offset by 55 basis points as supply chain benefits, including more favorable product costs. And 10 basis points of favorable product mix. SG&A decreased 4% to $557 million driven by lower marketing expenses and continued cost discipline across other expense categories.

Adjusted SG&A decreased 3% to $559 million excluding $2 million in transformation expenses related to the fiscal 25 restructuring plan and the $3 million benefit from the reversal of certain previously accrued litigation reserve expense. In the quarter, we recorded $13 million under the fiscal 20 restructuring plan, including $11 million in restructuring charges and $2 million in transformation related SG&A. Costs incurred to date totaled $280 million of the projected $300 million to $350 million. The plan is expected to be substantially complete by December 31, 2026. Second quarter operating income was $15 million or $25 million adjusted for restructuring and transformation costs. and the reversal of certain previously accrued litigation reserve expense.

Reported and adjusted diluted loss per share were both approximately breakeven. We ended the quarter with $1.1 billion in inventory, up 4% year-over-year. The approximate $200 million reduction in our revenue outlook in August left inventory above our planned sales needs. We ended the quarter with $285 million in cash $190 million of borrowings under our $1.1 billion revolving credit facility. We remain focused on liquidity working capital discipline, and investments supporting our transformation. Fiscal 27 capital expenditures are expected to be modestly below last year's level. Turning to our fiscal 27 outlook.

We are maintaining the expectation that revenue will decline at a mid single digit rate. And while current traffic and macroeconomic pressures could result in North America being down modestly more than the mid single digit decline we previously anticipated in that region. That potential downside is reflected within our unchanged full year outlook. For fiscal 27, gross margin, we now expect expansion of 170 to 22 basis points compared with our previous expectation of 22 to 72 basis points. This includes roughly 150 basis points of benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds related to cost expense in fiscal 26. Excluding that benefit, we expect gross margin improvement of approximately 20 to 70 basis points.

Supported by pricing actions, lower discounting and favorable channel and product mix. The 50-basis-point reduction in our gross margin outlook reflects ongoing elevated fuel and freight costs. Landmark downs to improve inventory alignment and a stronger U. S. Dollar. Keep in mind, our previous outlook assumed disruption from the Middle East conflict through September 30. Those pressures now extended into the second half. We reiterate our expectation for adjusted SG&A to decline at a low single digit rate, reflecting lower marketing spend and active expense management, while preserving priority investments. Our focus is not simply on spending less, but on making our marketing dollars work harder.

Reducing waste and duplicated content production, and deploying resources more efficiently behind priority franchises launches to improve marketing efficacy. Across the business, we are simplifying operations to strengthen profitability, by protecting investments essential to the transformation. The additional second half costs and planned inventory actions more than offset our second quarter operating income upside. As such, we continue to expect full year adjusted operating income of the $140 million to $160 million range. This excludes anticipated restructuring transformation expenses of approximately $44 million and the $3 million benefit from the litigation reserve accrual reversal, and includes about $70 million of benefit from IEPA tariff refunds related to fiscal 26 expenses.

This also assumes about $45 million of headwinds related to the ongoing Middle East conflict, up from the $35 million we cited previously. All in, we continue to expect full year adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.08 to $0.12 Turning to our third quarter, we expect revenue to decline approximately 8% to 9%. In North America, we expect the low double digit decline, which includes about a point of wholesale shipments that were recognized in the second quarter. In EMEA, we expect a high single digit decline, which includes about 5 percentage points of distributor shipment timing moving into the fourth quarter. And in APAC, we anticipate roughly flat revenue as the business continues to stabilize.

Third quarter gross margin is expected to increase 30 to 50 basis points with pricing and mix benefits partly offset by higher supply chain costs and foreign currency headwinds. Adjusted SG&A is expected to decline at a low single digit rate as we continue to manage marketing towards greater productivity and discretionary expenses. For the third quarter, we expect adjusted operating income to range from a loss of $5 million to a profit of $5 million with an adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.01 to $0.03 With third quarter adjusted operating income expected anywhere around breakeven at the midpoint our full year outlook includes a stronger fourth quarter.

In North America, we expect a couple of percentage points of revenue benefit from the youth transition, and a few additional points from wholesale initiatives to reduce excess inventory. In EMEA, distributor shipments shifting into the fourth quarter account for about 5 percentage points of improvement. That timing supports fourth quarter revenue without changing our full year demand assumption. Partly offset by the external cost pressures and inventory actions mentioned earlier. In closing, our second half priorities are clear.
