Power and Utilities revenue increased 18%. Rising energy demand continues to drive investment in generation, transmission, distribution and grid modernization. Larger developers are advancing multi-project substation programs, creating opportunities for successive assignments.

Our work includes technically complex projects from large utility programs to fire and storm hardening of high-voltage infrastructure. These programs underpin multiyear demand for our power delivery services. Cross-selling is also contributing to growth as our teams bring additional capabilities to existing clients and pursue work together across the platform. In power delivery, our teams are bringing in infrastructure specialists to support project execution with a long-term client. In transportation and infrastructure, engagement expanded to include bridge scanning by our buildings technology team, extending that team's capabilities into a new market. C&E backlog reached a record level, providing visibility into future activity.

As that work converts to revenue, we remain focused on disciplined project selection, staffing and execution to sustain margins. The timing and mix of project delivery, particularly on multiyear larger scale programs will influence the pace of revenue growth. Overall, broad-based growth, expanding client relationships and record backlog position C&E well heading into 2027. Turning to Geospatial. Third quarter revenue was $98 million, up 9.3% from the prior year, supported by increased activity in power and utilities and military programs and contributions from recent acquisitions. Strong sales activity increased backlog during the quarter. Recent awards include two large NOAA contracts for LiDAR data collection along Florida's Gulf Coast.

The work maps coastal land and sea floor to support safe marine navigation and track coastal erosion and shoreline changes. These awards reflect continued demand for our large-scale mapping capabilities and the recurring need to update coastal data, including after hurricanes. Our Geospatial Intelligence business also grew during the quarter. We were awarded a contract with the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency with a term of up to 5 years to provide access to commercial geophysical data and survey services. These data sets support mapping and navigation applications where accuracy is critical to mission success. The award builds on an established client relationship and our ability to source specialized data and coordinate surveys through a global network of providers.

Our commercial activity continues to grow, primarily in power and utilities. We conduct aerial surveys covering more than 1 million miles of power lines annually, helping utilities identify vegetation conflicts and support fire mitigation. Our Geospatial and Inspection teams are jointly pursuing utility work that combines aerial mapping with inspections, bringing complementary services to clients through coordinated proposals. Our Geospatial services are essential and scalable. We are pursuing opportunities in Canada, Asia Pacific and the Middle East with expansion guided by client demand. In newer markets, our proposals incorporate cost assumptions and contingencies that reflect local execution risks.

While Geospatial revenue and backlog grew, third quarter profitability was below our expectations, reflecting project timing, mix and execution challenges, including a high proportion of pass-through work on certain contracts. We've made leadership changes and are drawing on expertise and operating best practices from our C&E business to strengthen project management, improve forecasting and utilization and support more consistent execution. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kristin to review our financial results, provide an update on integration and offer more detail on our outlook.

Kristin Schultes: Thank you, Ben, and good morning, everyone. Unless otherwise noted, all prior year comparisons reflect results on a combined basis. C&E and Geospatial reflect legacy NV5 results and I&M reflects legacy Acuren to provide a more meaningful view of year-over-year performance. I am very pleased with our results this quarter with revenue growth across all three segments and continued progress on margin expansion. Cross-selling, cost synergies and operating improvements are driving results as we execute against our long-term plan. Total third quarter revenue was $640 million, up 12.5% from $569 million. Total growth was 13.0% in constant currency and organic growth was in the high single digits at 8.4%.

Growth reflects strong momentum across all 3 segments, favorable end market positioning and execution on our cross-selling platform. Another quarter of record combined backlog continues to support our outlook. Adjusted gross profit was $243 million, up 13.2% from $215 million. Adjusted gross margin was 38.0% compared with 37.8%, up approximately 25 basis points. This improvement reflected disciplined project selection, favorable business mix in C&E and I&M and strong operating execution, partially offset by GEO performance. Adjusted SG&A was $136 million or 21.3% of revenue compared with 21.8% last year.

The decrease as a percentage of revenue reflected net synergy savings and operating leverage from strong organic revenue growth, partially offset by higher nonbillable labor costs, incentive compensation and overhead from acquired businesses. We remain focused on continuing to drive SG&A leverage through cost management, integration, efficiency and automation initiatives as well as growth across the business. Adjusted EBITDA was $107 million, up 19% from $90 million in the prior year period, outpacing revenue growth of 12.5% as we continue to scale profitably. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 16.8% compared with 15.9%, an improvement of approximately 90 basis points, reflecting strong growth in C&E, margin improvement in I&M and SG&A leverage.

Third quarter adjusted diluted earnings per share was $0.18, up from $0.14 in the second quarter, bringing year-to-date adjusted diluted earnings per share to $0.36. Turning to segment results. Consulting and Engineering contributed revenue of $223 million, up 20.3% year-over-year. Adjusted gross profit grew 20% with adjusted gross margin holding roughly flat at 47.4%. Inspection and Mitigation generated revenue of $318 million, up 8.5% year-over-year. As Ben discussed, this growth reflected increased call-out, outage and capital project activity. Adjusted gross margin was 29.2%, up 80 basis points, primarily reflecting the contribution from this higher-margin work as well as indirect cost discipline.

Geospatial contributed revenue of $98 million, up 9.3% year-over-year, supported by increased activity in power and utilities and military programs as well as contributions from recent acquisitions. Adjusted gross margin was 44.9%, down 330 basis points, reflecting project timing, mix, project execution, including a higher proportion of pass-through work on certain contracts. Given the segment's mix of larger fixed fee contracts, GEO revenue and margins can vary quarter-to-quarter based on project timing and delivery schedules. We have taken actions to strengthen execution and backlog growth supports the segment's outlook. For the first 9 months of 2026, total revenue was $1.712 billion compared with $1.603 billion in the prior year period. On a combined basis, revenue increased 6.8%, including 4.3% organically.

Adjusted gross profit was $646 million or 37.8%. Adjusted SG&A was $389 million or 22.7% of revenue. Adjusted EBITDA was $260 million, representing a margin of 15.2%. For the first 9 months of the year, I&M generated revenue of $850 million, up 1.0% year-over-year with adjusted gross margin of 27.6%. C&E generated revenue of $617 million, up 15.7% with adjusted gross margin of 47.4%. GEO generated revenue of $245 million, up 7.5% with adjusted gross margin of 48.7%. From a capital allocation perspective, we deployed net cash of $170 million on M&A during the quarter, bringing year-to-date acquisition investment to $180 million.

This included the three strategic acquisitions Ben discussed and an additional bolt-on acquisition, which added technical capabilities and broadened our geographic and end market exposure. We believe these acquisitions offer outsized opportunities for growth and margin expansion while meeting our criteria for cultural fit and accretive financial profile. We remain focused on integrating these businesses and expanding the services we provide to existing and new clients. Capital expenditures were $14 million during the third quarter and $40 million year-to-date, representing 2.3% of year-to-date revenue, slightly below our typical range of 2.5% to 3%.

In July, we also repurchased approximately 900,000 shares at an average price of $7.94 per share for a total of $7 million under our previously announced share repurchase program. This brings year-to-date repurchases to 2.8 million shares at an average price of $8.20 per share for a total of $22.7 million. Our capital allocation priorities remain focused on investing in the business while also delevering towards our long-term leverage target of 2.5x. We plan to continue evaluating and pursuing strategic acquisitions while also evaluating these investments against other opportunistic uses of capital. Turning to the balance sheet.

As of September 30, total liquidity was $293 million, including $198 million of cash and undrawn capacity on our $125 million revolving credit facility. Bank calculated net leverage was 3.9x with the increase driven by the timing of working capital investments to support growth during our busiest quarter of the year as well as cash deployed for M&A. Interest rate movements since May have reinforced the benefit of our $800 million interest rate swap, which provides greater certainty around borrowing costs. Cash conversion reflected seasonal working capital requirements and investments needed to support revenue growth across the business. As previously discussed, shifts in I&M outage schedules moved revenue later this year, delaying associated cash collections.

We expect a portion of these collections in the fourth quarter with the remainder in early 2027. We believe this primarily reflects timing. We remain focused on billing discipline, collections and working capital management to improve conversion as the business grows. For the full year, we anticipate net cash interest expense of $195 million to $105 million, cash taxes of $25 million to $30 million and capital expenditures of $50 million to $60 million. Turning to integration. We continue to build a scalable integrated back office. During the quarter, we launched our integrated CRM platform, providing visibility into opportunities across the combined organization. We also continue to transition certain integration activities to business leaders as part of day-to-day operations.

Remaining work includes HR and financial system integrations and alignment of our IT environment. As of September 30, we had actioned approximately $22 million of our annualized run rate cost savings, up from $20 million at the end of the second quarter. We remain on track to deliver our previously announced $25 million run rate target by year-end and continue to expect approximately $15 million of realized savings in 2026. These savings are contributing to margin expansion alongside improvements in utilization, business mix and operating execution. I want to thank our teams for their continued effort and commitment to the integration as we continue building for our future. Turning to our outlook.

We are increasing our full year revenue guidance to $2.24 billion to $2.27 billion, up from $2.15 billion to $2.25 billion. We are also narrowing our adjusted EBITDA guidance range to $342 million to $350 million, updated from $330 million to $355 million. This raises the midpoint to $346 million. The updated outlook reflects our momentum and the growth in the business, both organically and through our recent acquisitions. Based on our results through September, our full year guidance implies fourth quarter revenue of $528 million to $558 million and adjusted EBITDA of $82 million to $90 million. The fourth quarter outlook incorporates the timing of backlog conversion, planned outage activity and contributions from our recent acquisitions.

At the midpoint, this represents year-over-year growth of approximately 7% in the fourth quarter for revenue and 13% growth in adjusted EBITDA. While we look forward to providing more formal guidance for 2027 at a later date, we want to share a framework for planning purposes. Consistent with the strategy outlined at our Investor Day in May, we expect a year of strong growth supported by current commercial momentum, record backlog and a full year of contributions from our 2026 acquisitions. For 2027, we are planning for mid- to high single-digit revenue growth with C&E and Geospatial growth again expected to outpace I&M.

We expect adjusted EBITDA to grow faster than revenue, driven by operating leverage, scale, synergies and contributions from our 2026 acquisitions. Total combined C&E and GEO backlog increased 23% year-over-year, including a 16% increase in our 12-month backlog, providing solid visibility into 2027. Our 2027 growth framework reflects the expected pace of backlog conversion, which depends on project schedules and execution capacity. We remain focused on converting backlog into profitable revenue. Our leading indicators remain strong, including proposal and commercial activity. We remain focused on execution, improved cash conversion and disciplined capital allocation as we progress towards our 2029 objective of $3 billion in revenue, 18% adjusted EBITDA margin and 85% free cash flow conversion.

With that, I will turn the call over to Robbie.

Robert Franklin: Thank you, Kristin. This quarter's results again reinforce the strategic rationale of bringing Acuren and NV5 together. Our teams are winning assignments that draw on multiple parts of the business, and the acquisitions announced this quarter extend the opportunity into additional services and geographies. Our priority is to translate those capabilities into sustained earnings and cash flow. That requires strong operating execution, accountability for site and project profitability and careful capital allocation. GeoVerra, WDI and Core Group each have capabilities we can bring to existing clients while introducing relationships that we can serve more broadly. As we evaluate further acquisitions, strategic and cultural fit must be matched by an appropriate purchase price, sustainable cash flow and attractive expected returns.

We also recognize the importance of reducing leverage, improving cash conversion and using that cash effectively will be important measures of our execution as we pursue our 3/18/85 2029 objectives. With that, Ben, back to you.

Benjamin Heraud: Thanks, Robbie. This was a strong quarter for TIC Solutions. We accelerated organic growth, returned I&M to growth, expanded margins and raised our outlook. We also added businesses that strengthened our technical capabilities and geographic reach. Cross-selling is translating into awarded work, increasing backlog and organic growth. Our teams are identifying additional client needs and combining services to address them. This is our life cycle model in practice, supporting clients from planning and design through construction and ongoing operations while expanding the scope of our relationships. Looking towards 2027, strong investment in infrastructure, energy and the built environment continues to support demand for our highly technical services.

Record backlog and our expanded capabilities put us in a position of strength, and we are confident in our ability to convert these opportunities into profitable growth and stronger cash flow. Thank you to our teammates for their continued focus on client service, their commitment to operating discipline and dedication to improving the business every day. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question will come from Chris Moore with CJS Securities.

Christopher Moore: So just the 8.4% organic growth was terrific. You said cross-selling is picking up. Just trying to get a sense as whether that had a meaningful impact on the organic growth yet.

Benjamin Heraud: Yes, absolutely. We're really gaining momentum with the cross-selling program. And I think this idea of us as a combined platform is really resonating with our clients and being a life cycle partner. One service is leading to another, and we're able to really drive additional business with our existing client base. Some common themes, we're just really able to serve our clients' needs better, expand our relationships geographically. And it's a competitive advantage when we're able to have this breadth of services that we have. So it's absolutely driving -- it's one of the driving factors of our organic growth for sure.

Christopher Moore: Terrific. And just on the three acquisitions, I think in total, you had talked about $90 million. Is any one of those meaningfully larger or smaller than the others? Just trying to get a sense as to kind of on a relative basis, the contribution that we should be looking for from them.

Kristin Schultes: Good morning, Chris. So I would tell you that there are four in total, two of them are a little larger than the other two. We are still in the range. We talked about our acquisition range and multiple range of 5 to 7x. We're on the high end of that for this quarter, but this was opportunistic for us. We remain very disciplined on M&A, but these were the right fit for us for the long term. So we're excited about them.

Operator: Our next question will come from Kathryn Thompson with Thompson Research Group.

Kathryn Thompson: Just on the implied Q4 guide, could you help us differentiate between onetime comps, acquired growth versus quarter-to-quarter revenue shifts and the run rate of the business into 2027? Really, what we're trying to parse out is just the organic growth versus acquired and differentiated between those two, particularly as we set up into 2027.

Kristin Schultes: Good morning, Kathryn. Yes. So if we look at our Q4 guidance, I think it's important to remember that the timing of these acquisitions in the quarter, they're seasonal businesses, and we do -- it does take some time for us to digest those. So if we look at the Q4 guide, it implies organic growth and I would call a very small contribution from the acquisitions given that timing.

Kathryn Thompson: Okay. Perfect. And last quarter and again this quarter, you discussed some bigger growth end markets for you, data centers, aerospace, industrial and energy. But big growth percentages on smaller numbers and they add up to real growth. How are you positioning the businesses to capitalize those into 2027? And can you put any framework around the magnitude of growth for these end markets and what you are expecting in 2027? Thanks again, and great job on the quarter.

Benjamin Heraud: Yes. Thank you. At our Investor Day, we talked about these megatrends that are really driving the growth of the business. And I think that those really do drive sustained growth for us. And just to touch on them, aging infrastructure, obviously, the digitization of the physical world and the rising energy usage and data centers relating to that. We're really happy with how broad-based our end market growth is across the organization. Data centers has been a driver of growth. But if you look outside of that, it is -- we're firing on cylinders on all cylinders across many end markets. So I think it's really setting us up.

We're really pleased with the momentum that we have as we go into 2027.

Kristin Schultes: And Kathryn, I would just add that we look through our end markets on a regular basis. We are truly bullish on all of our end markets. And as an example, the wind business -- the wind inspection business is a business that was strong for us in Canada in the legacy I&M business. And we've utilized resources and best practices and applied that to growth in the U.S. That piece of the business, that end market is up 60% this quarter. And so we're looking for pockets leadership opportunities to kind of cross share opportunities and resources to continue driving growth in all of our end markets.

Operator: Our next question will come from Josh Chan with UBS.

Joshua Chan: Really impressive backlog growth. And so I was wondering if you could talk about what are sort of the two or three primary drivers of your backlog growth? I know you gave a combined number between the two businesses. So just curious where you're seeing the greatest increase in demand.

Benjamin Heraud: Just as I mentioned before, the broad-based sort of performance across the organization, it's mostly organic that growth. So I'll sort of come back to the cross-selling being a key driver of that. But it really is broad-based across the board. We're really happy with -- we look every week at the new projects that are coming in, and it is very, very active across multiple end markets.

Joshua Chan: And I guess, Kristin mentioned that you expect EBITDA margin expansion in 2027 of 7%, which makes sense. I was thinking with, obviously, the capture of the remaining synergies and maybe kind of further operating leverage that I was wondering if -- what is kind of holding you back from having kind of a stronger language around margin expansion? Or are you just trying to be kind of prudent, kind of starting this far ahead of the new year?

Kristin Schultes: Thanks, Josh. Yes, I think if we align to our 3/18/85, it does reflect meaningful margin expansion on a yearly basis. If you look at our implied Q4 guidance, I think it's around 80 basis points of improvement. Our full year would be up about 60 basis points. It's early in our budgeting cycle. We're excited about that process progressing and being able to provide more clarity on expectations for 2027 margin expansion. But I would tell you that the team is very bullish on kind of the momentum we're seeing and some of the acceleration opportunities we have. We just returned to demonstrating operating leverage in the second quarter.

And so -- and again, we've talked about this before, but the levers we have from a margin expansion perspective are broad and meaningful and will deliver results.

Operator: Our next question will come from Andy Wittmann with Baird.

Andrew J. Wittmann: So I guess I wanted to start with the I&M segment here. You kind of mentioned some of the delays from second quarter pushed into the third and kind of sounded like thought that third was obviously a good quarter for you there. But you also had some comments later talking that this is going to be the segment that's growing slower than the others, which isn't new information. But I'm just trying to kind of put that all together on this segment in particular and just get a sense of what you think the underlying business is there, recognizing that you do have some of that run and maintain, which is very visible and recurring.

And obviously, the outage work is always going to be somewhat lumpy. But I'm just trying to get a sense to how to think about this business like you're thinking about it. Is this still kind of a low single-digit organic grower underneath everything, Ben, Kristin? Or how should we be thinking about that?

Benjamin Heraud: I think low to mid-single digits. I would just say really, really happy with the work that we've done, the results from the work that we've done through the year. The leadership changes we made, the commercial focus that the team has is really on the front foot, and we have a really, really robust commercial pipeline. So the quarter, Q3 played out as we expected. And we're looking for sustained growth within this business. I'm really happy with the momentum that we have going to 2027 with the I&M segment.

Kristin Schultes: Andy, we talked about site wins last quarter. We have some pending site wins as well. The momentum and the commercial progress we're making is meaningful. I'm excited also about when you look at service lines within I&M. So there's the core NDT business, which is about 70% of that business. But the rope access work that we're doing is growing meaningfully as well. That work is actually up over 20% this quarter and 15% year-to-date, which is exciting. The lab side of the business is also growing, up about 15% for the quarter.

And then if you look at the mix of the work that we're doing in I&M between the -- we call it nature of work, the outage activity, obviously was strong this quarter as expected. But we're seeing growth in call-out work, which is our higher-margin service work. We're seeing growth in our small project work, which is also high-margin work. So the momentum is there. We are putting out a high conviction number at this stage in the process, but feel very good about where this business is headed.

Andrew J. Wittmann: That's good detail. I guess want to do next. I guess I wanted to just kind of understand the cash and cash flow a little bit better. There's a couple of ways to kind of talk about this. We heard your comments that obviously, a big growth quarter, took some working capital and you expect 4Q and maybe some bleeding into 1Q. So I heard the comment on that. Just looking at some of the other things here, it looks like there's a pretty meaningful increase in current liabilities sequentially, like, I don't know, like $50 million. So I wanted to understand what that is.

Is it attached to -- last quarter, I asked about the purchase accounting and how the goodwill is now up over $20 million kind of creeping from when you first took a glance at it to now. It seems like there's probably some contracts that you're working on that's getting revised in terms of its cost outlook. Is that all related? What is the impact to cash from that? Kristin, maybe if you could comment on that. I just want to make sure that whatever project or projects are causing this are contained now and why we shouldn't expect -- I mean, next quarter would be income statement eligible.

And so I just want to make sure that we're talking about that now before anything else might happen in the future.

Kristin Schultes: Yes. So let me start with the measurement period adjustments. The growth in accrued liabilities is not related to that. That was largely completed in the second quarter. There was a minor adjustment not related to POC accounting in the third quarter. In terms of cash conversion, I think -- I mean, look, you're right to focus on it. In fact, I had your name down for this question. So there's a couple of nuances we talked about the growth in the quarter. Interestingly, if you look at our revenue spread during our busy months, typically, it's fairly even between May and October.

We had a very high concentration of revenue in August and September at the end of the quarter. That drove a spike in working capital and receivables. Our fourth quarter is typically our largest cash conversion quarter. We're working on an internal cash campaign to convert that. We did make meaningful progress on unbilled. We've shaved about 5 days off of our time to bill, which is positive. So working capital management proving and showing and demonstrating our ability to convert -- our billings and receivables to cash is a top priority for us. And we're focused on the typical people, process and technology.

Operator: Our next question will come from Tomo Sano with J.P. Morgan.

Brendan Shea: This is Brendan on for Tomo. With the life cycle partner model central to your thesis, are there any areas of greatest untapped opportunity to deepen your presence with existing clients that you'd like to call out? Or are those opportunities more kind of broad-based?

Benjamin Heraud: The opportunity is significant because there's so many clients that we currently only work within a very narrow scope of service. And so there's so many other services that we have within our purview that we're able to bring to them. So the trick really is educating our teams on what those services are and getting them in front of the clients, elevating our relationship and position with them and sort of really strengthening that relationship that we have with the clients. So I am very, very bullish and excited about the cross-selling opportunity that we have within the organization. We're only really just getting started, and I think the momentum is just continuing to build there.

Kristin Schultes: Yes. And I would add one of the integration items for bringing the businesses together was to get us on a consolidated CRM platform, and that just went live during the quarter. And we're excited about the way that's going to help increase opportunities and communication collaboration across our business.

Brendan Shea: And then you described implementing AI and technology work streams to improve productivity. Can you quantify measurable productivity or margin gains that you've realized so far? And what kind of investment is required to implement all of that?

Benjamin Heraud: We're not quite there in terms of quantifying it. What I will say is that we just -- we have a really strong history as a technology-enabled company, and we're very -- we have a very technical team. So they're naturally leaning into this in a big way. Getting subject matter experts into our business is one of our growth limiters, and I'm so excited about AI being a productivity lever for the business. So we're absolutely leaning into it. The CRM example that Kristin just brought up, AI is a big focus of that, our ability to react to web leads in almost real time for the Abilities team to understand cross-selling and the opportunity.

AI is a big lever there. But we're leaning into it in multiple work streams. The way I would look at it is it's been very exploratory to date, and we're really moving into an execution phase now where we identify the things that can be rolled out at scale across the organization, and we're really in that process at the moment. So more to come. We're absolutely in agreement that KPIs and being able to measure this is important, but we're not quite there yet.

Operator: Our next question will come from Jeff Martin with ROTH Capital Partners.

Jeff Martin: I wanted to dive into the acquisitions in the quarter a little bit deeper. It sounds like they are highly strategic in nature and bring unusual organic growth opportunities. I was just curious if you could speak to that.

Benjamin Heraud: Yes. Sort of it's showing us executing on our strategy. If we look at the GeoVerra acquisition in Canada, we've talked a lot about wanting to bring consulting engineering and Geospatial to that area. It's really executing on our land and expand strategy. We're already seeing a ton of cross-selling potential and leading into the leadership that we have up there. The Core acquisition was in response to client demand. They were asking for us on the data center side to be in Europe, and this was a great opportunity for us to set a platform up there.

And then WDI was a completely new service line and an end market that we really want to be in more in utilities. So highly recurring revenue base that also offers up a really big cross-selling potential between the clients that they have in the utility space and ours, which, as you know, is a really high barrier to entry into new utility clients. So sort of three different examples of our strategic acquisition strategy in play.

Jeff Martin: And then my second question, you've already answered the first part of it, which was, are we back on track to normal consistent I&M business? It sounds like we are. So maybe confirm that, that statement you agree with. And then on Geospatial, I was just curious if you could kind of characterize what kind of time line we might anticipate better execution with the changes that you're making there?

Benjamin Heraud: Yes. So we wanted to react quickly to some of the project-related issues that we have. And really, what it is, is we're bringing some of the best practices from our consulting and engineering business and just bringing those to the table within Geospatial. The quarter, Q3 was a really, really strong sales month. And I think that, that's setting us up for a good year next year around growth. So there are some problematic projects that we've dealt with and we're getting behind us.

And as I said, it was really just we wanted to react quickly to this and bring the horsepower that we have within the organization to the group to really strengthen it and support its growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Stephanie Moore with Jefferies.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: I was hoping -- really pleased by the rebound in the inspection business in the quarter. Maybe you could talk a little bit about what changed or what has kind of evolved as really this year has progressed, whether it's benefiting from some new wins, some project work. So anything that you can just speak to that's driven the rebound here as the quarters progress? And at the same time, maybe you could comment about how demand has exited the quarter as well.

Benjamin Heraud: Yes. So I mentioned earlier the work that we've done to date, it does really start with leadership and culture. And I think that we just -- that the tone within the group has completely changed and shifted towards a much more positive momentum and commercial focus. So the team is extremely focused on getting out, meeting with clients, elevating our position with the client and bringing -- moving ourselves up the value chain and bringing the C&E and Geospatial services to the table really, really enhance that. So we talked about new site wins last quarter. Those will start to ramp up through Q4.

And as we look ahead, I'm really excited about some of the commercial pipeline that we have. We've had a nice focus on project work, for example, and that's a great filler just seeing that grow and the callout work that we're doing. So it's quite broad-based. It's not one particular region. We're just seeing performance improve across the board. There's been a lot of focus and questions around the Gulf. I'm just really happy with the changes that we've made there, and that's behind us. The team is on a great growth path there.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: That's great. And specifically related to the work in the Gulf, was this more so from actions that you think are more in TIC's control? Or do you think this is just more of an underlying demand environment that maybe became a bit more favorable?

Benjamin Heraud: I think the changes that we made in leadership were absolutely key to getting us back on to a good growth path. I mean we did have some recessionary behavior from clients in last year and some of the oil and gas behavior around holding out on outages over a quarter or two that did hurt us in the past. So I think there's going to be a lot of pent-up demand for that work into 2027. So a little bit of both, some self-inflicted that we've fixed and some to do with the behavior of our clients, which we see as a positive opportunity into 2027.

Kristin Schultes: Yes. If I&M leadership were on the call, they would tell you that this is -- it's all the hard work on so many fronts that they've been executing against for the last year that is starting to show up in results, and it's coming from a number of different areas. And so yes, I agree with Ben. It's broad-based. It's not one customer, one site. It's structural improvements in the business.

Benjamin Heraud: Yes. Very proud of the team and what they've pulled off this year.

Operator: Our last question will come from Min Cho with Texas Capital Securities.

Min Cho: I had a question just basically on your data center business. Obviously, you added your European presence with the Core acquisition. Can you just talk about how your expansion into the U.S. is going and maybe talk about the outlook just based on geography?

Benjamin Heraud: Yes, sure. So just to sort of ground on where most of the revenue, it is about 80% still in Asia Pacific, 20% in the U.S. and a little bit in Europe. That business we acquired was actually -- in Europe was actually quite diversified. So it wasn't just a data center business, which is what we like that's nice. So I'm still really, really excited about the pipeline of work that we have in front of us. It continues to grow. Using Texas as an example, there were -- we were aware of some slowdown a couple of months ago.

And in conversations with our clients, because it's such a resource-constrained space, they said, look, if anything goes on hold here, we need you on a project over here. So we do expect some things to shift around in the U.S. with some of the recent changes, but we expect that capital to be diverted elsewhere. We have a very diverse client base. We work with approximately 80 end users. So as far as an end market that we're working in, we feel we're quite -- we're in a really good space when it comes to the data centers.

Min Cho: Excellent. And then, Kristin, maybe this is for you. In terms of the Geospatial end market, obviously, based on your commentary around kind of execution this quarter, but also just based on your outlook in terms of mix, should we expect the geo margins to be down sequentially in the fourth quarter? Just curious about your guidance there.

Kristin Schultes: Yes. So we haven't given guidance at the segment level. But that said, we're not anticipating degradation in the fourth quarter. Like Ben mentioned, the structural changes we're making in that business are providing improvements in results. And so on a combined basis for Q4, we're projecting about 7% growth at the midpoint.

Benjamin Heraud: I can just give a little bit of color on those gross margin drivers as well. It is depending on the mix during the quarter, it can swing the numbers quite significantly. The gross margin on different services within that segment can range from 30% to 60%. In the quarter, we also had a higher amount of pass-through than typical, and that was due to capacity constraints. A lot of our assets are fully utilized, and we needed to leverage subcontractors a little bit more. And we also had a data brokering opportunity or project, which is a really, really great business because it's pass-through.

So while it was a little bit dilutive to our gross margin, it was actually accretive to the EBITDA margin. So just a little bit more color on that gross margin.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer portion of today's call. I'd like to turn the call back over to management for any additional or closing remarks.

Benjamin Heraud: Thank you, and thank you all for your questions and your continued interest in TIC Solutions. I'm really proud of our team's third quarter delivery. We achieved what we set out to do and we've demonstrated scale. Inspection, Mitigation is back to growth and the combined platform is working as we intended. Cross-selling continues to gain momentum, and it's showing up in our organic growth and backlog. We remain focused on execution and delivering on our commitments, and we look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter. Thank you all, and have a good day.

Operator: Thank you, ladies and gentlemen. This brings us to the end of today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation, and you may now disconnect.

If you want to know what it looks like when a trillion-dollar tech bubble violently collides with physical reality, just look at yesterday. $2.5 trillion in tech valuations were wiped off the board as Wall Street panicked about AI’s leverage — punishing tech giants for incinerating cash on infrastructure that isn’t generating immediate profit.

Simultaneously, as we saw on Wednesday, the American voter rejected data center expansions in 40 out of 41 local ballot measures. The hardware hoarders are losing their grip, and the panic is palpable. The era of scrutiny is here, and I want to show you two possible timelines of where this could go.

But first, we have to go back over a couple things.

When faced with this stock crash, AMD CEO Lisa Su said, “We are a data center first company.” While I’d love to throw my hands up and get angry at this, I have to turn the BS detector on myself and address a brutal truth: she’s right. This market crash is a sentiment correction, not an overnight fab cancellation.

The big three memory foundries — SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron — operate on long-term agreements. 2026-2027 is already locked in at sky-high prices, and on top of that, enterprise AI accelerators consume roughly 3x the silicon wafers of standard consumer DDR5 memory.

As long as those massive AI server chips are shipping, conventional RAM capacity remains deeply suppressed.

So, if Wall Street is slashing valuations and data center permits are being blocked, why aren’t memory foundries pivoting back to consumer PC hardware right now?

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Hyperscalers are also starving for memory, and receive around 60-70% of what they ask for. If Microsoft and Meta get spooked by the market and pull back their massive order growth by 10% or even 15%, it wouldn’t trigger a supply chain pivot. It just means the foundries are a little less overwhelmed. Demand still vastly exceeds total factory capacity.

If foundries are still frantically trying to fulfill enterprise contracts, they have zero financial incentive to redirect back to consumer memory.

For them to actually panic and pivot, hyperscaler orders have to crater. A simple market correction like this won’t do it. But a sweeping wave of municipal zoning bans? That changes the math entirely.

Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence.November 4, 2026

If tech giants are legally barred from breaking ground on new server farms, they are forced to cancel their existing silicon orders because they physically have nowhere to plug the chips in.

We are not getting a massive surplus of GPUs and memory kits tomorrow morning. But the midterms and the stock market correction did put a concrete ceiling on the shortage. So let me take a stab at how I think this is going to unfold.

The stock rout has cracked the leveraged AI market for now, but contract prices remain firm. There is zero immediate relief, so don’t expect some banger Black Friday deals on RTX 5090s.

Memory shortages will hit their tightest consumer squeeze through early 2027. PC makers will fiercely defend a ceiling of 16GB-24GB on premium laptops and handhelds. If you’re hoping for 32GB in sub-$1,500 machines, shelve that hope through most of next year.

As hyperscalers face sustained stock and regulatory pressure from the midterm fallout, corporate boards will force company CFOs to look at their data center infrastructure plans again.

Instead of writing blank checks for server racks, the pace of subsequent purchase orders will slow. And for you reading this, I envision that PC hardware prices will finally stop climbing and plateau.

PC builders (Apple, Dell, Asus, Lenovo, etc) will gain massive leverage during mid-year procurement negotiations — putting an end to double-digit quarter-on-quarter price hikes.

A typical memory wafer run takes 3-4 months. Once the AI server orders officially ease in Q2, foundries will finally redirect their wafers back to consumer products. This is when the true price relief begins.

Standard desktop DDR5 kits will experience price drops, and holiday 2027 laptops will finally start normalizing 32GB unified configurations without severe margin penalties.

We aren’t completely out of the woods, and we still have to survive a brutal winter. But in my mind, those 2028 doom-and-gloom shortage predictions are officially dead.

The hyperscalers just hit a political and financial ceiling, which may lead to a peak in memory pricing this spring rather than running unchecked into next year.

Hold off on your PC upgrades — the local AI renaissance could be scheduled for the second half of 2027.

#3302. iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

#3301. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3300. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3299. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.
