#3297. Suzano S.A. (SUZ) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Arbex lifts revenue, but rising energy and logistics costs weigh on margins.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Suzano S.A. (SUZ +1.68%) reported a 36% year-over-year increase in net revenue as the company completed its first quarter consolidating the Arbex joint venture. Management reported that pulp market dynamics improved toward the end of the period, supported by inventory declines at Chinese ports and delays in competitor capacity expansions. The company focused on integrating the Arbex consumer goods business while navigating higher logistics and energy costs influenced by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Management prioritized deleveraging and structural competitiveness, noting that the full capture of efficiency gains from recent acquisitions remains a focus for future periods.

Operator: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for holding, and welcome to Suzano's conference call to discuss the results for the third quarter of 2026. [Operator Instructions] The presentation that will be addressed by the CEO, Mr. Beto Abreu and other executive officers. This call will be presented in English with simultaneous translation to Portuguese. [Operator Instructions] Before proceeding, please be aware that any forward-looking statements are based on the beliefs and assumptions of Suzano's management and on information currently available to the company. They involve risks, uncertainties and assumptions because they relate to the future events and therefore, depend on circumstances that may or may not occur in the future.

You should understand that general economic conditions, industry conditions and other operating factors could also affect the future results of Suzano and could cause results to differ materially from those expressed in such forward-looking statements. Now I will turn the conference over to Mr. Beto Abreu. Please, you may begin your presentation.

João Fernandez de Abreu: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. This is a special call for Suzano as it's the first one in which we are reporting Arbex results in our financial statements. The Arbex acquisition is perfectly aligned with the company's strategy. We see a significant value creation opportunity, and it gives Suzano a more resilient business portfolio. I'm happy to share that Arbex's first quarter with us came fully in line with our plan, once again showing Suzano's ability to deliver as promised since the transaction was announced more than a year ago.

Q3 was marked by solid volumes, sales and pricing, a declining cash cost, despite a challenging geopolitical environment and stable pro forma leverage of 3.4x in U.S. dollars, including Arbex's last 12 months EBITDA. Management's priorities are now fully focused on continuing to improve our structure, competitiveness, advancing our fiber-to-fiber initiatives, reducing net debt and leverage, starting already in Q4, our strongest quarter for 2026 and capturing the highly visible efficiency gains at Arbex. Nothing else is on our agenda at the moment. With that said, I turn the floor over to Fabio, who will continue the presentation.

Fabio Almeida Oliveira: Thanks, Beto, and good morning, everyone. Please let's turn to the next page of the presentation. Before we start, I would like to highlight that Suzano Packaging results in this quarter cover the June-September period. Since its inception, Suzano Packaging has been reported with 1-month lag for our Brazilian operations. We started this quarter to report and be fully synchronized across both businesses. Looking at our markets in Brazil, Print & Write demand grew 5% versus Q2 and 2% year-over-year, benefiting from seasonality and election-related coated paper demand. Paperboard demand remained under pressure, down 9% sequentially and 5% year-over-year amid softer domestic consumption environment in Brazil.

Imports continue to rise with Print & Write paper and paperboard imports up 76% and 18% year-to-date through August, respectively, reflecting global oversupply and a stronger FX. Turning to international Print & Write markets. PPPC reported a 2% decline in uncoated woodfree demand in North America and LatAm in the first 8 months of the year, while Europe fell 4%. Now looking at paperboard in the U.S., market fundamentals slightly improved during the quarter. Based on data from AF&PA, SBS shipments were 2% quarter-over-quarter and 4% year-to-date up, while the production disruption at Nippon Dynawave tightened regional supply, especially liquid packaging board, the main market for Suzano Packaging.

SBS operating rate is now at 85%, better on a quarter-over-quarter, but still below on a year-over-year and historical levels. During the quarter, our Brazilian operations performed well with a 3% growth in production quarter-over-quarter, even considering the annual planned shutdown at our Mucuri mill in August. Against last year, volumes from the Brazilian operations were stable. In our Suzano Packaging operations, the growth in production volumes in quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, reflecting the additional month reported as explained before. Our sales volumes grew 10% quarter-over-quarter and remained stable year-over-year.

While domestic volumes in Brazil were broadly stable, exports from Brazilian operations decreased 9% versus Q2 and 27% year-over-year, reflecting non-recurring impacts related to the implementation of our new SAP system in July. Export operations have since then improved, and we are now working to have our backlog cleared in Q4. Suzano Packaging sales grew on a quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year basis, but were limited to operational constraints at our Pine Bluff mill in Q3 and lower inventory levels. Despite higher import volumes in the Brazilian markets, our Brazilian operations delivered a price increase of over 2% quarter-over-quarter. Ex Suzano Packaging prices increased 6% in dollar terms over the same period.

Now looking at our EBITDA, our combined operations performance decreased 14% quarter-over-quarter. Our Brazilian operations delivered stable volumes and higher prices, but higher SG&A in the period due to corporate expense allocations and higher logistics costs and COGS impacted by annual planned maintenance shutdown at Mucuri mill, which affected our performance in the quarter. At Suzano Packaging, Q3 EBITDA was significantly impacted by operational challenges at the Pine Bluff mill, mainly related to asset reliability and production efficiency, resulting in lower operating rates, higher production costs and reduced inventory availability. In addition, raw materials and logistics costs increased in the quarter amid a more challenging geopolitical environment.

While price increases helped mitigate part of these inflationary pressures, they were not sufficient to offset the operational headwinds. The operational issues faced in Q3 were substantially addressed by the end of September and the mill has been operating more consistently since then. We continue to prioritize reliability, efficiency, safety and cost competitiveness as we advance the turnaround of Suzano Packaging, supporting gradual improvement in EBITDA performance and our path to positive cash flow by 2028, in line with the original business plan. Looking ahead in Brazil, we expect sales volumes to improve following historical seasonality, particularly in coated paper. Coated paper demand, on the other hand, should soften as the additional demand associated with the election cycle fades.

For paperboard, we expect stable demand with stronger year-end consumption, offsetting part of the softer economic backdrop. Now I hand over to Leo, who will present the Pulp business unit results.

Leonardo Grimaldi: Thanks, Fabio, and good morning, everyone. Let's now turn to our Pulp business unit, where I'd like to share with you the highlights for our third quarter of 2026 as well as my view for the upcoming months. This past quarter was marked by solid invoicing by Suzano, in line with last year. In China, paper and board production posted a slight growth when compared to Q3 '25. And as usual, our customers planned their pulp purchases in order to support the higher production pace from September to December, the strongest seasonal period of the year. Despite healthy demand, market pulp dynamics reflected 2 distinct business environments as the quarter unfolded.

In the first half of Q3, customers continued destocking in anticipation of new pulp supply coming from OKI 2 at the time expected to start up in Q4 '26. By mid-quarter and with the announcement that the project had been delayed into Q1 '27, customers rapidly increased pulp purchases to meet their late Q3 and their Q4 production plans, creating a significantly more favorable environment for market pulp producers. This supportive scenario was also fostered by pulp inventories at Chinese ports, which continued to decline during Q3.

At the same time, low pulp price levels in China in July and August, below the cash costs of some local producers led certain integrated players to reduce their own pulp production rates and shift to market pulp purchases. Despite hardwood-softwood price spreads remaining below historic levels, especially in Asia, fiber-to-fiber substitution continues at a healthy pace as customers seek every possible saving and recognizing that the current weak softwood market is unsustainable long term. As an example, in Europe, according to Europulp data, hardwood pulp consumption was stable in Q3 when compared to Q3 '25, while softwood consumption fell 9%.

The quarter was also marked by growing reports of permanent pulp mill closures as well as an increase in unexpected downtimes. According to market consultancies, more than 900,000 tons of bleached chemical pulp was removed from the market as Q3 unfolded, again, improving S&D dynamics. In such context, we have sold 3.19 million tons in Q3 with an average export price of $591 per ton, a slight decline when compared to Q2 '26 and 13% higher than Q3 '25. Looking at the right side of my slide, the BRL 4.8 billion in EBITDA, up 12% quarter-over-quarter with a 50% EBITDA margin was mostly driven by higher volumes, lower costs and a more favorable FX when compared to Q2 '26.

Now looking forward, I would like to highlight the following points. In October, we were able to implement our announced price increases globally, while maintaining our planned sales volumes. In China, at these new prices, our customers confirm their order intake with volumes at historic levels. At the same time, pulp production costs in China continues to rise.

On top of the $30 per BDMT over 2025 lows, which translates roughly into $60 per ton increase on pulp production costs, as I have mentioned during our previous call, our sources on the ground report an additional $10 per BDMT increase from this July to September, or $20 per ton of additional cash costs, bringing our estimated cash cost in China to a range between the low $500 to $560. And the cost pressure in our sector is not exclusive to China. Pulp producers worldwide continue to face a broad cost inflation in their value chain and the ongoing geopolitical tensions and weather-related events.

Now talking about the supply side of the equation, we are closely monitoring the impacts of El Nino globally and, more specifically, in Indonesia. Wildfires in this country, following a pattern similar to 2015, are reportedly affecting the forest base supporting the country's pulp production, although the impact remains unclear. Depending on the severity of the wildfires and their impact with haze or wood availability, the ongoing pulp project in Indonesia may face further start-up delays or have lower ramp-up curves. For the coming months, we also see the confirmation of our thesis that looking only at gross new capacity as a result of new projects in the pipeline is not enough to forecast price levels.

Permanent closures already reached over 1 million tons of bleached chemical pulp since the beginning of this year and expected downtimes are rising and reaching 2.3 million tons so far. Several pulp projects, both market pulp and verticalization, have been delayed during 2026, and we are enthusiastic to share that the first cases of the verticalization in Western markets are starting to materialize. Unfortunately, due to confidentiality agreements, we can yet publicly not disclose them. For Suzano, the fourth quarter is seasonally marked by higher sales volumes to support our customers' increasing demand, and we are prepared to deliver another strong Q4.

Today, we are running with invoicing backlogs in some cases, reaching more than 2 months, and we seek to reestablish normalized levels until the end of the year. With that said, I would now like to invite Carlos. Welcome back, Carlos, to address our cash cost performance during the past quarter.

Carlos Fernandes de Almeida: Thanks, Leo, and good morning, everyone. I will cover pulp cash cost, Page 6 of our presentation. Our cash costs, excluding downtime was BRL 825 per ton in the quarter, down 2% versus Q2 '26. The improvement was mainly driven by operational efficiency captured after the maintenance downtimes in the previous quarter with lower specific input consumption, better fixed cost dilution and lower wood costs supported by lower specific wood consumption. These gains were partially offset by higher chemical and energy costs, reflecting both direct and indirect impacts of the conflict in the Middle East as well as the stronger U.S. dollar.

It is worth noting that approximately BRL 14 per ton of our cash cost in the quarter was related to commodity cost pressures associated with this conflict in the Middle East. Adjusting for this exogenous factor, cash cost would have declined and again, would have declined 4% quarter-over-quarter, highlighting the underlying operational improvements captured during the period. Looking now to the year-over-year performance, our cash costs, excluding again downtime, increased 3%, mainly reflecting higher chemical and energy costs once again associated with direct and indirect impacts of the conflict in the Middle East on the global commodity and energy markets. We also saw higher wood costs, mainly driven by labor and maintenance inflation in our harvesting operations.

These headwinds were partially offset by operational efficiency gains with better fixed cost dilution from higher production volumes and stronger energy sales. The weaker U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real benefited the cash cost performance. Overall, we continue to demonstrate solid cost discipline despite a more challenging geopolitical and commodity cost environment. As we look to the year-end, our operational execution remains broadly in line with the assumptions underlying our original cash cost outlook. However, commodity and energy cost pressures have proven more persistent than initially anticipated as the conflict in the Middle East continues to impact -- to affect global supply chains and commodity markets.

Combined with a strong U.S. dollar, these exogenous factors have increased our cost base beyond our original assumptions. As a result, we are updating our full-year 2026 cash production cost, excluding downtime guidance from BRL 800 per ton to approximately BRL 825 per ton. Important to say that, absent these external pressures, we would be on track to deliver our original BRL 800 per ton cash cost target. Now I turn the floor over to Marcos, who will continue the presentation.

Marcos Assumpcao: Good morning, everyone. Moving to Slide 7. This is our first quarter after closing the Arbex acquisition and the first time we report Consumer Goods as a separate segment. João Fernandez de Abreu: Thank you, Marcos. What I can say to you is that we remain highly committed to improve the efficiency of our own operations. The change in the macro variable of FX, and we are also incorporating the efficiency gains that we expect for the business. And that's how we arrive at a TOD reduction from 2,060 level that was our realized TOD for 2025 to 1,980 in 2027. As Carlos mentioned in his initial speech, if it was not for the change in the macro variables, we will be 100% aligned with our guidance on the cash cost side. So I think that remains the case.

The main -- or the big difference that could arrive in the numbers for 2027 will be depending on the macro variables that we will use, okay? Second question regarding Arbex. Beto also mentioned that we expect the value creation program to kick in, in the upcoming quarters. As we mentioned before, we see room for SG&A improvement. We now have contracts that we have to still like -- Kimberly-Clark is offering some services to Arbex. #3296. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

#3295. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

#3292. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3291. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3290. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

“over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

The word “by” seems important here. That quote is clearly not about the apps used to track ICE, it’s about apps that ICE uses itself.

That makes me wonder if the original article is confused, though. Is ICE really “hosting” its own internal apps on the App Store rather than deploying through some enterprise/MDM distribution method? I guess Apple is involved in that process, too? And if the incoming Congress takes the posture that ICE has been operating an illegal human trafficking ring, then assisting them is a crime.

Apple was pathetic and ridiculous for removing ICEBlock and similar apps. It was also blatantly unconstitutional for the DOJ to threaten them into doing it.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

You can read the full Reuters report here, and The Washington Post’s here.

#3289. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD Review: Small, speedy, and easy on the wallet

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a simple, affordable way to make a 1080p TV smarter. The new Vega OS feels quick, its slimmer design can run straight off your TV's USB port, and setup is a breeze. It's limited to 1080p and can't sideload apps like Fire OS, so if you own a 4K TV, you should spend a bit more on the new Amazon Fire Stick 4K.

Responsive, easy-to-use interface with new Vega OS

Slim design that runs off your TV's USB port

No third-party app sideloading like Fire OS

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Streaming sticks don't need to be fancy to hit their mark, and the Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a great reminder of that. If you've got an older TV that's still going strong but has sluggish smart features (or perhaps none at all), a $35 streaming stick is an easy fix.

The 2026 Fire TV Stick HD runs Vega OS, Amazon's Linux-based software, which replaces the Android-based Fire OS that powered previous models. Amazon says the changes make it more than 30 percent faster, and it also brings a slimmer body, USB power, Wi-Fi 6 support, and free Alexa+.

It's not all pros across the board. The resolution caps out at 1080p, you can't sideload third-party apps anymore, and there's no support for Dolby Vision. But if you're shopping for a bedroom, guest room, or an older TV set that you don't primarily use, the Fire TV Stick HD is one of the cheaper streaming devices you should take a closer look at.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD launched on April 29, 2026, for $34.99, which is the same price as the 2024 model it replaced. It's Amazon's cheapest streaming stick, and it sits below the Fire TV Stick 4K and the Fire TV Stick 4K Max. Amazon ran a limited-time deal that brought the stick down to $21.99 shortly after launch, so we'll likely see temporary price cuts around the holiday shopping season.

Keep in mind that the stick's new "Direct Power" feature means that it gets power right from your TV's USB port. If your TV doesn't have a USB port, you'll need to pick up an adapter separately.

The Fire TV Stick HD is about as minimal as a streaming device gets, and Amazon says it's the slimmest Fire TV device the company has made. That makes it really easy to tuck behind a TV or toss in a bag for a trip, and it won't crowd the other ports and cables on your set.

The only other connection is a USB-C port for power, and thanks to "Direct Power," you can plug it straight into your TV's USB port with the included cable. That means you'll have one less wall adapter to hide, and your setup will look a lot cleaner as a result.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The included Alexa Voice Remote covers all the basics, including voice search, menu navigation, TV power, and volume controls. It doesn't have fancy extras like a remote finder or backlit buttons, but it gets the job done. (If you want Amazon's redesigned Fire TV remote, which I liked a lot more, you'll have to get the Fire TV Stick 4K.)

Setup is about as easy as it gets. Just plug the stick into your TV's HDMI port, connect the USB-C cable to your TV's USB port, and follow the on-screen prompts. You'll then have to connect to Wi-Fi and sign in with your Amazon account, and you're off to the races.

Since Vega OS only lets you install apps from the Amazon app store, you should make sure that the ones you use most are actually available. Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, and other popular streaming services all run natively, but niche apps may be missing due to the lack of third-party app sideloading, which the older Fire OS allowed you to do.

The Fire TV Stick HD has a quad-core 1.7GHz processor and 8GB of storage. It can stream up to 1080p resolution with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, and it supports Dolby Atmos through HDMI pass-through if you have a compatible sound setup. There's no Dolby Vision here, and it won't output 4K, so it's really only meant for 1080p TV sets.

Vega OS keeps menus and home screen rows moving smoothly, and apps open quickly. I didn't have any issues switching between my most used apps on the fly. Amazon's "30 percent faster" figure is its own claim, so I wouldn't treat it as fact, but it definitely felt faster than my past Fire OS experiences.

I also like that the Fire TV Stick HD isn't limited to video. You can pair a Bluetooth game controller and play cloud games through Amazon Luna or Xbox Game Pass, which is a fun bonus, and you can even connect a pair of headphones for late-night viewing. It comes with Alexa+ free of charge, which can come in handy when you're trying to hunt down something new to watch.

The downsides are pretty familiar to past Fire TV Sticks. A big chunk of the Fire TV home screen is taken up by recommendations and sponsored content, and you'll definitely notice it (especially if you're used to Roku's cleaner layout like I am).

Sideloading third-party apps is also gone, which will bug those who liked using older Fire TV Sticks for apps that aren't available in Amazon's app store. Neither is a dealbreaker for the average viewer, but they're worth knowing about before diving in.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a fast, simple, and affordable streaming stick that's a perfect match for older HD TVs and secondary rooms. Vega OS feels speedy, the slim design and USB power keep things neat, and setup takes just a few minutes. You won't get 4K streaming resolution, Dolby Vision, or third-party app sideloading, but for $34.99 (or less on sale), it's hard to complain.

If you're looking for an alternative pick, the base model Roku Streaming Stick ($39) also tops out at 1080p, but has a cleaner interface.

In Amazon’s ecosystem, the new Fire TV Stick 4K costs $25 more, but you get 4K resolution output and a redesigned (and much better) remote. And if you're a tinkerer who wants to sideload apps, the Fire TV Stick 4K Max is the only Amazon stick that still runs Android-based Fire OS.

If you've got an older 1080p TV and want a cheap way to get streaming apps on it, the Fire TV Stick HD is a solid choice that won't break the bank.

Dylan Haas is a Freelance Contributor and Lab Tester for Tom’s Guide. He’s a seasoned journalist with bylines at publications like Mashable, GameSpot, and Paste Magazine where he covered the latest in tech, gaming, and entertainment.

#3288. Verastem (VSTM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pancreatic data and a planned Phase III launch highlighted the call.

Verastem, Inc. (VSTM -10.34%) reported substantial year-over-year revenue growth for its lead oncology product while detailing clinical progress for its KRAS G12D inhibitor pipeline. Management discussed the transition of its commercial LGSOC franchise to a self-sustaining operation and the advancement of regulatory filings for patient-convenience enhancements. The company stated that alignment has been reached with the FDA regarding pivotal trial protocols, allowing for specific endpoint modifications in upcoming frontline studies. Strategic efforts are now focused on completing Phase II enrollment and initiating three Phase III trials across pancreatic, colorectal, and lung cancers by the first half of 2027.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to Verastem Oncology's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. My name is Didi, and I will be your call operator today. Please note, this event is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I will now turn the call over to Julissa Viana, Senior Vice President of Corporate Communications, Investor Relations and Patient Advocacy at Verastem Oncology. Please go ahead.

Julissa Viana: Thank you, operator. Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Verastem's Third Quarter 2026 financial results and recent business updates. This afternoon, we issued a press release detailing these results, along with the slide presentation that we will reference during our call today. Both are available on the Investor Relations section of our website. Before we begin, let me point out that we'll be making forward-looking statements that are based on our current expectations and beliefs. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially. We encourage you to consult the risk factors discussed in our SEC filings for additional detail. Additionally, today, we'll be discussing certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are provided in the press release we issued today. Joining me on today's call to deliver prepared remarks and take your questions are Dan Paterson, President and Chief Executive Officer; Dan Lyons, Chief Commercial Officer; and Dr. Michael D. Kauffman, President of Development; and lastly, Dan Calkins, Chief Financial Officer. I will now turn the call over to Dan.

Daniel Paterson: Thank you, Julissa. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining our call today. We're encouraged by the progress we've made across our commercial business and the VS-7375 development program. We generated net product revenue of $24 million in the third quarter with demand holding steady for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK and strong refills offsetting new patient starts after significant growth in Q2. As Dan Lyons will discuss, we feel that there's still considerable opportunity to be realized for the CO-PACK. While we continue to see a positive impact from the changes we've made throughout the commercial organization, we're making additional efforts to gather feedback from physicians to understand patient experiences and educate on new and existing initiatives.

We're also excited to share that our new blister pack NDA has been accepted by the FDA with priority review and a PDUFA date of February 2027. This is an important step we are taking to further support patient convenience and adherence to the CO-PACK. Turning to the VS-7375 program. In October, we announced new clinical data from our TARGET-D 101 trial, including for the first time, U.S. efficacy data and updated safety and tolerability results in KRAS G12D mutated pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers.

As Michael Kauffman will discuss in more detail, we set a new efficacy benchmark in pancreatic cancer with compelling and confirmed response rates across lines of therapy, and we demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity in both colorectal and non-small cell lung cancers. With longer follow-up, VS-7375 continued to demonstrate a favorable and manageable safety profile at both the 600- and 900-milligram dose level. Overall, we believe that VS-7375 has a potential best-in-class profile and with the recent agreement with the FDA to start our first-line PDAC study, we have an opportunity to bring a chemo-free option to patients with pancreatic cancer.

Building on these encouraging VS-7375 data, we further strengthened our balance sheet by raising gross proceeds of approximately $250 million in October. Together with our current cash position and expected revenues from AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK, the financing proceeds are expected to fund operations across our broad clinical development plans into the first half of 2028. This funding supports our opportunity to expedite the development pathway for VS-7375 Phase II trial readouts and initiation of 3 Phase III trials, including our Phase III PDAC trial. We look forward to advancing parallel development paths in pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers with multiple opportunities to create value along the way.

Lastly, in October, we announced that I'll be stepping down as President and CEO at the end of 2026, with Michael Bailey, current Verastem Board member, stepping into the role. This transition follows my planned retirement, though I'll continue serving on the company's Board of Directors and as an adviser. Michael is an accomplished biopharmaceutical executive and brings a wealth of experience in oncology drug development and commercialization experience. Most recently, Michael served as President and CEO of AVEO Pharmaceuticals, leading the organization to their acquisition by LG Chem and subsequently led the integrated company through June of this year. Michael will be an important leader through Verastem's next phase of commercial growth, clinical advancement and operational execution.

I'm extremely proud of all that we've accomplished in my 15 years at Verastem. Our work has benefited patients, physicians, families and the broader health care system, and I have great confidence that we'll continue to make positive impact with our promising future ahead. With that, I'll turn the call over to Dan Lyons for our commercial update. Dan?

Daniel Lyons: Thanks, Dan. In the third quarter, net product revenue for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK was $24 million. This revenue was driven by expanded prescribing across both community and academic accounts with increasing refill rates throughout the quarter, serving as the foundation of our performance. We also saw a moderation in new patient starts after significant overall growth in the second quarter, reflecting seasonal headwinds in the late summer. Given the episodic nature of treatment persistence in rare diseases like low-grade serous ovarian cancer, new patient starts can fluctuate quarter-to-quarter.

As we are in our first full year of the launch, we continue to see broader physician adoption and remain confident in our ability to grow the AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA business as more physicians gain experience with the CO-PACK. As the launch matures, prescribers are increasingly choosing the CO-PACK at a patient's first or next recurrence as appropriate LGSOC patients are prescribed their next treatment. We have shared before, we have seen physician-directed utilization outside of LGSOC, primarily in solid tumors such as pancreatic cancer. As a reminder, this is not an approved indication of the CO-PACK, and we do not promote its use in this setting.

With the recent availability of allele-specific and pan-RAS clinical trials as well as a recently approved RAS therapy in pancreatic cancer, we anticipate an impact on the business as the treatment patterns evolve. Importantly, our commercial strategy remains focused firmly on the approved indication in KRAS-mutated recurrent LGSOC and helping physicians identify appropriate patients and initiating CO-PACK therapy earlier in the course of recurrent disease. Our CO-PACK commercialization efforts remain centered around 3 priorities: driving consistent new patient demand, expanding use earlier in the treatment journey and helping patients stay on therapy to realize the full benefit of treatment. Let's talk more about our progress with these efforts. First, we are prioritizing growth in new patient starts.

While new patient starts moderated in the third quarter, we continue to see adoption broaden through the addition of first-time prescribers and new accounts across both academic and community settings. We continue to work closely with gynecologic oncologists as they are the primary prescribers of the CO-PACK and learn from their role in managing patients with LGSOC from diagnosis through the course of their disease. In the community setting, we continue to work with practices to identify patients through site-specific alerts and greater awareness around the disease and how to manage patients. Adoption in this market is influenced by both ongoing promotional engagement and physicians' experience with the treatment.

Many of our community gynecologic oncologists may only see 1 to 4 patients with LGSOC per year, making education prior to prescribing and continued support as they gain experience, especially important. Second, we are prioritizing initiatives to drive use in the right patients at the first or next recurrence. Throughout the third quarter, we continue to monitor several indicators that physicians are initiating treatment earlier. These observations are informed by our internal prescribing data, field insights, physician discussions and market research. As we have discussed previously, the early launch included a meaningful proportion of patients who are heavily pretreated and further along in their disease.

As we see treatment duration increase as the launch matures, we are confident the initiatives are working. Third, we are focused on helping patients to stay on the CO-PACK longer and making the treatment experience as simple as possible. Refills were a key contributor to third quarter revenue and strong refill rates tell us that our efforts to support patients in remaining on therapy are gaining traction. As prescribers gain experience with the CO-PACK, they are becoming more confident in proactively managing adverse events and helping patients remain on treatment. Patients who successfully navigate the early cycles of therapy tend to stay on treatment longer, creating a growing base of refill demand.

Building on that momentum, we are focused on further improving the patient experience through our new AVMAPKI tablet formulation and blister pack presentation of both AVMAPKI and FAKZYNJA. As Dan mentioned, the NDA has been accepted by the FDA with priority review and a February 2027 PDUFA date. If approved, the new formulation would replace the 4 0.8 milligram AVMAPKI capsules taken per dose with a single tablet, meaningfully reducing pill burden. The new blister pack presentation would also make it easier for patients to track and manage their medication, including dedicated packaging for reduced dosing while eliminating the current refrigeration requirement and making the CO-PACK easier to store and travel with.

Taken together, we believe these enhancements can simplify the day-to-day treatment experience, support adherence and consistent refills and ultimately help patients stay on therapy longer. Importantly, these proposed changes do not change the approved indication, efficacy or safety profile of the CO-PACK. In closing, we remain confident in our ability to capture the significant opportunity that remains in KRAS-mutated recurrent LGSOC. We are continuing to refine our commercial approach based on what we are learning from the launch and from physician feedback with a sharp focus on the 3 growth drivers: expanding adoption, driving earlier use at first or next recurrence and keeping patients on therapy longer.

As physicians gain experience with the CO-PACK and prescribing patterns evolve, we believe new patient starts and the growing base of patients receiving refills will support continued revenue growth and be amplified by the blister pack formulation. While we recognize that adoption in a rare disease market takes time and growth may vary from quarter-to-quarter, we believe focused execution against these priorities positions us to build a sustainable commercial business and capture the meaningful opportunity ahead. I'll now turn the call over to Michael Kauffman.

Michael Glen Kauffman: Thank you, Dan. Now I will cover key highlights from our VS-7375 R&D update in October. If you haven't viewed the webcast, I urge you to visit our website to watch the replay or review the slide presentation. We think you will find the clinical data quite compelling. VS-7375 is a highly selective, potent oral dual KRAS G12D on/off inhibitor with a long residence time on the target. These attributes are key to a strong efficacy and tolerability profile that may provide deeper tumor reductions and improved quality of life compared with pan-RAS inhibitors for patients fighting difficult-to-treat cancers, such as pancreatic cancer.

As Dan Paterson said, we have set a new KRAS G12D benchmark for a potential best-in-class profile with both compelling efficacy and a highly manageable tolerability profile. Progress in our CRC cohort is in an earlier stage, but we've shown that we can combine with EGFR inhibitors and are seeing early antitumor activity. In lung, while the data we've shared to date is at 600 milligrams and our go-forward dose is 900 milligrams, as more data are generated, we expect to see the same dose response in non-small cell lung cancer as we have seen in other tumors. A quick reminder on our data.

All patients who received 900 milligrams are included in our data set, meaning this is a modified intent-to-treat analysis, so-called mITT, which is what the FDA looks at. Secondly, all responses are confirmed, again, the way FDA and other regulators judge responses. Now jumping to our waterfall plot for PDAC patients in the 900-milligram monotherapy cohort. First, none of the patients on the study saw their tumors grow. Second, 4 out of the 8 patients who had second-line pancreatic cancer and had confirmed responses and 5 out of the 14 patients who had third and fourth-line disease had confirmed responses.

We also want to call out the unprecedented nature of all confirmed responses from a 22-patient data set of patients with heavily pretreated PDAC, including 2 single-agent complete responses. Here, we demonstrate the durability in the PDAC cohort with this swimmer plot. This highlights the need for multiple scans before observing response in some patients, but note that all responses are continuing except for one. That patient had progressive disease based on the CT scan, but is continuing many months now with stable disease and minimal side effects. In fact, he remains on the study today. Overall, we had 16 out of the 22 patients continuing with treatment at the time of the data cut.

We are highly encouraged that with a median follow-up time of 6. 4 months, we have not yet hit the median progression-free survival, and this is well beyond the 4.3 months PFS that was observed in third or fourth line PDAC in daraxonrasib's Phase I trial. To clarify, RevMed has not disclosed their actual PFS or overall survival for their KRAS G12D PDAC data set from their Phase III study, so we don't have a clear picture of a benchmark for second line. But we do know that our ORR, namely 50% in second-line PDAC is higher than the 24% ORR that daraxonrasib had in the second-line setting in the KRAS G12D population.

Let me reiterate, with a 67% landmark 6-month PFS rate, we feel confident that we are just beginning to uncover VS-7375's true potential and believe that trends in antitumor activity will continue to mature positively. Now while it's difficult to draw conclusions from direct comparisons between our data and that generated for other G12D selective or pan-RAS inhibitors, we've included key data points for ease of reference. In the second line, as noted above, we broke ground with a 50% confirmed ORR standing above daraxonrasib's 24% ORR in KRAS G12D-driven tumors recently disclosed in their FDA approval documents.

In the third-line [ frst ], we observed 36% confirmed ORR with VS-7375, while daraxonerasib demonstrated 21% in the third and fourth line G12X population, which leads us to believe that in the G12D, specifically the ORR is very likely to be lower for daraxonrasib relative to VS-7375 given the worst outcomes for patients experience. Looking across other molecules and data points on the slide and including updates from ESMO, we believe that VS-7375 has best-in-class potential, and we look forward to building upon that in the Phase II trial. Transitioning now to CRC, colorectal cancer, while the data are still early, we cleared the 600-milligram dose and are encouraged by the antitumor activity at the 900-milligram dose level.

We will provide an update on the CRC cohort with 10 patients worth of data in the coming months, dependent on CT scan schedules, but remain encouraged that 5 out of these 6 patients remain on treatment. Of the 6 patients in the mITT analysis, 33% demonstrated a response with median follow-up of 6.1 months. As you can see in this waterfall plot, every patient experienced tumor shrinkage, incredibly encouraging to see in heavily pretreated colorectal cancer. Next, we'll turn to lung at the 600-milligram dose level. With a 43% confirmed overall response rate, strong durability and a favorable tolerability profile compared to other available therapies, we believe these data support the potential for accelerated approval with VS-7375.

While one patient's tumor is slightly growing, our waterfall is still compelling with one patient closing in on a potential complete response. Patients previously treated with taxanes are in the gold bars, and we see great responses in these patients as well as in the other subgroups. Now looking across the swimmers plot, you will see that responses tended to occur very quickly. As of this data cut, all partial responses were observed in the first scan, and we feel very good about how well VS-7375 is penetrating the lung tumors as shown here. Lung cancer generally is more susceptible to these therapies, and every one of the partial responses here is confirmed and continuing. Moving to frontline lung.

These are the first 8 patients treated with VS-7375 at the 600-milligram dose, along with standard of care chemo immunotherapy. We have achieved a 75% overall response rate to date. Some of these responses are confirmed, some of these unconfirmed and some of these responses are just with KEYTRUDA because the patients who had a high PD-L1 or TPS score are indicated to receive KEYTRUDA monotherapy. The expected ORR in G12D lung cancer overall using upfront chemo immunotherapy is on the order of only 35% to 40%. To reiterate then, these KRAS G12D adenocarcinomas, therefore, fare much worse than the overall population with triplet treatment. And that's because G12D is a bad actor.

So again, very early data, but very exciting and a consistent water-only fell profile. Finally, I will cover the key points from our safety and tolerability profile from the 900-milligram dose level across 48 patients in the Phase I trial. Patients were consistently able to stay on the 900-milligram dose as best highlighted through the dose modification statistics. Only a single patient or 2% discontinued treatment due to either a treatment-emergent or treatment-related adverse event. Coupled with the median relative dose intensity of 97%, we believe the VS-7375's profile is extremely favorable compared to any class of targeted therapy. The vast majority of adverse events are gastrointestinal in nature.

And because the tolerability profile at 600 and 900 milligrams are practically identical, there is no reason for a dose reduction as it doesn't lead to a reduction in GI adverse events. Therefore, we consistently see dose interruption rates higher than reductions. A short interruption of 2 to 4 days can mitigate and effectively manage these AEs, supported by VS-7375's favorable half-life, long residence time and a 97% dose intensity. Patients who stopped the drug temporarily then restart at the full 900-milligram dose. Another important note is the lack of Grade 4 or 5 treatment-related adverse events. Only 10% of patients experienced a Grade 3 treatment-related event.

While the predominant adverse events again of VS-7375 are gastrointestinal disorders, only 1 patient experienced a Grade 3 GI TRAE, namely transient nausea, which rapidly responded to therapy. Looking deep at GI events, the most frequent were nausea, diarrhea and vomiting. These were predominantly Grade 1 with around 10% to 20% of patients experiencing a Grade 2 GI AE. Beyond GI AEs, VS-7375 showed a very low rate of rash and no reported mucositis or stomatitis in this study, highlighting the potential tolerability advantage versus pan-RAS inhibition.

As we look ahead to our future development plans and approaches, we believe that the safety data seen to date demonstrate VS-7375 is highly combinable and eventually can address a very wide population with KRAS G12D-driven cancers. Now let's talk about our broad ongoing program where we've made great progress. We have 3 ongoing Phase II trials, the TARGET-D 200 series in pancreatic, lung and colorectal cancer that are enrolling patients. We expect to complete enrollment in pancreatic and colorectal cancer around the end of the year and in the first half of 2027 for the lung trial. We then move to the frontline Phase III, which is the ultimate goal here.

We are very cognizant and focused and that we want patients to have the best chance to get their tumor under long-term disease control by moving expeditiously to the front. Along those lines, we recently reached agreement with the FDA on the protocol of the frontline Phase III TARGET-D trial in PDAC, and we expect to initiate the trial before the end of 2026. In parallel, we look forward to reaching alignment with the FDA on the protocol for the frontline Phase III TARGET-D trials in CRC and non-small cell lung cancer and plan to initiate these trials in the first half of 2027.

Before I hand it off to Dan Calkins, I want to spend a few minutes on the unique trial design of our Phase III first-line PDAC trial, TARGET-D 301. It's a 3-arm trial, 1:1:1 randomization. So 2/3 of the patients will be getting VS-7375 upfront. 1/3 will be getting standard chemotherapy. We went to the FDA with the argument that it is medically suboptimal for any patient in this day and age not to have at least a chance to get a RAS inhibitor if they have pancreatic cancer. As such, the FDA agreed to allow patients on the chemo arm to cross over once their tumor progress based on independently reviewed CT scans.

Given that all patients, therefore, have the opportunity to receive VS-7375 initially or on crossover, it becomes a study essentially of 7375 in the front line versus getting the drug in the second line. That makes overall survival as an endpoint very difficult to interpret. It confuses the endpoint. And FDA agreed with this logic. So far, as far as we are aware, for the first time ever, the FDA has allowed a Phase III randomized controlled trial for approval in frontline pancreatic cancer to move overall survival to a secondary endpoint. FDA also have allowed us to include overall response rate as a dual primary endpoint.

Some of you are aware of the program FDA has called the FrontRunner program, where you're allowed to potentially go to the FDA with data in hand and discuss the results of ORR analysis with them. We do not have explicit agreement that FDA will accept an accelerated approval based on ORR from this study, but FDA has allowed ORR to be one of the dual primary endpoints. In fact, FDA has also allowed other companies to include ORR in their primary endpoints in metastatic pancreatic cancer. So now we have the potential to use the FrontRunner program to garner accelerated approval in frontline disease.

This is potentially very important as ORR will mature before the other dual primary endpoint, which is progression-free survival. We believe these elements are really good for patients who have a very serious disease, PDAC. And recognize and applaud the flexibility of the FDA in this rapidly changing landscape. And we are actively contracting this trial across multiple international sites and reception has been extremely positive. It's why we expect to open this Phase III TARGET-D 301 trial by the end of the year, as I mentioned. With that, I'll turn the call over to Dan Calkins.

Research and development expenses were $68.8 million for the third quarter, increasing as expected from the second quarter of 2026.

SG&A expenses were $26.5 million for the third quarter of 2026 and roughly in line with the second quarter. These expenses continue to be driven by commercial activities and operations, including personnel-related costs to support the ongoing CO-PACK launch. We continue to expect SG&A expenses will remain consistent on a quarterly basis in the fourth quarter of 2026 as we remain disciplined in our expense management while making the right investments to support the ongoing commercial launch efforts. For the third quarter of 2026, non-GAAP adjusted net loss was $72.8 million or $0.72 per share diluted compared to non-GAAP adjusted net loss of $39.1 million or $0.53 per share diluted for the third quarter of 2025. Please see our press release for a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP measures. Moving to the balance sheet. We ended the third quarter of 2026 with cash, cash equivalents and investments of $172.8 million.

Based on our current cash position, proceeds from the October follow-on offering and expected revenues from the AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK sales, we believe we have the capital to fund operations into the first half of 2028 and deliver on our strategic priorities and key milestones, including completing our VS-7375 Phase II studies and starting our 3 pivotal Phase III studies in pancreatic, colorectal cancer and non-small cell lung cancer.
