Naturally, given the time of year, there are plenty of holiday movies now streaming on Paramount+, but making my pick was easy as Paramount+ just added my personal favorite Christmas film of all time. If you're not quite ready for festive-themed streaming, however, I'm also highlighting an iconic Sylvester Stallone action-thriller and an overlooked WWII drama.

Don't waste your weekend scrolling through the more than 120 movies just added to Paramount+. Here are the three that need to be at the very top of your watchlist.

"It's a Wonderful Life" is practically mandatory viewing over the holiday season. This 1946 Frank Capra classic isn't just the best Christmas movie of all time, but one of the greatest films of the 20th century. Charming, warm and sentimental, it celebrates the true reason for the season in quite some style. It's a feel-good movie that almost every new holiday movie takes inspiration from; it's quite simply a timeless masterpiece.

James Stewart stars as George Bailey, a selfless man who has given up his own dreams to help his family and community. On Christmas Eve, he reaches rock bottom and considers suicide. However, his guardian angel, Clarence (Henry Travers), intervenes and shows George what a lesser place the world would be if he had never existed. Also starring Donna Reed and Lionel Barrymore, "It's a Wonderful Life" lives up to its sterling reputation.

Watch "It's a Wonderful Life" on Paramount+ now

Sylvester Stallone's John Rambo is one of the 1980s most iconic action heroes, which makes his debut, "First Blood," a little peculiar. Sequels would depict Rambo as an unstoppable killing machine, but in his first outing, he's a traumatized soldier, scarred by what he saw and what he did during the Vietnam War. In fact, Rambo kills only a single person in the entire movie, and even that death is typically classified as accidental.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

If you're looking for '80s action pulp, go for one of the sequels, but if you want a tense thriller, then stream "First Blood." In my books, it's the best Rambo film of the lot. In "First Blood," Rambo (Stallone) finds himself on the wrong side of an arrogant small-town sheriff (Brian Dennehy); their confrontation spirals into a manhunt, as the law attempts to capture Rambo. But this former Special Forces soldier is a tricky man to catch.

The above picks are legendary movies. While they're still exceptional in 2026, you may have seen them before. So, for my final option this week, I'm going for "Allied." Directed by Robert Zemeckis (the filmmaker behind "Cast Away" and "Contact"), this 2016 wartime romantic drama stars Brad Pitt and Marion Cotillard. It was a box office flop and received lukewarm reviews upon release, but I believe it's worthy of a second chance.

Opening in 1942, during World War II, operative Max Vatan (Pitt) is paired with a French Resistance fighter, Marianne Beauséjour (Cotillard). The two pose as a married couple as part of a plan to assassinate a German ambassador, only for their pretend romance to become real. They settle in London, get married, have a baby, and all seems well. That is, until Max is informed by his superiors that Marianne might just be a German spy.

#3270. Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes – up to $500

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some GPUs will see bigger increases than others, while Intel and AMD remain mum on their pricing plans

Graphics are handled by an Nvidia Quadro M4000 card.

As the AI-driven global memory shortage rages on, Nvidia is notifying users that its RTX 50 series of graphics cards will see yet another significant price hike this week.

Also: I switched from Intel to AMD – here’s why I’m never going back

In August, Nvidia gave gamers and content creators fair warning that the company’s entire line of RTX 50 Series GPUs would get price increases of up to a 15%. The flagship 5090 is getting the highest: a nearly $500 increase on an already eye-watering $6,000 price tag at Best Buy. The lower-end 5050 and 5060 will get much more modest, if still grumble-worthy, $50-60 bumps, which puts the squeeze on consumers already caught between market hype and failed expectations.

Earlier iterations of the brand’s graphics cards, like the RTX 40 and RTX 30 series, won’t be directly affected by this decision. However, don’t be surprised if you see some resellers take advantage of the situation by adding their own price increases or snapping up stock to sell at a markup on the second-hand market.

Intel and AMD have been quiet about the possibility of a price hike on their own graphics cards, and neither company plans any immediate changes in response to Nvidia’s decision. Not yet, anyway. As companies like Nvidia continue to snap up the raw resources needed to manufacture AI chips and pledge their GPUs and motherboards to future AI data centers rather than the consumer market, it’s likely both companies will eventually follow suit with their own hefty increases.

Anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model between June 2024 and March 2025 is eligible to file a claim.

Dec. 21 is the last day to file a claim in Apple’s $250 million settlement over delayed Siri features, and payouts could reach $95 per eligible iPhone.

The class covers anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or any iPhone 16 model between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, the stretch when Apple was promoting a more personal Siri that hadn’t arrived yet. Filing takes a few minutes online, and each qualifying phone gets its own claim.

The iPhone 16 went on sale in September 2024 with Apple Intelligence at the center of its marketing. However, the first AI features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, several weeks later, and the most heavily promoted one, a Siri that could pull personal context from your apps, was further delayed in March 2025.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The opt-in form is available only for a limited time, so get your name in the pool before it closes. Eligible buyers have until Dec. 21 to file, and each qualifying iPhone gets its own claim.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. Apple denies all of the lawsuit’s allegations and denies that it did anything unlawful or improper.

If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme.

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

Tech > Services & Software > Online > Online Services

You get two subscriptions for the price of one. But the credits have some major limitations.

Lyft and DoorDash are teaming up for a new plan that essentially gives you two subscriptions for the price of one. But is it worth it?

The rideshare company announced the Lyft Go with DashPass subscription Thursday. Lyft says you’ll earn 8% back in credits to use toward your next Lyft ride or DoorDash order. Lyft Go with DashPass includes DashPass, DoorDash’s $10 monthly subscription — which includes no delivery fees and additional savings on select DoorDash orders.

Lyft is accounting for common mishaps. Lyft Go allows three trip cancellations per month and unlimited use of the Lost Item Fee Waiver in case you leave something behind in somebody’s car. Lyft currently charges $20 for drivers to make the return trip. And if you opt in to Lyft’s Round Up and Donate feature, Lyft will match 100% of your charitable donation.

Since Lyft Go with DashPass is $10 per month, you’ll basically get DashPass and Lyft Go for one price.

There’s also Lyft Go Core, a lower-tier monthly subscription that’s $5 per month. It won’t include DashPass, and you’ll earn 5% instead of 8% in credits. You’ll still get three ride cancellations and donation matching.

There are some caveats that may make you think twice. You won’t be able to earn credits through DoorDash orders and then redeem them with Lyft. And credits expire after 60 days. If you cancel your Lyft Go subscription, those credits may also expire sooner or become unavailable. And these subscriptions only work in the US. Lyft didn’t respond to a request for comment.

So if you earn credits within your free trial, you may want to use them before the trial ends if you’re considering canceling before your card is charged.

The new subscriptions give me pause given what we already know about US adults and subscriptions. CNET’s annual subscription survey found that only 10% of US adults are paying for meal and food delivery subscriptions and even fewer (3%) for automotive subscriptions.

However, subscription spending is up 23% compared to last year’s average of $1,080. Now, US adults are spending an average of $1,332 annually on subscriptions. However, most are paying for streaming services (61%), retail platforms (48%) and music (35%). If this isn’t a subscription you’ll use regularly enough to redeem the credits, it could be another subscription that sucks $10 out of your monthly budget. And you’ll need to do the math to see if the savings add up enough to justify paying for the rides, your DoorDash orders and the monthly subscription.

The new subscription comes the same day Amazon announced that Uber Eats is the new meal delivery perk after ending its GrubHub partnership.

Both Lyft Go with DashPass and Lyft Go Core are now available in the Lyft app nationwide, and a one-month free trial is available. However, if you already have DashPass, you can link your account with Lyft to have Lyft Go with DashPass at no extra cost. And if you have Lyft Pink, you’ll automatically be transitioned to Lyft Go with DashPass at no extra cost to the current price. However, Lyft Pink All-Access and Lyft Business Travel Rewards aren’t changing.

#3266. Oracle Just Sold $10 Billion of Stock at $116 a Share. Is the Stock a Buy at That Price?

The cloud giant maxed out its new four-year fundraising cap in five days. What did it cost shareholders?

Oracle (ORCL +0.82%) set a cap at its investor day on Oct. 28. Through fiscal 2030, it would raise up to $20 billion of new money in the stock and bond markets, which it expected to split equally between shares and debt. Five days later, on Nov. 2, it raised it all.

The cloud giant sold 86.2 million new shares at $116 each, netting around $9.9 billion. A separate $10 billion of notes, in five issues maturing from 2029 to 2046, carries interest rates between 7% and 8.65%. Both deals closed on Nov. 4.

As I write, the stock trades around $116 -- about where the new shareholders bought in, and near its lowest close in the past year. And I'd say the price Oracle got matters more than the size of the deal.

Oracle sold the stock about 11% below the $130.67 it closed at on Oct. 30, the last trading day before the deal. Shares had closed at $144.54 on investor day itself.

This gap matters because the limit was set in dollars, not shares. When I covered the cap last week, I figured $10 billion of stock at around $145 a share would mean about 69 million new shares. At $116, the same $10 billion took about 86 million -- about a quarter more.

Still, using the full limit at once has an upside. Oracle's promise spans its fiscal 2027-to-2030 investment cycle (its fiscal years end May 31), and only refinancing of existing debt sits outside it. By its own commitment, then, Oracle shouldn't have to sell more stock or new debt in the capital markets through fiscal 2030.

This should ease worries about further share sales, which Oracle relied on heavily this year. It sold $20 billion in stock using an at-the-market program in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (which ended Aug. 31, 2026) alone.

As for the dilution, the stock sale boosts Oracle's share count by about 3%, from the 3.02 billion outstanding at the end of August to about 3.11 billion. Future profits now get spread across that many more shares.

But in cash terms, the new stock is cheap to carry. At Oracle's $0.50 quarterly dividend, the 86.2 million new shares add around $172 million a year in payouts.

The notes cost far more. Across the five issues, the $10 billion carries about $780 million in interest per year. And that adds to an interest bill that was already rising fast.

Oracle's interest expense grew 29% year over year in fiscal 2026, reaching $4.6 billion. Growth then sped up to 47% in the fiscal fourth quarter and 55% in fiscal Q1, when interest expense hit $1.4 billion for the three months. Put simply, the new notes add over half a recent quarter's interest bill a year.

And the $20 billion doesn't go far at Oracle's current spending rate. The company spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal Q1, more than triple the $8.5 billion it spent a year earlier, as it expanded its cloud infrastructure business. The whole raise covers around 70% of that one quarter.

The rest needs to come from the business, which is growing fast. Oracle's operating cash flow hit a record $23 billion in fiscal Q1, up 184% year over year. Contracted revenue it hasn't recognized yet, called remaining performance obligations, reached $664 billion at the end of August. And management expects revenue to rise somewhere between 30% and 34% year over year in the fiscal second quarter.

But capital spending topped operating cash flow by around $5 billion in fiscal Q1. Oracle doesn't expect to have positive free cash flow until the second half of fiscal 2028.

At about $116, Oracle stock costs about 10 times fiscal 2028's expected adjusted earnings per share (that fiscal year ends in May 2028). For a company growing revenue by roughly 30%, I think this price is low enough to absorb an additional 3% of shares and the added interest.

That said, Oracle's borrowings were already about $125 billion at the end of August, before the new notes. If AI customers cut back before free cash flow goes positive, that debt might matter much more than the dilution.

I'd consider buying Oracle around the $116 its new shareholders paid, maybe adding shares bit by bit. Oracle expects capital spending to peak this fiscal year and next, so the highest spending isn't over yet.

#3264. What to Know About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent keeps a running profile of everyone who uses it. Yes, even if you deny it permission to do so. And by doing so, it’s effectively made Jolly, its “cute and cuddly” mascot, a harbinger of concerning security architecture.

Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

#3263. SUSE lays off 1 in 10 workers – citing AI and automation

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but explicit ties to AI remain inconsistent.

According to exclusive reporting by The Register, enterprise Linux provider SUSE will lay off one in 10 of its nearly 2,000-person workforce due to “automation and AI,” CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff via email.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

We also continue to benefit from our integrated infrastructure model. With our extensive gas gathering and processing, water super system and electrical infrastructure across New Mexico and Texas, we are able to lower our cost of supply and capture more margin across the value chain. Our complementary assets in the Anadarko, Marcellus and Rockies provide high-return investment opportunities that generate significant and durable free cash flow at low reinvestment rates.

We expect to create meaningful upside from the continued application of technology, operational efficiencies and synergy capture. Projected well economics in these basins are highly competitive and provide significant optionality between oil and gas investments. The Eagle Ford divestiture fits the same logic. Over the past several years, we have created substantial value in the Eagle Ford by lowering costs, increasing productivity and coring up our acreage position. The market valued the asset meaningfully above our internal view, so we opportunistically chose to divest the position and create immediate shareholder value. This strategic sale actually increases inventory life, lowers our breakeven, reduces our base decline and is accretive to per share cash -- free cash flow and NAV.

While our post-combination portfolio review is complete, our active portfolio management remains one of our 3 pillars to enhance go-forward value. We will not stand pat. We will continue to explore and execute ideas that are in the best interest of our shareholders. High-grading our portfolio has long been a core competency of our strategy and the multiple actions that we have executed in 2026 have further strengthened the quality, depth and returns of our portfolio. Next, I'd like to spend some time discussing our go-forward plans to enhance shareholder value through strong execution and disciplined growth underwritten by our deep high-quality inventory.

Over the next few years and beyond, we expect to generate low single-digit oil growth with conservative reinvestment rates of 45% to 60% of free cash -- of cash flow. This will result in 5% to 10% annual growth in free cash flow per share, fueling accelerated shareholder returns. This modest oil growth will be driven by the Permian, where we will direct roughly 75% of our 2027 capital program. Furthermore, as we look ahead, we're excited to get to work on the federal lease sale acreage acquired earlier this year. We expect to spud our first wells around midyear and will have meaningful production in early 2028, which will provide a noticeable step change in capital efficiency.

Synergies from the Coterra combination compound these gains as we apply shared learnings and leverage our expanded scale and infrastructure across our Delaware and Anadarko positions. Shareholders should expect sustained multiyear improvement in our capital efficiency. We are excited to accelerate and enhance our shareholder returns program through buybacks, future dividend increases and debt reduction. We see substantial value in our equity today and accelerating buybacks creates immediate and lasting value for our owners. Finally, I would like to discuss how Devon is fueling our future. As we show on Slide 4, we have 3 pillars that will guide us. Pillar 1, make Devon a better Devon.

This is a focus on improving our core business every day through engineering, innovation and technology. As a top operating company, this means increasing productivity, driving down costs, improving our margins and never settling for status quo. Pillar 2, organic growth opportunities. Leveraging our differentiated scale and skill set to capture ground floor value-creating opportunities have the potential to deliver the highest risked returns on anything we do. Examples include investing in our leasehold ground game, shale exploration, midstream enhanced value like Solitude. Pillar 3, active portfolio management.

High-grading our portfolio has long been a core component of our strategy and the multiple actions we've executed in 2026 have further strengthened the quality, depth and returns of the assets we own. Our leadership team and Board remain objective and will not hesitate to explore and execute any future opportunities that are in the best interest of the shareholders. As I wrote in my letter to shareholders, I'm extremely proud of what the team has accomplished to date, but we are never satisfied. We will not settle for anything less than being the best E&P company. With that, Shane, I'll let you take us through the numbers.

Shannon Young: Thank you, Clay, and good morning, everyone. The third quarter was our first full quarter as a combined company, and we delivered strong results. Today, I will focus on how we increased free cash flow during the quarter, accelerated our share buyback program, developed our capital-efficient preliminary outlook for 2027 and how we continue to methodically improve on our fortress balance sheet and our liquidity position. Let me first share a few thoughts on the third quarter numbers. Oil and total production were both within guidance and reached all-time highs. Importantly, we saw a strong rebound in natural gas realization to almost $2 per Mcf during the third quarter.

This was largely driven by the Permian Basin, where realizations averaged $1.74 or almost 60% of Henry Hub. At the same time, we beat our cash cost guidance midpoint by 2%. This all resulted in discretionary cash flow for the quarter of $3.5 billion, which was over 20% higher than the prior period. At the same time, we invested $1.5 billion of capital for a disciplined 43% reinvestment rate, resulting in $2 billion of free cash flow during the quarter, up meaningly from both the first and second quarters. Now turning to the remainder of the year.

For the fourth quarter, we expect oil volumes of 550,000 to 560,000 barrels per day and total production of 1.66 million to 1.7 million BOE per day. We anticipate capital will be between $1.29 billion and $1.395 billion, which puts us right near the midpoint of our 2026 guide. For the full year 2026, we are reaffirming our production ranges as well as cost and capital guidance with efficiencies offsetting modest inflationary pressures. For clarity, we have included Eagle Ford activity for the remainder of the year in all of these figures. Now to our initial outlook for 2027, which is based on current market conditions.

Assuming the Eagle Ford sale closes in early 2027, we expect oil volumes of approximately 525,000 barrels per day, total production of approximately 1.6 million BOE per day and capital of approximately $5.3 billion, of which 75% would be directed to the Permian Basin. This number excludes potential land acquisitions or ground game and our equity investment in the Solitude Pipeline, which we expect to be approximately $400 million next year. In total, we expect Devon's Solitude investment to be $500 million for the entire project, including almost $100 million we have invested year-to-date.

On a full year basis, we will have a disciplined low single-digit production growth on both oil and total volumes on less capital than the pro forma combined company spent on the same assets during 2026. In other words, 2027's capital program will show meaningful improvement in capital efficiency over 2026. That $5.3 billion of capital compares to a pro forma 2026 baseline of $5.9 billion. The Eagle Ford sale removes a little over $400 million and synergies and efficiencies, net of modest current inflation take out another $300 million.

This is partially offset by a small increase in infrastructure spending in 2027 for an investment in our Permian water super system, which has a great return and will further enhance basin margins in the future. As I'm sure many of you saw on Slide 15 of our investor deck, we project that based on current costs and commodity prices, we will generate approximately $12 billion of cash flow in 2027. And when paired with our $3.5 billion of Eagle Ford net proceeds expected in early 2027, we could have $15.5 billion of cash inflows during the year.

After funding our capital program, paying our dividends, handling debt maturities and investing in the Solitude Pipeline and our ground game, we could have $6 billion of excess free cash flow that we could use to support our buybacks and for enhancing liquidity. Turning to the balance sheet and shareholder returns. Our philosophy has not changed. Leverage at or below 1x through the cycle, strong investment-grade credit ratings, a gross debt target of approximately $9 billion, all while maintaining a strong liquidity position. In the third quarter, we retired the remaining $750 million of our term loan, bringing total debt reduction since the merger closed of $1.25 billion.

In 2027, we plan to retire an additional $1.5 billion of long-term debt and achieve our gross debt target of roughly $9 billion. Regarding third quarter shareholder returns, we paid our quarterly dividend of $0.32 per share or $366 million and repurchased nearly 9 million shares or $414 million of stock. This was over double the second quarter's buyback activity and when combined with dividends and debt retirements resulted in over 75% of free cash flow returned. We expect share repurchases to further increase to more than $1 billion during the fourth quarter, well over doubling again.

We continue to view our shares as an attractive use of our free cash flow and expect to continue to lean into repurchases during 2027. To rehighlight our framework, we intend to use up to 70% of our annual free cash flow returns, including dividends, repurchases and debt repayments. With the net proceeds from our Eagle Ford sale, we will be differential towards buybacks and work closely with the Board on the pace and timing of those buybacks during 2027. Expect to hear more on this early next year. In summary, we used our strong third quarter results to accelerate our buyback program, and Devon is set up for a great finish to 2026.

Our outlook for 2027 provides disciplined growth with a conservative reinvestment rate and increased capital efficiency. That, coupled with our Eagle Ford sale sets up nicely for robust shareholder returns program in 2027. Our balance sheet and liquidity are in great shape and will position us to thrive throughout the commodity cycle. Finally, looking forward, Devon is a multiyear rate of change story with regards to improving capital efficiency. Capital reallocation to the Permian, activity starting on our recently acquired New Mexico leasehold beginning in the second half of '27, coupled with synergy capture hitting a run rate at year-end 2027, uniquely positions Devon with visible multiyear improvements in our capital efficiency.

With that, I'll turn the call back over to the operator for our first question.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Doug Leggate from Wolfe Research.

Douglas George Blyth Leggate: Clay, the letter was quite informative. Obviously, there's a lot of news on the screen today. But I wonder if I could try and address the issue, the kind of 800-pound gorilla in the room, which is the decision after the portfolio review to basically, as you put it, we're not standing pat. But there seems to be an interpretation that the end of the portfolio review means the end of the portfolio high grading. There's a big difference between those 2.

So I wonder if you could address that and maybe share any color on how far down the road you got to exploring potential alternatives, whether it be selling other assets or whatever and what the barriers were that prevented you from doing that, whether it be value, gas prices or whatever.

Clay Gaspar: Yes. Thanks, Doug. Great question. I know that's on everyone's mind. Let me address it. As I think about the portfolio review, the opportunity that we had, it's rare in a company's history where you have 2 high-quality teams that have been working so intently to evaluate each other. And so we took full advantage. We said, look, how do we take all of the best ideas and challenging perspective from the Coterra side of the family and the Devon side of the family, and let's do a fulsome review. And we're going to be very open and transparent with our investors that we're going to be open and transparent to new ideas.

That served us in a couple of very strong and positive ways. First, we were honest about exactly what we're saying. This is incredibly objective. There were no -- nothing held back. We had rigorous debate internally. We had rigorous debate with our Board. We had great outside perspective. The other real significant advantage that we brought in is when you're so open and transparent, there's all kind of ideas that come out of the woodworks. We heard from everybody in the industry, Hey, Clay, old friend, old pal, let me help you out on this.

And I can tell you, some of it, these are all wonderful people, but some of it was certainly trying to just take advantage of the situation. We were absolutely clear that we were never desperate sellers on any of this. Starting with a really strong balance sheet and a strong financial position allowed us to capitalize on opportunities. And so it was easy to dismiss any of those that were just kind of way out of bounds on completely value destructive. But I would tell you, there was lots of ideas that came our way that we said, you know what, that's something we really need to evaluate.

And the teams ran through, again, a very rigorous process to understand the validity of those opportunities, how would it ultimately make us a better company. And I can tell you, we went down several paths. That is a strong opportunity for the company, and we took full advantage of it. Now the downside of running such an open and transparent process is it is taxing on the investors, and it is taxing on the organization in multiple levels. Let me start with the investors. From the investors' perspective, the question was very simply, are you this or you that? What's the go-forward company? Are you selling this?

I hear from one angle, you're selling this asset or combining this asset or doubling the size of this asset. And what we had to say very routinely was, guys, we are in the process. We are wide open to who we are going to be. Okay? The second part I want to address is the challenge for the organization. As you can imagine, these are all exceptionally hard-working individuals that care about their families, that think about their own best interest and have to think -- and we're challenging them with day jobs and night jobs and how do you think about the best tool or process or even piece of software as we're doing this integration.

This is 3,000 families that we're dealing with. It is a massive distraction and overhang to think that maybe it's my asset that they're talking about, sell it. So we owe it to our investors to, one, be thorough, very transparent and very open, but we also found it very important that we drew a line and said, this is the close of this period, this chapter, okay? This chapter being everything is on the table. We don't know who we are. We're going to be very open and transparent that we could go right or we could go left.

What we wanted to do is close the box on this portion and then reiterate, there's great ideas that come through our door every single day, and we remain objective and very open to whatever those opportunities are to create shareholder value as we always have been, as we always will be. So while this is the end of this chapter, this in no way means you shall never see another opportunity for us to proactively move in the shareholders' best interest. That's core and part of who we are.

And while we, it feels a little bit like we're talking out of both sides of our mouth, I think this is a clear and present turning of the page to our new go-forward 3-pillar strategy. And of course, one of those pillars is always thinking about how do we transactionally enhance shareholder value. So thanks for the question, Doug.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Neil Mehta with Goldman Sachs.

Neil Mehta: I mean, Clay, I appreciate all those comments. I would just love your perspective on how you interpret the market, right? It's been a frustrating period, I think, since the close of the transaction and the stock has underperformed over the last 6 months, and you see in the valuation as well. Do you think it's just the market is looking for clarity of who Devon is going to be on a pro forma basis? What do you make of the market reaction? And then how do you build that confidence going forward?

Clay Gaspar: Yes. Again, great question. This is on the top of folks' mind. I appreciate us hitting this right upfront. Absolutely, we are not satisfied with where -- how our shares have performed. I personally have met with nearly 200 investors in the last 6 months. Our team has met with over 300 investors. What I would tell you is there is not a single monolithic view of here's what we need to do. But what we hear very often, especially from those investors that have probably better alignment with our long-term shareholder value creation focus is we need to know who you are and what you're doing. Are you pure play this or focused on that?

Are you more gas-oriented or oil oriented? Are you doubling down in this basin in that basin? And meanwhile, we're going to sit on the sidelines, near the hoop and ready to understand who you are and then be able to make an intelligent investment decision. So what we hope is after this very methodical, very transparent process that we are open with the investors, this is it, this is who we are. This is the opportunity, the investment opportunity that we present. And by the way, we're going to work on getting better every single day for the best interest of the shareholders.

So I think that clears the path to close this valuation gap, and we look forward to being on the road as soon as Monday to meet with more investors, get that feedback and really talk to the opportunity ahead and really, I think, excite the organization and the shareholders about our clear path forward.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Arun Jayaram with JPMorgan.

Arun Jayaram: Clay, maybe just a follow-up to Neil's question. You've clearly done an exhaustive review of your asset base post the merger and as part of this portfolio review. I was wondering if you could help us think about your view of the intrinsic value of the company. Your stock right now is trading in the low 40s. And maybe just help us think about where you perceive that gap is? What do you think the market is missing? And maybe Shane could talk a little bit around your thoughts around the buyback and how you maybe take advantage of this perceived dislocation in the share price.

Clay Gaspar: Yes. Thanks for the question, Arun. This is, I think there's 2 points to it. One, I think what the shareholders have missed is a clearly articulated strategy on here's who we are and here's how we're going forward. And hopefully, we've taken the first step in delivering that today. I think the second piece, and Shane is welcome to pile on this. We've been very clear. We're going to move differentially towards share buybacks. We see our -- this is a great opportunity for us to buy back shares. We've talked about $1 billion-plus share buyback in the fourth quarter and then accelerating from there beyond that.

We have a really a great opportunity to invest in ourselves in this period, and we're not going to lose that opportunity. Shane, other comments?

Shannon Young: Yes, Clay, and Arun, look, as we sit here today, we see very compelling value in our shares in the marketplace. And we believe that buying our stock is an attractive use of our free cash flow, and we just happen to be in a fortunate position where we have a lot of free cash flow coming. And so that's why we've accelerated. We've really leaned in leaning in last quarter, the third quarter, continuing to lean in this quarter and frankly, probably leaning in further in 2027 as we go. I mean I can tell you, for one, cannot wait to be out of our blackout period so that we can continue to get after it.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Devin McDermott with Morgan Stanley.

Devin McDermott: So I wanted to shift over to that capital efficiency, attractive rate of change. And one of the drivers of that is just the synergy and integration opportunity. And alongside the release today, you did take up the 2027 expectations. So I was wondering if you can just talk about where you're seeing delivery of synergy faster than planned, some of the milestones you're focused on for next year? And should we take this progress and accelerated timing as potential upside to that $1 billion target as we look out over the next year or 2?

Clay Gaspar: Devin, I really appreciate the question. I was afraid we're going to have to just talk about the portfolio or the lack of moves on the portfolio all day. But I can tell you the team is doing some incredibly, incredibly good work that we probably get -- could get buried in all in this news flow. So man, I'm incredibly proud of the team. We are ahead of track. As you saw in the projections, and Blake is here, he can talk about some of the specifics on what's going on in his view of that rate of change that's incredibly exciting.

Blake Sirgo: Yes. Thanks, Devin. Really excited to be here and be able to talk about just, frankly, a lot of the wins we've had since bringing these 2 companies together. Our operating teams have come together really fast, and it's really showing in our results. Right out of the gates, we leaned in hard to Devon's embedded AI tools. And really, what those have allowed us to do is just capture best practices, identify top performance and then immediately extrapolate it. We're currently running 34 rigs and 9 crews. There's a lot to extrapolate on, and we're seeing the results in the field. Just since coming together, the amount of wells we're simul-fracking has increased from 68% to 75%.

As we walk into 2027, our average lateral length is going up over 10%. That's on the back of 53 4-mile wells across 4 different basins. You roll all that up, and it's allowing us to deliver an expected dollar per foot in 2027 around $750 a foot. That's all in drilling, completions, facilities, flowback. That's the number we use to make an investment decision. And at the same time, we are leaning into larger fracs driven by our AI subsurface models. We're adding surfactants, and we're continuing to fight off cost pressures. So when you add all that up, it is truly more for less.

That's what we're delivering in the field, and we just, we couldn't be more excited to see where the teams take us next.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Betty Jiang with Barclays.

Wei Jiang: I want to talk about and ask about the leasehold, ground game, the spending that you guys are doing. Can you maybe talk about how you underwrite the return of that investment? And how does that compare to drilling or buying back stock? And how does that, the durability of this leasehold spend? And how does that impact your long-term inventory or replenish what you guys draw down every year?

Robert Lowe: Yes. Betty, this is Trey. Thank you for the question. We continue to be excited about what we're doing on the ground game across the board. We've really focused a lot of that investment in the Permian Basin and the Delaware where we already operate. And one of the things that we came out of the merger with was a really aggressive growth team based out of our Midland office, and they have been very active picking up what we think are some of the best returning dollars that we've spent.

And to the second point that you raised, all of these investments, whether it's our ground game, our infrastructure investments or whether or not we're drilling a new well, these all compete against each other on a heads-up basis. And we continue to look at all of those both on a PVI basis, rate of return and a net present value basis. And so the team has a really, I would say, sophisticated and now mature process for evaluating the financials on those.

But you're going to continue, just as we signaled in this earnings release to lean in and to find new opportunities, and we're excited about the opportunities that the team has been able to uncover, and we expect to do more of that in the Permian.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Neal Dingmann with William Blair.

Neal Dingmann: Clay, my first question is -- or my only question is for the organic opportunity specifically. Could you speak to the type, you mentioned this, I think, in the prepared remarks that you listed, the type of some midstream investments. I know you have some current and maybe looking at some non-E&P ventures and then even exploration. I mean there's a host of things in there. I was wondering how, what type of things these days you find attractive out there.

Clay Gaspar: Yes, Neal, I think this is really important. When we think about how do we expand the multiple, our trading multiple and really create value for the shareholders. I think one of the things that E&P companies can really do is, one, display a high-quality and deep inventory. And then as a complement to that, display a capability to creatively and constructively invest for the extension of that quantity and quality of inventory. And so when I think about that, we did a really strong exercise really over the last 1.5 years, kind of broadening what that can mean. Does that just mean how do we create more oil inventory or BOE inventory?

And what we really came up with is how do we create more really strong investments so that the product we create is sustainable free cash flow. And so what are those opportunities as we broaden the sense to really think about how do we invest our precious dollars into systems, into processes into opportunities that allow a full cycle return that's competitive, that's accretive and that really extends the quantity and quality of inventory. And so that's how we started really opening up to think about, for example, the Solitude Pipeline. If we were just solely focused on driving oil production, Solitude would have never ranked.

What we saw was an opportunity for us to lean in to some of the best gas inventory in the world was already under our feet in the Delaware Basin. The challenge was it was constrained by a limited infrastructure system. And so we went to our good friends and partners at WhiteWater, put this concept together and really created something that's groundbreaking, that's forward leaning and is incredibly value creative. As we look through the full cycle of that value creation, that's how we create value for our shareholders. There's lots of other things on the list. We'll have more to come in time.

I just want to put that placeholder together that leveraging our scale, our differentiated scale and skill set can really create value above and beyond just drilling that next horizontal well. And so as we've opened that aperture, we have lots of exciting things kind of on the list as Trey just talked about, every one of these things has to compete full cycle on a fully risked basis for capital. And I think that's the work that we've done over the last year, in particular, has really differentiated our ability to compare apples and Chevrolets and really get to the heart of what's the best investment for our shareholders.

And so more to come on that, some exciting opportunities, but know that we hold these to an exceptionally high standard that on a full cycle risk basis, they have to deliver return to the bottom line.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Phillip Jungwirth with BMO.

Phillip Jungwirth: I think the multiyear outlook you presented here of low single-digit oil growth, 45%, 60% reinvestment with improving capital efficiency and 5% to 10% free cash flow per share is highly competitive across peers, can be achieved at a conservative price deck. The question is just more in the portfolio review. I know you ran a lot of different scenarios. So I was hoping you could talk about why this portfolio outlook is a better longer-term outcome for the company versus what you could have achieved with less scale or fewer assets.

Clay Gaspar: Yes. I mean when you look at Slide 8 of our deck, the left side of it, we talk about some of the attributes of the Permian, and it's really the same attribute list that we started looking at when we start talking about other assets. We think about the scale, the depth of inventory, kind of that ability to create value. We have this recent merger. We're just on the front end of capturing all of these synergies, specifically in the Permian and the Anadarko, but I can tell you, it doesn't limit there. We're learning things and transferring skills every single day between all of these assets.

And so when we think about how do we build a better company, we think about these characteristics and we think about how do they stack up, not just for this quarter or calendar year, but as we run through this next decade of opportunity and we continue to build for the future of Devon, how do these attributes really stack up? We love the Eagle Ford. It's a high-quality asset. But I can tell you that the steepness of the base decline was very challenging, and it dragged the overall maintenance capital of the organization. The inventory as it became challenged late in life, but teams are incredible. We're going to drive more value.

We're going to get smarter every single day. But I can tell you that the differential value creation that we were able to make was probably in our rearview mirror, and this was more valuable to the market than internally. I have no hesitation.

And when we see that opportunity, we're going to act on it, accelerate that value for shareholders and then go redeploy that into more share buybacks, future dividend funding and then, of course, building liquidity in this volatile industry displayed over the last few days in perfect form, you certainly want to have your financial house in order and a little bit of cash on the sidelines never hurts in this business as future opportunities come our way.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Josh Silverstein with UBS.

Joshua Silverstein: Clay, you mentioned the significant gas growth coming out of the Permian and your asset contributing to that. I'm curious how that makes you think about the value of your Marcellus asset, capital allocation there and the role that has in your portfolio.

Clay Gaspar: Yes. To me, it's exciting. This is a perfect example of you have one side of the family that's lived with this asset that knows this asset. And then you have another side of the family that's brand new to the asset and have our own kind of maybe outside-in-looking perspectives. When those teams really sat down and started just tearing apart what's the inventory, what's the quality, how does it compete? What's the upside potential? Where do we take these synergies and apply them there? How do we think about the evolving technology, both operational and digital to further enhance value?

How do we think about vertical integration and application of all of the tools in our toolbox to create more value, we get pretty excited. And I think there is true incremental value creation in that asset. There's no doubt about it. It's a coveted asset that like all of our assets are. And so understanding how that the market values it. And what I could tell you is I feel very confident that we have exceptional upside value in this asset that we will create for the shareholders. And again, I'll go back to the words that we used in our prepared remarks, the leadership remains objective on any and all of these assets as opportunities present going forward.

But man, our first and foremost priority it's Pillar 1, make Devon a better Devon. It's a perfect example of how do we drive even further value from this high-quality assets.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of John Freeman with Raymond James.

John Freeman: The Slides 19 and 20 are really interesting in the deck on the lateral lengths and the progress that you all are making. And just trying to make sure that I'm not, that these aren't like apples and oranges slides I'm looking at, but it would appear that based on the guidance for the Delaware in '27, it sort of implies about $765 a foot. And as you all move toward more and more of the program being 3, 4, 5-mile laterals are all like the 4 miles you'll highlight $630 a foot. Like if we look out 2, 3 years, I mean, is there anything I'm missing?

Otherwise, just as the program gets longer on average, you've got a pretty good line of sight to where that cost per foot is going to go down, I mean, pretty dramatically.

Blake Sirgo: Yes, John, this is Blake. Happy to take that one. Our teams just continue to push the edge on what we can do in the long lateral game. This really started up in the Marcellus, where kind of driven by our land position, you had to get creative on how you're going to access untouched rock, and we started putting 5-mile wells in the ground, and it wasn't long before the other basins were chomping to get there also. So the name of the game is try to grab that capital efficiency everywhere we can with lateral lengths. We're really excited about the 4 milers going in the Permian. We're calling out with some pretty creative well geometries.

They're 2x2 U-turns. So they're 4-mile wells, but it actually has a U-turn in the middle. And where our acreage position is really defined and maybe we don't have the opportunities to extend the acreage, we can still chase these long lateral efficiencies with really creative wellbore geometries. And so I think you see that in these numbers. You see it in the 53 4-mile wells we're going to execute next year. And my hope is exactly what you said. We're going to keep pushing the limits on this, which will, of course, drive our dollar per foot down.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Scott Gruber with Citigroup.

Scott Gruber: It sounds like the low single-digit growth can be sustained here for several years at flattish capital. But I'm curious on the drivers and how would you compare the drivers? So how would you compare the benefit from developing the newly acquired federal acreage and overall well productivity relative to base decline management relative to more kind of process-driven efficiency gains? Kind of how would you rank the key drivers behind delivering some growth at flattish capital?

Clay Gaspar: Yes. Scott, I appreciate the question. This is -- this was a difference between how Devon saw the world and Coterra saw the world. And this was one of the outstanding questions that honestly, we needed to do the work. Number one, you need to understand the portfolio. Two, you need to really think about the macro, what is the world calling for? Do these barrels really need to go incrementally, incremental barrels onto the market. And when we did the work, we came back together and we said, you know what, we got the quality and the longevity of the inventory.

We got the confidence in our ability to recreate quantity and quality of inventory beyond this that we can lean in. And that was different than what we saw from Devon. What you heard from me, say, even a year ago was, man, it feels like the world is pretty saturated in oil. I don't know that there's an incremental need for our incremental barrels. And also objectively, we didn't have the length of inventory that the new combined company does. Part of that is certainly the benefit of the Coterra merger, certainly the acquisition of the federal lease sale.

But I can tell you, it's also the incredible synergies that we're creating from this combined company extend that inventory run life. And what it gives you is the confidence to say, hey, we still have 12-plus years of fully understood delineated opportunities, really 15-plus when you start thinking about some of the downhole potential that we're continuing to work today, that gives us confidence that we can accelerate some of that for the shareholders in a market that I can tell you, looks pretty radically different than it did a year ago when it comes to inventory, global storage and supply-demand numbers. And so that's how we feel good about the low single-digit growth.

You know that's a rough guide. The oil side is where we start. Certainly, BOEs are going to be even higher than that. And then, of course, we talked about the very impressive 5% to 10% growth when you talk about per share of free cash flow. Shane, is there something else you'd like to add on that?

Shannon Young: Well, yes. Look, Scott, I would just say, as I was saying, we looked at a whole range of scenarios that we could potentially look at. And we found that low single-digit growth actually maximized free cash flow over the near and the longer term, particularly with, as you highlighted, some of the paybacks on some of the newer acreage acquired in New Mexico. The other thing I would say I want to just make sure it's clear, we didn't lean into low single-digit growth strategy because oil price was higher. This is something that's very durable. Down to $60, $70 a barrel. We still have very, very competitive reinvestment rates on this capital program.

So it's something that's not just for the oil price we see today, but frankly, through the cycle.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chris Baker with Evercore ISI.

Christopher Baker: You all described the Anadarko, Marcellus and Rockies as complementary assets that have strategic value to Devon. And you started to talk about this play a minute ago with the Marcellus. Would just love to hear more about the strategic value that you all see in the Anadarko and Rockies, and how you plan to capture it.

Clay Gaspar: Yes. I think the Anadarko is one that's, it's just very obvious. There is so much synergy potential. You look at the quality of the wells that Coterra was drilling, you look at the D&C cost from the Devon side, you start marrying those things together and it's like, wow, I have to tell you, 6 months ago, I was excited about Anadarko Basin, but I feel much more excited today seeing what that combination, and this is a perfect synergy example, how do you combine 2 great teams and take the best of and really lean that together, it's pretty compelling.

You compound that, we've talked for the last 6 months about the potential of the midstream opportunity both sides of the history have opportunities to renegotiate some pretty long-dated contracts. We're working with counterparties now. I think there's real value creation and more vertical integration. And there's no doubt about it. I mean the Anadarko Basin being more gas-oriented in a very good position in the country geographically can really satisfy a lot of that Gulf Coast call for gas as well as all of the electrification that we see a lot around the planet. So you put all that together and it's like, wow, this is really compelling. And there's no doubt about it.

There's a lot of interest in the market. We are absolutely 100% aware. What I would tell you is we look at this as we can create more value than what we see in the market today. And as with anything, we remain really focused on driving value first. When I think about the Rockies, we have 2 complementary pieces of business there. The Williston, man, still it's just the same story that Blake was talking about with the Williston -- excuse me, with the Marcellus. In the Williston, we're driving longer laterals. We're improving well cost. It's in that graphic.

I think that might have been Slide 20 or so on what we're doing with well costs, extending those laterals. We do have a preferred, a little better midstream position there, extracting more value. And I think that just is a great opportunity for us to also create incremental value from a very oily-oriented asset that generates a ton of free cash flow. The Powder is unique. It's probably, it is the least mature of all of our assets. It gets the benefit of all of this knowledge and the technological innovation, both on the operational and digital side.

And then those long laterals, I was in a meeting the other day and the team pointed to a map and they said, this is the shorter laterals over here. And I said, wait, I thought that was the 3-mile laterals. And they said, yes, yes, that's the 3-mile. And I said, wait, when did short become 3-mile? And they said, no, no, standard's now 4 mile, and we're going out further than that. So again, operational innovation is really unlocking future potential in these incredible portfolios.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Gabe Daoud from Truist.

Gabe Daoud: I appreciate all the responses so far and the shareholder letter very informative. Yes. I was hoping we could maybe just talk a little bit about Permian inventory. You mentioned earlier the 12 years inventory overall. But could you maybe just unpack the Permian, some of the deeper zone testing that you guys are kind of embarking on and maybe just highlight what you're seeing in the Woodford and maybe even the Penn Shale.

Robert Lowe: Yes, Gabe, this is Trey. Appreciate the question. We continue to be just amazed all the time with what we're finding in the Permian from the entire stack. We are going to continue to work through our inventory. We're collecting data. We're obviously watching all of the industry activity that we see, both in the Woodford and the Penn and the, all the deep Wolfcamp as well. We will start to appraise that. We're going to start understanding where it fits in our longer-term portfolio as we derisk these things. It will continue to be evaluated over the next year.

But strategically, our development programs are going to move forward in the way that we have been, which is co-development, maximizing the value of the assets that we have. And we also, just as a reminder, we have a giant position in the BLM lease acreage that we just picked up last year that we're going to insert into the program this year as well. And so we've got lots of moving pieces. We're continually looking at the upside. We think it's promising. The asset teams are excited about it, and we're excited about where that will take us over a longer period of time.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Matt Portillo from TPH.

Matthew Portillo: Picking up on your comments for Solitude and gas resource in the Permian. As we add up the pipeline capacity that's been announced and look at impacts to egress out of the Permian over the next 5 years, it looks like we'll probably see a 50% increase in capacity. I was just curious, given your size and scale in the basin and your position on pipes, what your perspective is for your oil cut for your assets through the end of the decade kind of thoughts around the zone mix moving forward, as I know that's been quite topical. And then should the market expect Devon's gas production to keep up with that industry CAGR from an egress perspective?

Clay Gaspar: Yes. So Matt, there's a lot there. Let me start with, we are, the deep and high-quality inventory we have today is driven by the oil economics, okay? So right now, with the price realizations, even with a relative run-up in gas price, man, we are limiting our gas production for much over the last couple of years, we've tried to really, really limit our amount of gas production. And every quarter, it continues to increase. It is, there is such a hydrocarbon-rich environment in the Permian Basin that it's incredibly valuable. The challenge has been the realized prices aren't where we wanted them to be. So we made the proactive step.

And then when we get this locked in, when the pipe is in place, we lock in our value, we're able to maximize the value potential of that, not on the Waha side, but on the Gulf Coast side, that really unlocks even further potential kind of firming up the realizations. And that's where I think the upside is just unlimited in the position that we have. So incredibly excited about that position. When I think about our current just under 50% oil cut, there's a few things at work. As we start going a little bit deeper into the section, certainly, that will be more gas oriented.

And then the natural tendency of these, the gas oil ratios of these wells also get a little gassier in time. So that will continue to migrate that way. But until we have the real value creation steps in place, you're not going to see us move differentially into gas production. But when those real material steps are in place and we have the full realized prices, I don't know of another basin in the U.S. that will compete for gas valuations because it's always going to come with a nice complement of oil that will probably carry the economics and you essentially get all the gas for free. So I think there's tremendous value creation.

Our position, specifically on the Delaware side of the Permian, I think there's just so much more runway and we get so excited about the additional value creation and the steps that we're making proactively to really get the true value of these precious resources for the U.S.'s benefit and beyond. So we look forward to more steps on that and more value creation from this incredible resource.

Operator: Our final question comes from Kevin MacCurdy with Pickering Energy Partners.

Kevin MacCurdy: For my question, I wanted to come back to the ground game spending in 2027. If I'm doing the math right, I think you've implied about $500 million, which is higher than the historic run rate. And maybe you can expand on the opportunities you're seeing there and how that's different than before? And is this part of the lateral length increase? Or are these brand-new locations?

Clay Gaspar: Yes. I'll start and then Trey may want to add some comments. This is another, I would put it in the category of synergies. So Devon didn't have a Midland office. Coterra had a Midland office. And Trey talked about the outstanding team that we have on the ground doing this work, and we've really leaned in. In fact, in 2026, we'll have about $500 million, $600 million. Is that right, Shane?

Clay Gaspar: Yes. And on that bulk, about $500 million of investment. These are incredible -- over $600 million of investment in 2026. These are incredible returns. As you talked about, maybe it's extending that lateral, which we see from Blake's slides, the value creation opportunities there. Maybe it's some trade without even cash out the door that enhances our position that moves opportunities that a little further out in our portfolio to something more near term. We always have a little more incremental value creation perspective.

We've talked about the very sophisticated infrastructure we have from gas gathering, processing, the water infrastructure, that can change the economics of these positions, and we're really leaning forward and that team in Midland is doing a fantastic job. So we'll continue to lean in. It counters about $500 million is the plan for next year. But honestly, I hope that, that team continues to be as successful as they are because it's such phenomenal returns, full cycle returns on those investments.

We're taking stuff down at roughly about $2 million to $3 million per stick last time I looked at the math, which is highly competitive and exciting and something that, honestly, we're doing better than either legacy company, and it's a great synergistic win for the combined team.

Robert Lowe: The only thing I would add to that is the pace of change or the rate of change that we're seeing in the Permian right now continues to give us confidence. That performance improvement from the long laterals that Blake mentioned, the success we're having with surfactants today with a lot of the other subsurface work really gives us the ability to marry that up with our infrastructure and our scale position that we have in the basin, be really competitive in our ground game. And you marry that with this team that we've got that have been, they have the mandate to go help find those opportunities, and that's driving some real success for us across the business.

And we've got all of these synergies coming from the merger as well as just the cultural benefits that we're seeing right now around technical excellence and putting our people together and they're finding new opportunities for us to go pursue these new ideas, and that's what's paying off. And that's where we're trying to give everyone a peek at where we think we're headed with our ground game. Great question, though. Thank you.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3261. The Swift Observatory Dropped Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

NASA believes most of the space telescope burned up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may have made their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, has reached the end of its journey. Launched into orbit in 2004, the space telescope completed an extraordinary 22-year mission when it plunged back into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope hit the atmosphere Wednesday at 7:39 am ET, just four hours after the space agency predicted.

The space telescope entered orbit over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, just west of Malaysia. NASA says that most of the space telescope likely burned up upon reentry but that some components may have survived.

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work.

It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended in 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA extended its operations to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, Nousek said.

The volume of science research conducted using Swift’s data is difficult to match. According to NASA, Swift scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said.

The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.
