#3238. A Wall-Mounted Smart Garden Is Peak Winter Decor (and a Great Gift)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I tested Modern Sprout's handsome Growframe for a pop of green during fall and winter.

My pursuit of good houseplant tools means I’m always looking for shops and resources. That led me to Modern Sprout, a Chicago-based online store that sells plants and plant-care accessories. When they reached out offering a chance to test some of its high-design indoor garden tech, I decided to see what, if anything, is worth considering for your houseplant needs or as a place to get gifts for the plant parents in your life. I found a few pleasant surprises.

Whether I’m tending to houseplants in winter or gardening in summer, I’m always looking for tools to improve plant care. For houseplants in particular, this means watering, trimming, fertilizing, occasionally repotting and providing as much real estate in sunny windows as possible. When that’s not enough, I harness the power of full-spectrum LED grow lights, so I can have greenery in practically every room of my apartment.

A quick look at Modern Sprout’s website shows it sells most of what you’d expect from a boutique plant nursery: live plants, potting soil, gardening accessories, grow lights, grow kits, candles, bird feeders and gift sets. While Modern Sprout carries plenty of its own products, it also curates items from other small businesses instead of relying on large mainstream gardening brands. This is a nice bonus for folks who prefer to support smart business owners. Modern Sprout also offers wholesale accounts, so you might even see it at a nursery near you.

For my tests, I stuck to the Modern Sprout brand, which is also available on Amazon. Since I review a lot of smart home gear, I wanted to try out the Smart Landscape Growframe ($229) and compare it with other plant light options I use. I also wanted to see if Modern Sprout’s tools are any good, so I rounded out my experience with three essentials behind effective houseplant care: Pruning Shears ($20), a Glass Watering Can ($48) and Dissolving Plant Food Sheets ($20).

I don’t think anything could’ve prepared me for the size of the Smart Landscape Growframe: 32.1 inches long, 11.5 inches tall and 5.3 inches deep. For some context, that’s wider than my kitchen table and large enough to require a careful survey of my home to find a suitable location. I found a nice spot above my stairs next to the front door.

Additionally, its durable powder-coated steel frame weighs an incredible 8 pounds. That’s roughly the weight of a gallon of milk, which makes wall mounting tricky. I agree with Modern Sprout’s recommendation to place the mounting screws in studs, so you’ll need a stud finder, a level, and a power drill if you want it on the wall. You can use drywall anchors, but they aren’t included.

Make sure you visually line up the Growframe’s mounting holes with your marks before driving screws into the wall. This is easier with a second person, but I managed it alone. However, I relied purely on my measurements and had to redo the screws after one was slightly off. I suggest marking one stud first, then holding the planter and using a level to see where the other should go. Similarly, keep in mind that the 9-foot power cord needs to reach an outlet.

The app isn’t complex and is really easy to use. I really like that there are preset schedules for shade, partial sun and full sun light levels — these options always start at 8 a.m., providing 8, 12 and 16 hours of lighting at different intensities, respectively. The presets aren’t customizable, so you must use one of the app’s two other scheduling options to adjust the timing and other settings. I noticed that toggling a preset works as intended, but closing and reopening the menu shows an inactive toggle — a minor visual bug that doesn’t seem to affect the feature. (It might even get patched by the time you read this review.)

You can also set a schedule using specific times of day in the Growframe device menu. While this particular scheduling menu lacks an option to tie the lighting controls to sunrise and sunset, you can find that on the Scenario tab. (Sunrise/sunset automation isn’t necessary for most tropical plants and herbs people put in the planter, but it’s nice to have a temperate lighting option that changes throughout the year.)

The Scenario tab offers a few automation options based on device status, scheduling and weather changes, plus a way to set up manual Tap-to-Run automations. Beyond that, there isn’t much else to the app, which makes sense and aligns with the company’s goal of keeping things simple. However, folks wanting smart home integrations with a platform like Home Assistant or Samsung SmartThings might be better off using a smart plug with a different grow light brand.

Speaking of grow lights, the full-spectrum unit inside the top of the Smart Landscape Growframe can reach up to 1,480 lumens, which is very bright considering most plants in the planter will be within 6 inches or less. Given the size limit on the plants you can put in the planter, I doubt you’ll have any issues with giving your plants enough light. I want to note that the adhesive holding one of the grow light strips in my sample unit came loose during shipping, but it was easy enough to reattach.

Planting in the Smart Landscape Growframe is fairly easy. It comfortably holds up to seven potted plants (2- to 3-inch pots), though I ended up putting five 4-inch potted herbs in my setup. One pot in particular is a little taller than the planter box lip, but it doesn’t bother me.

Be mindful of pot size in the planter, as rims that press up against the side can cause water to overflow onto the floor, as it did with mine. The best solution is to remove a little soil from overfilled pots and to add a small notch or hole in a side of the pot that drains into the basin.

The potted herbs I got from my local garden center needed a little trimming before I could put them in the Smart Landscape Growframe, so it was a good opportunity to try out the Pruning Shears. I’m a huge fan of the all-metal design, which is easily one of the most comfortable pairs of gardening shears I’ve used. The nifty locking latch at the end of the handle isn’t metal — it doesn’t need to be — but it’s easy to use and doesn’t require any fiddling.

I also love the needle-nose blades, which are easy to maneuver into tight spaces when trimming dead growth off plants — they are great for trimming all of my herbs. Although I’ll admit that the densely packed chives tested my patience, that’s hardly the shears’ fault.

Of the items I tested, the glass watering can was my least favorite. For instance, the borosilicate glass may be more durable than other types of glass, but it’s still glass and still fragile. I’m not sure if I trust my clumsy self with it when I water my plants. Similarly, the 1-quart size is great for folks caring for a handful of plants, but it can’t keep up with the gallon-size watering can that I sometimes empty completely just to water my dwarf lemon tree in a large container.

Another issue I had with the glass watering can was the upper rim. While I like that the flared rim makes it easy to fill from my bathroom sink, it can get in the way when watering the Growframe. This is especially tedious when you need to tilt the watering can nearly vertical to get the last drops out. Fortunately, you can see when the water is almost gone, but that’s the only real advantage it has over my normal watering can.

I often put off fertilizing houseplants because it feels like a hassle. My main reason is that most of the carnivorous plants I grow don’t like fertilizer, so I skip it on other houseplants. (I get around this with plant food spikes, but I’m hardly consistent at that either.) A secondary reason is that keeping the fertilizer out where I’ll use it isn’t the best use of space in my apartment. While Modern Sprout’s Dissolving Plant Food Sheets don’t really solve the former problem, they’re very convenient for the latter.

Just like when I tested dishwasher detergent sheets, I really like how easy it is to toss Modern Sprout’s fertilizer into the watering can. A full sheet treats a gallon and has perforations so you can tear it into segments to fit your watering can. Since the glass watering can holds one quart, I needed only one-quarter of a sheet. The sheets dissolved a little slowly, and I had to stir them for a minute or two before no fragments were left.

I’m a fan of the seaweed sheets, which are a great option for plant food that isn’t entirely a collection of processed chemicals. Despite the seaweed ingredient, the sheets don’t explicitly state they’re certified organic, so keep that in mind if you use them for herbs or microgreens.

All of the Modern Sprout products I tested have a premium design and build quality that makes them easy to recommend for people who value form as much as function. I consider the Pruning Shears the best value in the bunch. They feel incredibly sturdy and capable for $20 and are a huge step up from my $10 Vivosun Gardening Scissors in every way. I haven’t tested Modern Sprout Bypass Hand Pruners, but I suspect they’ll easily rival the Fiskars Shears I use for thicker growth.

While $229 is a lot to ask for the Smart Landscape Growframe, keep in mind that premium heavy-duty steel planters without smart lighting already cost more than those made from other materials. Likewise, more affordable — and more powerful — grow lights are on the market, but Modern Sprout’s intuitive app includes every scheduling and customization feature I consider essential. Even people who don’t use other smart home gear should find it easy to navigate.

I think the Dissolving Plant Food Sheets are a fairly nice option for seaweed-based fertilizers, but the 20-pack will treat only 20 gallons of water at the normal dilution. This makes the sheets generally more expensive per feeding than liquid kelp fertilizers from brands like TPS Nutrients and Grow Queen. That said, Modern Sprout is more convenient to measure, and it won’t cause a liquid or powdery mess if you knock the package over. It’s a great gift, but not necessarily for an enthusiast with a large collection of houseplants.

I wouldn’t buy the Glass Watering Can, but I don’t think it’s a bad product. It’s undeniably attractive, but $48 is more than most. I’ll stick with my cheaper, larger plastic watering can. Overall, Modern Sprout suits folks with higher budgets or as an attractive gift option for your favorite plant nerd.

#3237. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3236. You Should Update to iOS 27.2 Now to Patch Hundreds of Bugs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The update fixes some bugs that could expose your sensitive iPhone data or worse.

Apple released iOS 27.2 on Monday, Oct. 26, just a few days after the launch of the iPhone Duo. While iOS 27.2 brings Siri AI to more languages and updates a few other features, it also patches 141 bugs and security issues, including some that could allow a third party to access data or run commands on your iPhone or leave your device inoperable.

You can download iOS 27.2 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

According to Apple’s release notes, iOS 27.2 patches dozens of issues across your iPhone. Some of these issues can cause some serious problems for you and your device.

Nine of these bugs address issues that could lead to kernel corruption on your device. The kernel is the core of your device’s operating system, and kernel corruption can cause your device to freeze or crash. The blue screen of death, for example, could be caused by kernel corruption.

Apple also wrote that seven of these bugs could lead to arbitrary code execution. That means the bug could allow a third party to steal your data or use your device for other nefarious purposes.

The update addresses a lot of other bugs, including one that you might run into if you plug a malicious USB into your device. Apple didn’t write that any of these bugs were being actively exploited, but you should still update to iOS 27.2 now to give yourself the most protection.

For as many bugs as 27.2 fixes, it’s actually a slight decrease from earlier updates. Last month’s iOS 27 update patched even more bugs at 157. The number of bug fixes in both iOS updates are unusual based on data over the past few years. In iOS 26, the most bug fixes included in an update was 88 with iOS 26.6. The update with the next highest number of patches was iOS 18.4 with 75.

Apple didn’t say why there’s been an uptick in the number of bug fixes in iOS updates. Artificial intelligence has been used recently to find and address huge numbers of software bugs; however, that doesn’t appear to be the cause behind the surge in iOS 27.2 or iOS 27. Apple usually notes when a bug is found with the help of AI, yet OpenAI is mentioned four times in iOS 27.2’s release notes, and Claude’s Anthropic is only mentioned thrice.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to my request to comment.

For more iOS news, here’s what you should know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1. You can also check out our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

#3232. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

This includes additional regulated generation investment in Kentucky required to meet continued increases in potential demand growth. This represents $6 billion to $7 billion of incremental investment opportunity through 2032, which includes $3.5 billion to $4.5 billion through 2030. This investment opportunity alone supports meaningful upside that could increase our EPS CAGR to over 9% through 2030. In addition, we see at least $6 billion to $9 billion of potential future investment from Invitium Energy through 2032. These amounts reflect PPL's 51% ownership share and are based on 5 gigawatts of executed reservation agreements for combined-cycle natural gas turbines.

And those investment opportunities exclude any bridge solutions such as fuel cells or battery storage, though Invitium Energy also provides meaningful shareowner value potential. And focusing on Invitium Energy, we're pleased to announce that Invitium and QTS have agreed to collaborate on about 2 gigawatts of generation capacity in Pennsylvania, which I'll cover in more detail on the next slide. This represents a significant milestone for Invitium and an important step toward converting strong customer demand into tangible generation projects. Just as importantly, these projects help meet rising energy demand while strengthening the PJM grid and supporting long-term energy affordability. Our updated business plan excludes any financial impacts of Invitium, including the QTS announcement.

Let's turn to Slide 5 to provide some additional details about the Invitium Energy announcement. Invitium signed a letter of intent with QTS to be their generation solution provider in portions of Pennsylvania. Under that LOI, we've agreed with QTS on all key commercial terms for approximately 2 gigawatts of generation capacity for its Salem Township data center project with a 20-year initial term allowing for multiple 5-year renewals. We also signed a cost reimbursement agreement that provides reimbursement and risk mitigation for specified development costs and commitments in the event certain approvals and conditions for project development are not achieved.

The proposed generation portfolio includes 2 combined-cycle natural gas plants, complemented by fuel cells and battery storage or BESS, with the final technology mix between the fuel cells and BESS still being finalized. Using current cost estimates of $2,500 to $3,500 per kW, 2 gigawatts of generation would represent an estimated $5 billion to $7 billion of total project investment with PPL's 51% share representing approximately $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion. The fuel cell and BESS generation could be online as early as 2029, and the combined-cycle plants are expected to be online in 2032 and 2033. This structure aligns with the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge and Governor Shapiro's clean and firm energy requirements under Pennsylvania's GRID standards.

The structure provides a regulated like risk profile designed to deliver stable, predictable and growing long-term earnings and cash flows. A fixed monthly payment with annual escalation covers the return of and on invested capital and fixed operating costs. Variable payments cover fuel and other operating costs when the plants run. The ultimate data center customer will also be required to meet minimum credit ratings or credit support requirements, mitigating counterparty credit risk. In summary, the combination of the negotiated key commercial terms and the cost reimbursement agreement creates a durable foundation for disciplined investment, attractive long-term returns and meaningful growth with appropriate risk protections and provides for about 2 gigawatts of new generation in Pennsylvania.

It demonstrates the strength of the platform we're building and the growing momentum behind Invitium Energy, which is in active discussions with multiple counterparties for additional generation projects in Pennsylvania. Turning to Slide 6. This slide demonstrates how the updated plan has changed from our prior plan and just as important, what hasn't changed. First, the key change is the 100 basis point increase in our annual EPS growth target. That growth is supported by a larger investment program, primarily paid for by our large load customers. Our base capital plan is $2 billion more than the prior plan, primarily from an additional CCGT in Kentucky. Rate base CAGR over the plan period remains at about 10%.

We're also maintaining strong cost discipline with overall planned O&M growth at roughly 0.5% annually through 2030 to benefit our customers. Our financial foundation also remains strong. We continue to target an FFO to debt ratio of 16% to 18%, and the plan has our credit metrics improving towards the midpoint of that range over the plan period. Our dividend commitment is also unchanged as we're targeting the low end of our 4% to 6% annual dividend growth range while we fund our significant CapEx plan. The bottom line is that we have a stronger growth outlook, continue to focus on affordability and efficiency for our customers and are exercising the same financial discipline you've come to expect from us.

And beyond the strong base plan, we have the additional capital investment opportunities I discussed, stemming from the potential for additional Kentucky generation and Invitium Energy. Let's turn to Slide 7 for a brief regulatory update. In Kentucky, the Public Service Commission partially granted our request for reconsideration of its decision in LG&E and KU's 2025 rate cases. The commission approved several elements of our request, resulting in an additional $7 million in annual revenues. In total, LG&E and KU received approval for an aggregate increase of approximately $240 million in annual electric and gas revenues.

While the commission granted part of our reconsideration request, the sharing mechanism that would have allowed us to stay out through 2028 was not approved. As a result, LG&E and KU expect to file base rate cases in the coming months. In Rhode Island, new base rates became effective September 1, with the commission approving $138 million annual revenue increase following Rhode Island Energy's first base rate review since 2017. The order is a constructive outcome that supports our capital plan to modernize Rhode Island's electric and gas networks.

We were also successful in securing a settlement for our hold harmless commitment, which provides $163 million in bill credits to our electric and gas customers from October 2026 through September of 2027. These are meaningful savings for our customers during the winter heating season and helped to offset the base rate increases. While the Rhode Island PUC approved an increase in annual revenues, it did not approve our requested second year revenue increase. As a result, Rhode Island Energy plans to file another rate case as early as next year. And as a reminder, PPL Electric's rate case settlement became effective July 1 with a positive outcome for both customers and shareowners.

The approved increase of $275 million supported critical investments we're making while reflecting less than a 4% increase across all of our rate classes. The settlement also included a 2-year stay-out provision, but we expect to be able to stay out longer than the 2 years agreed to in the settlement. Across all our jurisdictions, our focus remains consistent, investing responsibly in the infrastructure needed to support reliability and economic growth, engaging constructively with regulators and maintaining a strong focus on affordability for our customers. Turning to Slide 8 and speaking of customer affordability. Keeping customer bills affordable remains one of our top priorities, and it shapes how we run our business and execute our plan.

Through constructive regulatory outcomes, along with a steady focus on cost efficiency, we've kept the average residential bill at each of our utilities below the relevant state or regional averages. Across our utilities, the portion of the bills that we control are about 10% lower than our state averages. And in Rhode Island, we are lower by about 16% compared to the rest of New England. We expect that trend to continue, even including the results of our recent rate case outcomes. Importantly, we're also ensuring that growth pays for growth, reducing cost pressures on our existing customers.

Our large load tariffs, the first of their kind by investor-owned utilities in Pennsylvania and Kentucky, require data centers to cover the cost of serving them. So existing customers don't bear that burden. And we're looking to build on those protections even further. In September, PPL Electric filed a proposed Customer Protection Transmission Rider, or CPTR, to further strengthen our protections around large load growth. The benefits of additional load will be felt every year over the next 5 years, and this has measurable affordability value for our existing customers. At the full 11.4 gigawatts currently under ESA, we estimate that our customer protection framework could reduce the average residential customers' annual transmission cost by $300.

We expect a decision by the commission on our CPTR filing in the summer of 2027, targeting implementation in Q1 2028. And finally, we continue to remain focused on cost. This includes holding our O&M growth to about 0.5% on a compound annual basis through 2030. And we're not planning on stopping there. We continue to see AI as a game changer for the utility industry, one that will come with significant cost savings. And while broad deployment of AI is a key part of our utility of the future strategy, we've taken a conservative approach in our planning process and have not baked significant AI-related savings into this updated plan.

We see this as a meaningful opportunity, which could further enhance system reliability and the customer experience at a lower cost, further supporting our customer affordability strategy. Turning to Slide 9. Data center development in Pennsylvania continues to progress. The pipeline of projects in advanced stages increased for the 11th consecutive quarter to 35.3 gigawatts, up 3.5 gigawatts from the second quarter. We're also continuing to see projects advance within that pipeline. Load converting to signed ESAs increased by 300 megawatts from the second quarter to approximately 11.4 gigawatts. Of that data center load, approximately 8.5 gigawatts are now under construction, an increase of 2 gigawatts from last quarter.

We've already connected 2 data centers and to date have energized 300 megawatts of that contracted load, which will ultimately ramp to about 2 gigawatts. This progression of the pipeline is critically important. As projects move from initial agreements to ESAs and then into construction, we gain greater visibility into the infrastructure and generation that will ultimately be needed to serve this load. This continued data center interest in Pennsylvania also further supports new generation opportunities at Invitium Energy. Turning to Slide 10. We're seeing similar momentum in Kentucky with another quarter of strong economic development growth and increasing conversion of projects in the pipeline.

Our total economic development pipeline has increased another 1 gigawatt since the second quarter to 14.7 gigawatts of potential load growth through 2032. Data center load has increased to 12.8 gigawatts, while the non-data center load remains at approximately 2 gigawatts. Importantly, we're also seeing significant progress in converting that pipeline into more committed projects with 2.3 gigawatts of load under reimbursement agreements, up from 1.3 gigawatts at the end of the second quarter. In addition, projects with a probability of success of 50% or greater have increased to 4 gigawatts of additional peak demand with the average probability for these projects sitting at almost 85%.

The generation investments in the updated plan that I discussed earlier support approximately 2.4 gigawatts of that demand. Additional generation needed to serve the remaining 1.6 gigawatts represents $3.5 billion to $4.5 billion of investment needs through 2030. Bottom line, we continue to see a significant opportunity in Kentucky to support economic development and invest in the generation needed to serve that growth. And importantly, these incremental investments are expected to be primarily paid for by large load customers and not our existing customers. Our next CPCN filing will occur once we have signed a data center ESA, which is currently anticipated in Q1 2027.

These opportunities are good for the state, good for our existing customers and create additional long-term value for our shareowners. With that, I'll turn the call over to Joe for the financial update.

Joe Bergstein: Thank you, Vince, and good morning, everyone. Let's turn to Slide 12. PPL's third quarter GAAP earnings were $0.49 per share compared to $0.43 per share in Q3 2025. We recorded special items of $0.05 per share during the third quarter, primarily due to system and other integration-related costs and PPL's Rhode Island Hold Harmless commitment. Adjusting for these special items, third quarter earnings from ongoing operations were $0.54 per share, an improvement of $0.06 per share compared to the same period a year ago. This increase was primarily supported by base rate recovery resulting from rate case outcomes in all 3 of our jurisdictions, timely recovery of capital investments through tracking mechanisms and higher sales volumes.

These favorable drivers were partially offset by higher depreciation expense from additional plant in service, higher operating costs and higher interest expense. As we look at the first 9 months of 2026, our ongoing earnings increased by over 7% compared with the same period in 2025. And as we head into the final quarter of the year, we've narrowed our 2026 ongoing earnings forecast range to $1.92 to $1.96 per share and are on track to achieve at least the midpoint of $1.94 per share. We also have continued to execute on our capital investment program, having deployed $3.6 billion of investments through the end of the third quarter.

This is more than a 20% increase from what we deployed during the first 9 months of 2025, including great progress on our major generation projects in Kentucky, which remain on time and on budget. Moving to Slide 13. Building off our strong momentum in 2026, our updated business plan supports strong EPS growth heading into next year. For 2027, we are forecasting earnings of $2.06 to $2.14 per share with a midpoint of $2.10 per share, representing 8.2% growth from the midpoint of our current 2026 ongoing earnings forecast.

That puts us squarely in the top half of our new 7% to 9% growth target from the outset of the plan, and we expect to be in the top half of the range annually. Growth in 2027 is expected to be driven by improved rate recovery from rate case outcomes approved earlier this year and higher revenues associated with the recovery of ongoing capital investments. We expect these drivers to be partially offset by higher operating costs in Kentucky as well as higher depreciation and higher financing costs across all segments. Moving to Slide 14. We have a high degree of confidence in our updated base plan, which supports our higher EPS growth targets.

That outlook does not depend on any of the upside opportunities that we discussed this morning. Beyond our updated base plan, we see additional generation investment opportunities to serve 1.6 gigawatts of Kentucky demand. Those investments could support an EPS CAGR over 9% through 2030. The upside case includes 2 additional natural gas combined-cycle plants, the 266-megawatt Lewis Ridge Pumped Storage Project and 400 megawatts of additional battery storage to bridge power to data centers coming online in our territory. Based on this case, we estimate that earnings contributions could start as early as 2028, ramping as the units come online.

Critically, these incremental investments would be primarily paid for by large load customers driving the need and not our existing customers. We'll begin to add these opportunities into the formal plan once we have signed agreements with these large load customers. This provides a visible and credible path to extend growth beyond our updated base plan. Turning to Slide 15. Our updated capital plan totals $25 billion of customer-focused investments through 2030, approximately $2 billion more than our prior 4-year plan. As we roll the plan forward to 2027 through 2030, the $5.2 billion of capital investments in 2026 rolls off and we add a projected $5.7 billion in 2030.

And on a comparable 2027 to 2029 basis, investment is $1.5 billion higher, primarily reflecting the expected need for another natural gas combined-cycle unit with a commercial operation date of 2032. From a generation standpoint, our business plan now includes 4 NGCCs totaling over 2.5 gigawatts, 240 megawatts of solar projects and 525 megawatts of battery storage. Slide 25 in the appendix of today's presentation provides additional details on the generation units assumed in the business plan. As Vince noted, continued conversion of the Kentucky economic development pipeline could support another $3.5 billion to $4.5 billion of generation investment through 2030, which could increase our EPS CAGR to 9% plus as discussed on the prior slide. Turning to Slide 16.

Our rate base is projected to grow from about $33 billion this year to nearly $48 billion in 2030, a 10% compound annual rate. That growth is driven by the $25 billion capital plan and is the foundation of our 7% to 9% EPS growth target. This is the base plan only. It does not include the Kentucky generation upside opportunity outlined on the prior slides, which would be incremental. Moving to Slide 17. Our financing plan is designed to fund our growth while preserving balance sheet strength and strong credit ratings.

We continue to target 16% to 18% FFO to debt with the ratio improving towards the midpoint of the range over the plan period, while maintaining holding company debt below 25% of total debt. We expect approximately $3 billion of equity needs through 2030 beyond the more than $1.5 billion we've already executed on a forward basis. This $3 billion covers the unissued equity under the previous plan and the remaining $2 billion supports our updated capital plan, which includes additional AFUDC versus the prior plan and to support our current credit ratings.

We expect to use our ATM program as a primary funding vehicle for this equity while opportunistically evaluating other equity-like structures that offer an attractive cost of capital. We're also targeting annual dividend growth at the low end of our 4% to 6% range with a payout ratio expected to be about 50% by 2030. Together, these actions provide a balanced path to fund our $25 billion capital plan, maintain strong credit quality and support stronger durable earnings growth. This concludes my prepared remarks. I'll now turn the call back over to Vince.

Vincent Sorgi: Thanks, Joe. Let me close by summarizing the investment proposition we've outlined today. At its foundation is a stronger base business. Our $25 billion capital plan supports 10% annual rate base growth and annual EPS growth of 7% to 9% through at least 2030, with results expected to be in the top half of that range beginning in 2027. We are supporting that growth with disciplined financing and a strong balance sheet. We also continue to target annual dividend growth at the low end of our 4% to 6% range, retaining capital to help fund all of this growth. Just as importantly, we are delivering this growth while keeping customers at the center of our strategy.

Our investments support safe and reliable service and our cost discipline and rate case strategies help maintain affordability. This is demonstrated through the portion of the bills we control being about 10% lower than our state and regional averages. And moving forward, our large load tariff protections are designed to ensure that growth pays for growth, further supporting customer affordability. Together, these elements support a compelling 10% to 13% total return proposition from the base plan. And beyond that base plan, we have meaningful potential upside. Continued conversion of the Kentucky economic development pipeline could drive further regulated generation investment and support our EPS CAGR to over 9% through 2030.

Invitium provides another source of potentially significant value, beginning with the QTS collaboration we announced today. In short, we have a stronger base plan, a disciplined customer-focused approach to funding growth and significant opportunities to outperform the commitments we made today. We are confident in our ability to execute this plan and are excited about the long-term value these opportunities can create for both our customers and our shareowners. With that, operator, let's open the line for questions.

Vincent Sorgi: And then just the cash flow. So maybe talk about the delta between, right, this and, say, a regulated, I think you forgot.

Joe Bergstein: Sure. So sorry, on the cash flow and financial structure of this, yes, I mean, it is different than a regulated utility. We're confident that we'll be able to finalize an ESSA with QTS, again, given their track record, the CPs that will kind of carry us to the ESSA and what both parties have to do that and our collective confidence in being able to do that. So no concerns that we'll be able to get to the ESSA. And again, those terms have financial and nonfinancial have been negotiated already.

Steven Fleishman: Okay. And then just as we think about -- let's say, you have the ESSA and you get that full run rate 2032, '33. Are you thinking then you might look to kind of move the growth rate out longer term to capture that kind of like NiSource has done? Or are you going to wait for it to get into your window? Like is finalizing that the kind of -- that when you kind of put it into your growth rate plan?

Joe Bergstein: Yes, I think that's right, Steve. When we finalize all of those terms and have all that nailed down, I think that's when we can provide more of the financial guidance around this and then obviously, extending the forecast horizon so that you know what that means from an impact of overall PPL Corporation.

Vincent Sorgi: Yes, Steve, I would say it's probably more in conjunction with the final notice to proceed, right, the FNTP, which we would need the ESSA signed to get to FNTP, right? But that's where we have the equipment contracts locked down the ESA -- sorry, the EPC contracts locked down. That's where we true up the cost of the project based on those contracts being executed. Obviously, the ESSA being executed is a key step in order to then get the financing, which is all needed to get to FNTP. And that's when we kind of lock everything down, right, and then we're finishing the development and the construction of the project.

Steven Fleishman: Got it. And one other question, sorry, different topic. We just had the elections and I think Pennsylvania Senate went Democrat majority. Just any kind of sense on whether the governor is going to bring back the GRID plan law and just how to think about potential legislation next year?

Vincent Sorgi: Yes. Well, first of all, I'd say I don't really have any concerns in terms of the -- at least on the data center side and the pipeline that we have. I actually think that the national election results could actually support our pipelines that we have both in Pennsylvania and Kentucky. Not just Shapiro, but both of our governors have signed executive orders for developing data centers and doing it the right way, right? And they're actually similar in terms of the requirements of those EOs with having a stakeholder engagement at the local level, right, no harm to power and water customers, et cetera. So neither have put a moratorium on data center development.

So I don't see that really coming as a result of the election results. And I say that because I think both of the EOs really protect our existing customers and the communities, especially when you combine them with the larger tariffs that we have in both states. So I do think some of the election results could in some other states potentially have a chilling impact, which could drive some of those projects or future development projects to both Pennsylvania and Kentucky, where we have pretty significant pipelines and have demonstrated the ability to work those. So at least on that side, no major concerns.

I think on just general legislative agendas, in particular, in PA, which I think is what you were hitting at. Again, we just have a long history of working with both Democrats and Republicans in Pennsylvania. Fully expect that, that will continue following the results. I would expect affordability and energy policy to continue to be important issues here in PA. But I think there's policy and legislative areas that we actually have mutual agreement on. And we've talked about a lot of ideas, some of which we've expressed on these earnings calls on how we could improve affordability in the state of PA.

And we believe that the new legislative session may actually provide a more receptive environment to advance some of those ideas. So again, we're open to working with whoever is in power in our states, and we share a lot of the same goals and look forward to engaging with them to achieve what's in the best interest for our states, our customers and our communities. So no overarching concern, Steve.

Operator: The next question comes from Richard Sunderland of Truist.

Richard Sunderland: Following up on some of those points at the end around affordability, there's a lot in motion on the PJM side. Just curious what you have an eye to right now from kind of progress or lack thereof over the past few months, both from a PPL Electric perspective and then also from a competitive landscape for Invitium perspective.

Vincent Sorgi: Yes. Well, look, I think this announcement today, right, we're putting our money where our mouth is on helping to support the affordability concerns in PJM, and ultimately get generation built not just within PJM, but within Pennsylvania. And so I think that's very positively viewed by our governor, our commission, ultimately, the legislature. So again, I think Invitium fits right in with pushing for more generation to improve that supply-demand dynamic that we've been talking a lot about in PJM. For PPL Electric, just, again, I think EU has been leading the way on affordability, the affordability agenda in Pennsylvania, again, with the large low tariff.

We talked about the CPTR filing, which will just take that another level in bringing additional bill support to our customers. Again, the support of the utility-owned generation in the state to try to balance the supply-demand. So again, I think EU continues to play a leadership role. We have the PUC working group on ratemaking. I expect we'll have an active role in that. Again, I think we're a trusted source in the state. We've earned that position. I would expect us to play a role in that as well. And in fact, we look forward to doing that.

Because, again, I think we share the same goals on bringing a reliable service to our customers, making sure that it's affordable, but at the same time, ensuring that the utilities are financially strong to be able to invest in the grids that deliver all of those services for our customers. So we look forward to bringing all of that to the discussion with the PUC working group. So again, a broader affordability agenda that we've been focused on has been core to our strategy, not just in PA, but across all of our jurisdictions.

I would even throw in the hold harmless settlement, which was a way to help with affordability up in Rhode Island on the heels of the rate case increases. So look forward to engaging in all of our states on affordability discussions because I think we lead in each of our jurisdictions on that topic.

Richard Sunderland: Got it. And then switching gears to Kentucky. The 1.6 gigawatts and $3.5 billion to $4.5 billion upside, are those the numbers to key into with the CPCN filing next quarter? I guess I'm trying to read the tea leaves of the data center and economic development pipeline overall relative to what gets you to that 9% plus side of the EPS growth range?

Vincent Sorgi: Yes. I think it's early to know for sure what we're going to put into that CPCN filing, right? We have 4 gigawatts of load that we talked about that has 50% or higher probability. Actually, the overall probability of those projects is close to 85%. So we'll parse through that to determine how comfortable we are putting some or all of that into the next CPCN. Of course, we'll put some of that. The plan has 2 to 2.5 gigawatts that's 90% or above in that group of projects. So feel very confident about what's in the plan going above and beyond that.

Look, I personally think we're going to be building generation for the foreseeable future in Kentucky, just given what we see with the quarter-over-quarter movement in the pipeline, even within the pipeline projects moving to more mature stages, just knowing what other things we have going on in the state that are not in the 14.7 gigawatts of total pipeline. I just think we're going to be building gen for a long time in Kentucky and with the supply chain constraints and the cost pressures, right, the sooner we lock those prices in and get that generation built, the better our customers will be and the less they will have to pay for those assets.

We saw that with the original CPCN we filed. We didn't get everything approved. The second one was about $1 billion more than the first one. So we want to try to stave that off. Of course, the commission is going to be diligent in their review of all of that, but conservatism is not cost free. And sometimes being overly conservative in regulatory outcomes ends up costing our customers, and we've seen that in the past. And I clearly want to try to stave that off in this next CPCN. So we may end up putting more in there than less, but we're still working on that.

Operator: The next question comes from David Arcaro of Morgan Stanley.

David Arcaro: Most of my questions have been answered. I guess I was just going to ask about the O&M growth trajectory. I mean keeping it at 0.5% through 2030 is very low, very impressive considering the inflationary backdrop. Wondering if you could give color around the confidence level in doing that and any kind of any improvements even from there that you're working on.

Joe Bergstein: Yes. Sure, David, it's Joe. So I mean, look, cost discipline is something that the team here has been focused on for a long time, and it's really become part of how we run the business day-to-day. We've worked hard over the last several years, as you've known, to find efficiencies across the organization. And I think that the effort is showing up in the results. And I would say it's really just that relentless focus to improve operating costs and get more efficient and support customer affordability. Inflation, as you mentioned, it's certainly a factor that we're mindful of, and we've tried to be realistic about that in our planning.

But I think given the path that we're on and the focus that the entire organization has had, the success over the last several years in driving cost out of the business that this approach is sustainable. We'll, of course, continue to balance cost management with reliability and service for our customers.

And beyond the 0.5% that we have in here, I think there's further opportunity, as we mentioned during the prepared remarks, from AI deployment, which we don't have anything materially baked into the plan from that perspective, but I think that's another opportunity and one where we're focused across the organization on how we can use AI to drive better results, get more efficient and work at a lower operating cost.

Vincent Sorgi: Yes. David, I would just add that the grid hardening and grid automation parts of the capital, which are significant in the T&D aspect of the plan, they harden the grid, right, which reduces the amount of customers that go out storm event, less truck rolls, less O&M, et cetera. So the capital plan itself continues to drive O&M out of the business in particular, the grid hardening and automation pieces of it.

Operator: The next question comes from Nicolas Woods of Bank of America.

Nicolas Woods: On the incremental Kentucky generation, you mentioned earnings could begin in 2028. How much of the contribution through 2030 would come from AFUDC versus like the earnings coming into service?

Joe Bergstein: Yes. From an incremental perspective, over the last plan, it would be AFUDC as those units don't come online during the plan period.

Nicolas Woods: Got it. And then my second question is on the Kentucky 9% plus EPS CAGR illustration, does that incorporate any associated financing costs and equity dilution for that plan? And if so, like could you give me a broad sense of what the mix is between cash flow, debt and equity?

Joe Bergstein: Yes, it certainly assumes full financing for those assets in that 9% plus. I mean look, from an overall financing perspective, we would keep our credit metrics in mind as we're doing that and making sure that we stay in that 16% to 18% range. It's traditional utility CapEx, expect roughly to 30% to 40% equity to support capital programs. So I don't really think it would be different. Obviously, we'll have to see ultimately the mix of the units when they come online, when they produce cash flows, but that's generally how I think about it today.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the call over to Vince Sorgi for any closing remarks.

Vincent Sorgi: Great. Thanks for joining us, everybody. Really excited about the update we provided today, including the Invitium announcement with QTS. I think that's the start of, again, a lot of momentum within the Invitium business and looking forward to building on that. And look forward to seeing everybody in a couple of days at the EEI Conference. We'll see you soon.

Operator: The conference has now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation, and you may now disconnect.

#3230. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3229. The Step-by-Step Guide to Shutting Off Apple Intelligence Features in iOS 27

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With the master Apple Intelligence toggle gone, opting out in iOS 27 means turning off Siri AI, Writing Tools, Image Playground and other features separately.

Screen Time, the iPhone feature most people know for limiting app use, has become the most direct way to block Apple Intelligence in iOS 27. That’s because Apple removed the single switch that used to turn every AI feature off at once. The Settings section once called Apple Intelligence & Siri is now just Siri, centered on the new Siri AI, and the remaining AI tools are scattered across several menus. Screen Time’s restrictions can shut down Writing Tools and image creation together, and a few other features need their own toggles. Here’s the full map.

Individual features can still be disabled, but they’re scattered across several menus in Settings and Screen Time rather than consolidated in one place. Here’s the current map of what can be turned off and where to find each control.

If your device is not running the newest software, turning off Apple Intelligence all at once only takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

You can still disable some of Apple’s AI features if your iPhone is running iOS 27. It just won’t be as easy as tapping the main toggle.

To disable Siri AI, go to Settings > Siri and toggle off the control. Beware, though, that this will disable your voice assistant entirely, as well as disable conversations in the new dedicated Siri app and block you from using Apple’s Visual Intelligence. Additionally, your HomePod speakers will not be able to recognize your voice or help with personal content if they’re on the same iCloud account as your iPhone.

Keep reading for how to disable some of the individual Apple AI features.

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Read more: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? Here’s what’s actually going on.

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas should be for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the new iPhone 18 lineup, the iPhone Duo, iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. This is what it looks like running iOS 26, but the settings flow is the same.

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, the storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an “Apple Intelligence & Siri” option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features.

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. This is what the settings look like with iOS 26. It may look different if you are using iOS 27. The settings flow is the same.

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 27 yet, make a good backup first.

If you aren’t on iOS 27, you can turn off Apple Intelligence with one tap. (You can see what software your iPhone is running by going to Settings > General > About and seeing what iOS version you’re running.)

If you’re on iOS 26 or earlier, here’s how to disable Apple Intelligence. Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch if you are running iOS 26 or an earlier software version.

Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.

#3228. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.
