#3226. Will Democrats Rein in Big Tech? It Starts With Privacy and Data Centers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech critics say that real change will depend on newly elected officials keeping their campaign promises.

In this week’s midterm elections, Democrats won back control of both chambers of Congress, with stunning victories in battleground states that have voters and tech critics asking: Was this the AI election?

Artificial intelligence was central to the national conversation during the midterms, alongside concerns about affordability and the Iran war. From data centers needed to power AI to how it’s used in surveillance tech like Flock cameras, many Democratic (and a few Republican) candidates campaigned against AI.

Despite tech leaders like Elon Musk pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, tech critics say voters’ choices show a strong distrust in Big Tech and give the newly elected leaders the necessary momentum for change. But how, exactly, they deliver on those goals remains to be seen — and will have real consequences for tech consumers and companies.

“It is time for lawmakers to get real about reining in unchecked tech power and to hold these companies accountable to the people,” Butler says.

More than any other tech issue, data centers took center stage in the midterm elections. It isn’t surprising; these facilities are popping up everywhere and require vast amounts of water and electricity at the expense of nearby communities’ health and environments.

Voters showed their frustration at the ballot box. Across the country, voters rejected more than 40 ballot measures that would’ve supported data centers. It was a rare national consensus on an issue that is usually debated in city councils and statehouses. As such, “action is more likely to come on the local and state levels, at least in the short term,” says Paris Marx, tech critic and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast.

Governments may continue to adopt moratoriums on new data center construction, like New York’s first-in-the-nation pause implemented earlier this year, as they try to figure out how to mitigate the harms. State and local legislators need to continue setting environmental rules, managing electricity demand and finding real community benefits, Marx says. (OpenAI, for its part, is tackling the issue by renaming data centers as “compute campuses.”)

In many ways, “data centers are a symptom of the larger problem,” says Samir Jain, vice president of policy at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Tech companies are so focused on “winning” the global AI race that they forget (or didn’t prioritize) the impact on everyday people, he says.

But neighbors living next to data centers cannot forget. In that sense, the overwhelming public backlash to data centers and the midterm election results are “a real repudiation of that kind of approach to technology,” Jain says.

But we’ve seen very clearly over the past decade that when left unchecked, tech companies can collect and use our data in concerning ways. Despite stalled progress on a national bill in the past, there may be a new push for it, thanks to recent tech headlines. Flock cameras and other automatic license plate readers have sparked immense public concern as many cases show law enforcement officers misusing the tech to stalk and harass people.

It isn’t just major tech platforms; it’s also data brokers that sell data to companies you don’t interact with. That industry is worth more than $277 billion, and it’s the engine behind much of how Big Tech operates.

“If you are mad at this whole surveillance pricing situation where we’re going to charge you more if we feel like you can afford it, that is because of data brokers,” says McKinney. “If you are mad that the federal government can just buy information from data brokers that [it] would otherwise have to get a warrant to get, that’s a data broker problem.”

“We can’t lead the world in AI and support transformative AI innovation with a patchwork of conflicting state laws that make life harder for startups and small businesses,” Fabrizio says.

While the Democrats will have a firm majority in both chambers of Congress, many of the most contentious tech issues have bipartisan support, tech critics told me. And we’ve already seen how that can result in actionable legislation, such as the Take It Down Act, which passed nearly unanimously in 2025.

This fleeting moment of bipartisan agreement on reining in Big Tech could help lawmakers achieve the elusive task of actually fulfilling their campaign promises. But part of the challenge will be getting lawmakers to focus on real-world harm and basic protections, not whatever dystopian tech prediction is trending that day.

“It’s very likely we’ll see companies continue to push lawmakers to focus AI regulation on so-called ‘existential risks,’ meaning their claims that more advanced AI might kill humanity or end the world,” Marx says, “rather than addressing the impacts of data centers and the present-day harms.”

Those existential risks only serve to make tech companies more powerful. “These elected representatives don’t just have the power to rein in these powerful corporations; they have the obligation to do so to promote the interests of the constituents they serve,” Butler says.

We saw this election cycle how much money Big Tech is willing to spend to try to get its preferred candidates and policies. Elon Musk alone reportedly spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates such as Ken Paxton in Texas, who lost by 12 percentage points to Democrat James Talarico. Despite that, most of the tech experts I spoke to said the results showed a real desire from voters to rein in tech companies and the harms they wrought.

But that will depend on how willing the new Congress is to buck Big Tech. “If we have a new electorate that is newly emboldened to stand up to bullies,” McKinney says, “let’s start there.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3225. Sunstone (SHO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management raised 2026 guidance and sees stronger group bookings ahead.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Sunstone Hotel Investors, Inc. (SHO +1.38%) reported third quarter results that management attributed to better-than-expected industry fundamentals and disciplined capital recycling. The company sold the Hyatt Regency San Francisco at an attractive private market value and redeployed the proceeds into common and preferred stock repurchases, which management indicated increased net asset value and funds from operations per share. The company updated its full-year 2026 guidance upward to reflect strong performance in the urban and resort segments and higher expected contributions from recently renovated assets. Looking ahead to 2027, the company highlighted a stronger group booking calendar and reduced fixed charges resulting from its recent capital structure improvements.

Operator: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Sunstone Hotel Investors third quarter earnings call. [Operator Instructions] I would like to remind everyone that this conference call is being recorded today, November 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time. I'll now turn the presentation over to Mr. Aaron Reyes, Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead, sir.

Aaron Reyes: Thank you, operator. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that this call contains forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties, including those described in our filings with the SEC, which could cause actual results to differ materially from those projected. We caution you to consider these factors in evaluating our forward-looking statements. We also note that the commentary on this call will contain non-GAAP financial information, including adjusted EBITDAre, adjusted FFO and hotel adjusted EBITDAre. We are providing this information as a supplement to information prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.

Additional details on our quarterly results have been provided in our earnings release and supplemental, which are available in the Investor Relations section of our website. With us on the call today are Bryan Giglia, Chief Executive Officer; and Robert Springer, President and Chief Investment Officer. After our remarks, the team will be available to answer your questions. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Bryan. Please go ahead.

Bryan Giglia: Thank you, Aaron, and good morning, everyone. The third quarter saw solid performance all around, as better-than-expected industry fundamentals added to earnings growth generated from disciplined cost controls at the corporate level and from our meaningful share repurchase activity. Our well-located portfolio benefited from broad-based strength across all segments and contributed to total portfolio RevPAR growth of 11.4%. Excluding Andaz Miami Beach, comparable RevPAR still increased by a very impressive 10.3%. The stronger-than-expected revenue performance allowed us to deliver nearly 9% growth in adjusted EBITDA compared to last year. Since the start of the third quarter, we repurchased an additional $130 million of common and preferred stock, bringing our year-to-date total to nearly $200 million of accretive buyback activity.

This has not only helped to grow NAV, but also contributed to a nearly 18% increase in adjusted FFO per share this quarter and lays the groundwork for additional growth in per share earnings in 2027. I will share some additional thoughts on our capital allocation strategy shortly, but first, let's review some highlights from Q3 operations. For the fourth quarter in a row, our resorts led the portfolio with combined RevPAR growth of over 22%, including the benefit of Andaz Miami Beach. Wailea Beach Resort delivered another impressive performance as RevPAR grew nearly 27% in the quarter and total RevPAR increased almost 31%.

The resort has recovered its competitive position, growing occupancy by 19 points in the quarter and demonstrating the strength of the current appetite for leisure travel. As we shared with you last quarter, we were encouraged by the momentum we saw in Maui, with strong production through midyear. This trend accelerated through the third quarter with group pace for 2027, now up over 20%. Our Wine Country resorts also saw increased demand with third quarter occupancy growing nearly 8 points and combined total RevPAR 11% higher. At Andaz Miami Beach, we opened the resort's signature dining destination, Bazaar Meat by Jose Andres in late October, and Jose was on site to help kick things off.

This is an exciting milestone as the full resort campus is now activated, and we look forward to benefiting from significant growth over the coming months as we move into Miami's high season. Our urban hotel portfolio drove the greatest degree of outperformance relative to forecast with combined total RevPAR growth of 12.8% in the quarter. The strength was broad-based with each of our urban hotels generating at least 10% growth. While rate performance was solid at 5.5%, strong demand from group events and corporate travel also drove a healthy lift in room night volume. We continue to be pleased with the booking patterns we are seeing at our urban hotels as we move into the fourth quarter.

Group pace for our urban portfolio is up meaningfully, and we are seeing strength in corporate transient rates. This combination should allow our operators to take advantage of the compression and maximize yield. The setup looks particularly good for the Marriott Boston Long Wharf and the JW Marriott New Orleans, as these 2 very well-located hotels can drive significant premiums to the market. Performance at our convention hotels reflected a continuation of the same trends we have seen all year, with incremental transient demand partially offsetting a more subdued event calendar in a couple of our larger markets.

San Antonio was our best-performing convention hotel, with the Hyatt Regency on the Riverwalk, generating total revenue growth over 40% in the quarter on a much more favorable group event calendar and the benefit of our recently renovated meeting space. While our other convention hotels generated lower growth, overall performance was better than forecast. As we have shared with you on prior calls, we expected some headwinds this year due to less favorable event calendars in some of our key group markets. The good news is that as of the third quarter, most of that is behind us, and the outlook is much more encouraging.

In Orlando, quarterly group revenue production for all future periods was up over 40% and set a record for third quarter booking activity. While year-to-date performance in San Diego has been soft, we are moving into a stronger backdrop for the market and expect substantially better results in the fourth quarter and into next year. We are off to the right start with October RevPAR at Hilton Bayfront up over 20% to last year. Across the country in Washington, D.C., where the group calendar and local market dynamics have been challenging, we have seen some recent positive signs with 2027 group pace at the Westin increasing several points since last quarter.

Overall, we are encouraged by a more constructive group setup for our portfolio next year. On the expense side, our occupancy-driven growth resulted in an 8.9% increase in total comparable portfolio expenses during the quarter, or 2.7% per occupied room, which led to EBITDA margin increasing only 50 basis points. Our margin performance during the quarter was impacted by renovation work at the Hilton Key West and by several onetime items that skewed comparability. Adjusting for these impacts, we estimate margins would have expanded nearly 200 basis points. As we shared with you on prior calls, a more transient heavy mix of business at our largest group hotels this year has limited their ability to operate at peak efficiency.

We expect a return to more normalized segmentation for these hotels next year, which should drive meaningfully better flow-through and increase profitability. We expect our Hilton San Diego Bayfront, with group pace up over 10% in 2027, could have a meaningful benefit to margins next year. Additionally, our other large group hotels in Washington, D.C. and San Antonio also have strong group pace growth that should support better flow-through next year. We continue to focus on driving labor efficiencies where possible and working with our operators to mitigate growth in other property level costs. We expect that increased utilization of technology will help drive down operating costs over time.

And while it is difficult today to forecast the exact cadence and magnitude, we think it is reasonable to assume that we will begin to realize some of these benefits of our operators' recent technology investments as we move into next year. We have also been focused on minimizing expenses at the corporate level and ensuring that our overhead costs are aligned with the needs of the company. As I noted on the start of the call, we have now repurchased nearly $200 million of common and preferred stock so far this year, recycling about 70% of the proceeds from the sale of the Hyatt Regency San Francisco.

This has been a very successful and efficient round trip of capital done without earnings drag created from holding cash for an extended period. We realized an attractive private market value for an asset that was expected to remain low yielding and deployed most of those proceeds back into our common and preferred stock at a much higher implied yield and at an attractive discount to NAV. The revised full year outlook that Aaron will discuss shortly reflects not only the benefit from stronger trends across the portfolio, but also the contribution from this repurchase activity, which also gives us a head start on per share earnings growth for next year.

To put this into perspective, we sold an asset at a strong value, repurchased a meaningful amount of common and preferred stock, increased NAV and FFO per share and did all of this on a leverage-neutral basis while still retaining capital to deploy. Our nimble size and decisive action allowed us to quickly realize value and acquire our equity at a significant discount to NAV and to today's stock price. We have remaining proceeds from the sale together with balance sheet capacity that we can use to further drive growth in earnings per share. We expect to remain opportunistic with our repurchase activity as pricing allows.

At current levels, our buyback efforts will be focused on preferred stock over common stock. We are also continuing to monitor opportunities in the transaction market, but expect to remain disciplined in our approach and ensure we retain full strategic optionality as it relates to our ability to create value for our shareholders. With that, I'll turn the call over to Robert, to give some additional details on our capital investment activity.

Robert Springer: Thanks, Bryan. We have made solid progress on our 2026 capital plan, delivering several key projects that should position us for future growth. In San Diego, we completed a meeting space renovation earlier this year and are already seeing the benefits of that investment in our booking velocity. We expect to see significant revenue growth as we move into the fourth quarter of this year, and our 2027 group revenue pace is more than 10% higher compared to the same time last year. At Andaz Miami Beach, the property's transformation is now complete with the resort's signature dining destination, Bazaar Meat, now open.

We will conduct a formal grand opening celebration early next year to coincide with peak season, but initial response has been great with a variety of press and media coverage bringing additional energy and awareness to the resort. Work is also underway on a room refresh and facade restoration at our recently converted Hilton Key West Resort & Marina. We are scheduling the work in phases through mid-2027, to minimize disruption and take advantage of peak demand periods. This renovation work and the resort's new brand and manager affiliation are intended to drive incremental earnings as the property benefits from Hilton's stronger distribution channels, operating expertise and lower customer acquisition costs compared to its prior independent operating model.

And last, we are moving into the final phase of remediation work at Wailea Beach Resort, following the damage incurred from the storms that impacted the Hawaiian Islands earlier this year. Work in the guest rooms and public spaces is complete and the roof and facade repairs are underway now, so that we can have them done by the busy festive season. While this was not a project that was on our to-do list at the start of the year, our team mobilized quickly to complete significant repair work while not disrupting the strong demand recovery we are seeing at the resort this year.

While this work added several million dollars to our total capital investment in 2026, nearly all of this incremental spend is being reimbursed by our insurance programs. We are working through our capital planning for 2027, and we'll have more to share with you next quarter. As it stands now, we expect a significant portion of our capital spend for next year to be funded from existing FF&E reserves, with a smaller contribution of owner capital relative to prior years. With that, I'll turn it over to Aaron. Please go ahead.

Aaron Reyes: Thanks, Robert. As we noted at the top of the call, our earnings results for the third quarter came in ahead of expectations, driven by broad-based strength across the portfolio. Rooms RevPAR for the total portfolio grew an impressive 11.4% in the quarter, including a 110 basis point benefit from Andaz Miami Beach. Total RevPAR for all hotels increased 10.5%, including a 90 basis point benefit from Andaz. The stronger top line performance in the quarter contributed to earnings that were ahead of our expectations, including adjusted EBITDAre of $54.5 million, an increase of 9% relative to last year.

When combined with the added benefit of our accretive repurchase activity, adjusted FFO per diluted share was $0.20, an increase of 18% from last year. As of the end of the third quarter, we had $237 million of unrestricted cash and over $80 million of additional cash held in FF&E reserves. Together with full availability on our credit facility, this equates to nearly $820 million of liquidity. Net leverage as of the end of the quarter stood at only 2.8x trailing earnings or 3.7x, including our preferred equity.

Despite deploying a significant amount of capital into buyback activity this year, we have been able to preserve our low leverage position by taking advantage of opportunities to repurchase our preferred stock at attractive discounts. These repurchases have not only reduced our preferred dividends by nearly $4 million per year on a run rate basis, but have also contributed to growth in NAV. Included in our press release this morning are the details of our updated outlook for 2026. We are once again revising our expectations higher to capture the outperformance in the third quarter and to reflect the improved near-term trends we are seeing as we move into the fourth quarter.

Our updated guidance also includes the benefit of incremental savings in corporate G&A and the benefit of higher FFO and FFO per share created by our accretive common and preferred stock repurchases. Based on what we see today, we now expect that rooms RevPAR for all hotels in the portfolio will grow between 9.5% and 10.5% or an increase of 200 basis points at the midpoint to a range of $245 to $247. This reflects the full year benefit of Andaz Miami Beach, which is expected to contribute approximately 450 basis points of growth at the midpoint.

Total RevPAR is now expected to increase between 8.5% and 9.5% to a range of $409 to $413, with a similar 450 basis point benefit from Andaz. As we noted in our press release and supplemental, our year-to-date RevPAR and total RevPAR growth for the total portfolio was a robust 10.8% and 9.9%, respectively. Based on the midpoint of our updated ranges, this would imply a mid-to-high single-digit revenue growth expectation for the fourth quarter, with approximately 150 basis points of benefit from Andaz. This revised revenue growth is now expected to translate into adjusted EBITDAre in the range of $254 million to $259 million.

Our FFO per diluted share has been revised higher to also incorporate a further reduction in preferred dividends and a lower share count as a result of our repurchase activity, and is now expected to range from $1 to $1.03. Given that our repurchases were concentrated in the second half of this year, we will continue to see the benefit of this activity in our per share earnings as we move into 2027, with approximately 178 million current shares outstanding, a reduction of nearly 6.5% from the start of the year and nearly 20% since the start of 2022. Turning to our return of capital.

Since the start of the year, up to this week, we have repurchased approximately $143 million of common stock at a blended price of $10.43 per share, a meaningful discount to consensus estimates of NAV and our current trading level. In addition, we have also repurchased nearly $54 million of our preferred stock at a blended price of $21.03 per share or a 16% discount to its liquidation value. This common and preferred stock repurchase activity has been accretive to both NAV and earnings per share. While we expect to continue opportunistically repurchasing common and preferred stock when pricing is compelling, our revised 2026 outlook does not assume the benefit of additional buyback activity.

Our Board of Directors has authorized a $0.09 per share common dividend for the fourth quarter. Given the tax impact associated with our sale of Hyatt San Francisco earlier this year, our current dividend will satisfy our distribution requirement this year. If we adjust for the sale impact, the portfolio is generating cash flow per share meaningfully in excess of our current payout rate and should support incremental capital return as we move into 2027. Our Board has also declared the routine distributions for our Series G, Series H, and Series I preferred securities.

While an attractive combination of implied yield and NAV growth has focused our preferred repurchase activity on our 2 publicly traded series, we retain the option of redeeming some or all of our Series G preferred at any time at our election and is another lever we can pull to drive growth in FFO per share moving forward. Before we conclude our prepared remarks, I'll turn it back over to Bryan, for some additional thoughts.

Bryan Giglia: Before we open the call to questions, I want to provide an update on our 2026 objectives and our progress towards them. In July, we sold the Hyatt Regency San Francisco at attractive pricing of nearly 20x trailing EBITDA, realizing a private market value that far exceeded its valuation inside our portfolio and appropriately capturing the present value of its future growth. Importantly, we promptly redeployed most of the proceeds into the repurchase of common stock at a discount to both NAV and our current trading price and into the repurchase of preferred stock at a 10% to 20% discount to redemption value. Our combined repurchases increased value and FFO per share while maintaining a leverage-neutral balance sheet.

At the same time, we retain additional capital and balance sheet capacity to deploy into the most compelling opportunities available to us. Looking ahead to 2027, the combination of embedded growth in our portfolio, reduced corporate G&A, lower fixed charges from preferred stock repurchases, a lower share count and the remaining proceeds we have to deploy, has increased our expected distributable income per share despite the earnings we forego from selling San Francisco. Taking all of that into account, we expect our 2027 quarterly dividend distribution requirement to be between $0.11 and $0.12 per share or approximately 20% to 30% above our 2026 quarterly distribution.

This is based on what we see today, and we will revisit our 2027 dividend payout approach early next year. Taken together, our 2026 capital allocation decisions demonstrate our ability to unlock and create shareholder value by selling assets when private market valuations are compelling and dynamically redeploying that capital where we see the best risk-adjusted returns. We remain disciplined and nimble with the balance sheet capacity and liquidity to continue opportunistically allocating capital across acquisitions, investments in our portfolio, share repurchases and other opportunities that we believe will generate superior long term value for our shareholders. With that, we can now open the call to questions. Operator, please go ahead.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Smedes Rose with Citi.

Bennett Rose: I guess I wanted to ask my first question, just a little more if you could just discuss group pace, I guess, portfolio-wide for '27. I know you mentioned it for a couple of your assets, but what are you seeing so far for the whole group?

Bryan Giglia: Yes, we're up -- we are up right now mid-to-high single digits right now. But when you look at the big components of that and you look at especially one of the hotels that has struggled this year on the group side, which we knew going into it, is San Diego, is one of the big ones that has meaningful -- over 10% growth. Wailea also has significant growth, and then also San Antonio and D.C. So when you look at our largest hotels from both a top line and then the ancillary spend and the margin impact you'll get, those are big movers for the portfolio and will benefit the portfolio next year.

Bennett Rose: And then I guess I wanted to ask sort of along the same lines, I feel like a focus on this quarter's call has been kind of issues or expectations around flow-through. And some of the feedback has been that higher transient-driven occupancies have driven up variable costs and maybe impacted some of the flow-through. It sounds like in your remarks, you anticipated kind of a more normal segmentation for next year. But could you maybe talk about that a little bit and maybe what some of the margin implications are for the portfolio?

Bryan Giglia: So starting with the group hotels first, both San Diego and D.C., that had a weaker group pace for this year, 2026. We were able to partially backfill a good portion of that with transient demand, because short-term transient demand year-to-date and looking forward for the next 6 months continues to be very strong. That was able to backfill some of that demand. But then hotels that typically do larger group percentages of their overall revenue, San Diego and D.C. specifically, they become less efficient. And so banquets is a big piece of that, meeting room rental, AV, those are all more profitable than what the transient guests will spend.

So that was a portion of the flow-through that we will see, both San Diego and D.C. revert back to their normal -- more normalized segmentation next year. So that's a tailwind for margins. And then for this year also, there were some tougher comps to 2025. We had some real estate tax credits. We also had a lot more cancellation and attrition in 2025, which has a better flow-through. So that is something we won't have to compare to next year. And then we had across the portfolio, you look at Wailea specifically, large pickups in occupancy.

And so as we look at transient bookings going forward and even some of the group bookings going forward, while this year, occupancy was a bigger component of it; next year, rate will be a bigger component. So that will also benefit. And then last, even though Wailea is having a phenomenal year in the year we talked about and expected with regaining its position on the island -- third quarter, they didn't do damage to the hotel like we had in the second quarter, but there were several storms that moved through Maui. And so each one of those has its own level of disruption.

And then on the repairs and maintenance, landscaping, cleanup there, there's a lot of costs running through the P&L that we won't -- hopefully will not have next year.

Operator: Your next question comes from Conor Peaks with Wells Fargo.

Conor Peaks: [Technical Difficulty] Francisco bought back nearly $200 million of stock and worked to 13 hotels at this point. How do you think about the right size and mix of the portfolio from here? And what does Sunstone look like in 2 or 3 years?

Bryan Giglia: Conor, I think we got -- yes, I think you cut off a little bit, but I think I got your question. So if I miss anything, just please we can follow-up on it. As far as what is the right size for Sunstone, we like being the size that we are. We like being nimble and being able to allocate capital in a manner that is meaningful to all aspects, our NAV per share, our FFO growth, our overall impact to share price through reducing share count.

So we like to be able to, with San Francisco specifically, look to sell an asset into a market and realize a private market value that is well in excess of where it is valued in our portfolio and getting the value of the future cash flows today and then being able to then take that -- those proceeds and allocate them in the manner of which we think we're going to get the best risk-adjusted return. And at that moment in time, our stock was trading at a level that was a significant discount and well outside of where assets were trading in the market.

And so the right allocation at that time was to repurchase our own portfolio, also being able to repurchase our preferred stock at a discount, being able to do all that leverage neutral and retaining capital to go deploy further. And so lowered the share count, kept the leverage level the same, which should benefit our taxable income and distributions next year and have some dry powder to deploy after all that. Where we stand today with the stock where it has moved, preferred is still very attractive. Acquisitions are more attractive now. But again, we need to find the right one.

And looking at the transaction market in -- specifically going in Q3, you see that overall transactions are up. But when you dig into it a little deeper, you see that very small transactions are up and very large $250 million-plus transactions are up. But when you look at the sweet spot of where we would want to acquire -- that's, call it, the $50 million to $200 million range. Those transactions were actually down. I think the market is improving.

And so where we stand today and where we'll stand in the future will be dependent on all the factors I just went through, but we will continue to allocate capital in a manner that is going to benefit our shareholders the best. And I think overall, we have -- we've made the right changes from overhead costs and make sure that we are adequately sized for our current portfolio and have capacity to grow the portfolio under the right circumstances.

Conor Peaks: And sorry, am I coming a little clear now?

Conor Peaks: So maybe shifting to Wine Country. It looks like it could contribute about $0.07 on the stabilized FFO bridge. What kind of -- how is that pacing today? Maybe what's the main constraint or area of improvement you're looking for to drive this recovery?

Bryan Giglia: It's -- we continue to see steady growth year-over-year from both the assets. Both of them are having very good years this year. The demand -- and the short-term demand in the market has been very strong. So you can see in Q3, we picked up quite a bit of occupancy. The short-term demand is both on the transient and the group side. And so -- and part of that is a little bit of a surprise, especially the booking window for these hotels can be within a few days for weekend travel.

And even on the group side, we were just speaking with the hotel, and they're picking up group -- 1 or 2 weeks out still, smaller groups, mainly from the Bay Area. So when we look forward, we look at -- both of them have great transient demand patterns for the next 6 months. And we're seeing more -- picking up more on the rate side. So we'll look to continue to compress rate going forward. And then as we have seen a big jump in the occupancy levels this year, again, then it's time to go and really try to fine-tune the overall cost model of each of these resorts.

And our expectation is we'll continue to see steady growth in EBITDA next year and continuing on.

Operator: Your next question comes from Duane Pfennigwerth with Evercore.

Peter Laskey: This is Peter on for Duane. Could you just discuss what's implied for the fourth quarter? If our math is correct, it seems like RevPAR may be in the mid-single digits. So just kind of describe the puts and takes on what changes from 3Q to 4Q and maybe some of the clues that you saw in October?

Bryan Giglia: Let me start, and then Aaron can cover some more of the specifics. Looking at Q4. It's -- mid- high single-digit growth for the quarter, I think is what's implied. October is the strongest month and obviously, the one month that's behind us. So October was from a comp basis and especially with some of our larger hotel -- group hotels starting to have a -- have some of that group pickup that I talked about earlier, starting to materialize in the fourth quarter. October was a strong month. November of the 3 months will be the lowest growth month.

And then as we get into December, specifically the back half of December, we see strong festive demand across our resort portfolio, Wailea, Hawaiian Country, and Miami.

Aaron Reyes: Sure, Peter. What I might just add to that, I think Bryan hit the high points, but we had anticipated that October would be the strongest month of the quarter from a RevPAR growth perspective and that would come in kind of in the mid-teens area, and then we would step down for November and December just based on the cadence of the booking patterns that we had at the start of the quarter. We've been pleased with what we've seen in October. So I think what we can see from preliminary data is that occupancy came in generally in line with that. That rate was a touch better. So some encouraging signs for October.

But we'll overall expect a kind of a mid- to high single digits as we move through the quarter with October being the best.

Peter Laskey: And I guess just quickly, Bryan, you finished up on Miami there, so I'll follow-up. Was this a -- was there anything to note about the 3Q performance? I know it's low season, but was it a pretty typical 3Q that kind of aligned with your expectations? And then just talk about some of the transient pacing into 4Q and next year.

Bryan Giglia: Q3 was, I would say, generally within expectations for Miami. We didn't get a lot -- and we talked about this on the last call. We didn't have a lot of the FIFA impact of this hotel specifically. So one, that was either where we were positioned or we didn't see that, but that will obviously not be a headwind for this hotel next year.

And I think we have a game plan also for next year when we look at Q3 in this market, kind of taking the blueprint that we have used in Wine Country in Q1, where you have a highly seasonal market with some pretty big variances in rate and occupancy between your low season and your high season.

Really, what we're focused on with the resort and what we did in Wine Country was to really push that group base as best as you can and -- which that means going to get group customers that not necessarily that customer in the high season, but they're in other local markets or other regional markets and going in and pulling that group base. And as we saw in Wine Country, it will be at a lower rate, but it comes with all of the ancillary spend. And then that allows you to then compress the transient business. So I think for year 1, post-renovation, Q3, it's a good start.

We've got a long way to go, and I think that there's a lot of upside here where we can do much better. Now looking forward, there's Q4 festive period specifically, we're seeing really strong transient demand. We're seeing rates pick up like we would want. Festive is several hundred dollars higher in rate than it was last year. Still have a lot of room to go to the market, which is good. But I think we're going to make another major stride this year, which was our expectation.

Also the -- our Basel time period with all of our meeting space available this year and also having the Bazaar restaurant done, which can be used for buyouts, just further enhances the entire resort and the resort experience, especially for the group customer. So I think the combination of those two will have a very good festive season. But like Q3, and as we said before, these are all building blocks. And so that will just carry us into '27. And we have a lot of growth that we expect and that I believe we're on target to achieve.

Operator: Your next question comes from David Katz with Jefferies.

David Katz: I think you've talked about this a bit. And so if I'm triple clicking on it, I think it's worthwhile. You made a mention about Orlando and booking pace, I believe, plus 40%. And broadly on the portfolio, group booking pace was at 10%, right? Can you just go back through what the drivers of that are and just make sure that we're getting that right? Group revenue pace is more than 10% higher, I think, is what you said. And where specifically in the portfolio that is that we can sort of point to?

Bryan Giglia: And so for total group pace, we said mid- to high single digits for the entire portfolio. The 10% you referenced, I believe, was San Diego. So let's just -- why don't we start with the building blocks for next year and then you can double back. So when we look at where the -- how the portfolio is positioned next year, both from a top line and a margin standpoint, we can start with where the most EBITDA comes from, and that would be our large group hotels. So like I said, our group pace is up mid- to high -- mid-single digits. Looking at the specific hotels, San Diego is up 10% in group pace.

Wailea is up in the 20s. And then our larger group hotels in San Antonio and D.C. are all -- are both up meaningfully. So those -- looking at the EBITDA generation just between those hotels, that is a big plus to not only top line growth next year, but at the group hotels, San Diego and D.C. specifically to really get that ancillary revenue and rightsize their margin performance. When we look at transient pace, transient pace is up, and this is -- transient is a shorter window, so it's the next 6 months. Transient pace is up 9% for the portfolio. That is pretty much all rate. And it's really across the board.

Certain hotels maybe have -- if they have a lot of group on, like San Diego, the transient pace might be down a little bit. But really, that's building on the occupancy that we built in 2026, going to rate in 2027, that should be very beneficial for our margin growth also. And we've seen and probably the biggest surprise this year has been that transient demand and how broad-based it is. It's not just the leisure, it's business transient, and it's throughout the portfolio. Then one-offs for next year is for growth, you have Andaz. So Andaz, we expect significant growth. We have significant growth this year.

As it ramps up, it will continue to provide additional growth to the portfolio next year. So I think those are the major building blocks. And then on top of that, our markets are -- have a great supply picture for the next several years at or around historically low levels of supply in the majority of all of our markets. And then from an earnings perspective, you've got the full year benefit of our share repurchase, which will be fully annualized next year, which will help. And then also our balance sheet capacity and additional liquidity we have from the San Francisco sale to redeploy.

So I think all those together, you look at -- we're pretty well positioned for 2027, and having our largest hotels with the best growth is a good formula for the next 12 months.

David Katz: I just want to confirm one detail. I thought what I heard on Orlando was pacing -- group pacing plus 40%. Is that the right -- did I hear that right?

Aaron Reyes: David, it's Aaron. The metric that we're referring to is quarterly group revenue production. And so you did hear that right at 40%, which is a great indicator of booking velocity there. Just to note that the quarterly booking patterns can fluctuate as you move from year-to-year, but it's certainly nonetheless a good story of what we're seeing in Orlando.

Bryan Giglia: But beyond Orlando, year-to-date, we're having the best production year we've had in a decade. And so like all of the group hotels are booking business, part of that into '27, part of it beyond '27. But as far as when you look at all the different segments, transient has -- is great pace booking into the next 6 months. Group is booking into the out years and booking at a rate more than we've seen in the last several years.

Operator: Your next question comes from Michael Bellisario from Baird.

Michael Bellisario: So two parts there. I'll hit the first part here. Just in terms of the buybacks and the step-up there, I mean how much of that was due to fundamentals getting better and you getting ahead of that versus you not seeing attractive enough acquisition opportunities? Sort of what are the puts and takes that you were thinking about there in the quarter?

Bryan Giglia: Yes. Mike, I think it's -- when we look at our -- we have proceeds from San Francisco. And while we need to make the best capital allocation decision with those, and we don't have to do something immediately, we are also aware of the cost of that cash sitting on the balance sheet for an extended period of time.

And quite honestly, when we looked at our portfolio and we looked at where we saw things going and in line with where we've guided things going, is that we felt that the value in our own shares compared to what was available and where current pricing was in the market was just too big of a discount that it would be very difficult to make that up through a hotel acquisition. And so I think we were measured and still didn't deploy everything.

But between the combination of common and preferred and then having some capital left to deploy, we were able to -- on a stabilized basis -- buy back our stock probably close to a mid-8s to 9% cap for the stabilized portfolio and do that on a leverage-neutral basis that we believe that was a superior allocation of capital.

Michael Bellisario: And then just one more on transactions. It sounds like maybe volume might not have been the best, but perhaps getting directionally better. What did you see in terms of pricing expectations, underwriting returns, how have those been trending? And if you're seeing any changes in seller expectations or the bid-ask spread?

Bryan Giglia: Yes. I think you're seeing a little bit of a convergence on the bid-ask spread, but it depends. And some of the larger deals we've seen, the pricing seems a little bit more reasonable, but sometimes that's for specific reasons, whether it's a structural issue with the hotel or some reason, there's usually always a reason for the pricing. I think as we see in that, call it, $50 million to $200 million range, there were very few deals, and I think that those were more of a seller's market for that type of hotel. If you could give something that's relatively needs not a lot of capital, is in a good market, is in a good labor market.

Those are -- were highly desirable and for whether it be REIT or private equity, those were bite-sized deals that I think investors wanted and were willing to do. And then -- so those were a little bit fewer and far between in the quarter. My hope and what I think we've seen a little bit now is we're starting to see more of those. And as there's more capital out to deploy, that should bring more of these to the market in, call it, in that 8-cap range.

Operator: Your next question comes from Chris Woronka with Deutsche Bank.

Chris Woronka: I was hoping we could circle back for just a minute on kind of the mix dynamic that I think affected you in Q3, where you had more transient and it may have been at a pretty good rate, but you didn't get the group with all the higher-margin ancillary. Is that something you contemplated at the beginning of the year? Or was this more of the shorter end kind of groups that didn't fill in? Just trying to square it all up because you're not the only -- it affected all your peers as well. It just seems like a little bit of an odd dynamic that unfolded.

Bryan Giglia: Chris, yes, I mean this is something with San Diego, you know 1, 2 years out where your group sits. So that was something that we were aware of D.C. -- also aware of it going into the year. I think where we were a little bit -- we were a little bit more concerned and where we were pleasantly surprised is that the transient demand was greater than we thought, but you're exactly right. That transient customer does not spend what the group customer does at those hotels. And so while I don't know if this was a -- other markets had strong group quarters and strong citywide. So I don't know if this is an industry thing.

And what we obviously focus more is our specifics of our portfolio. And so for us, this was something we knew going in, and we knew that it would be a tougher year on the margin front at these larger hotels. I think on Wailea, we were a little bit surprised at the amount of shorter-term transient demand. So that's a plus, and that's something that came up in the year. The other thing in Wailea is we weren't expecting the number of storms we had. And typically, during the hurricane season, you're focused more on the Atlantic than the Pacific, but that was the opposite this year.

And so that cost associated with each one of those that came through is even with little damage or no damage, it's still a couple of hundred thousand dollars each time of cleanup and other work. So I think to answer your question, most of it we expected. And most of it is -- our expectation is that it will reverse itself next year. So I think that we're in a good position going forward.

Chris Woronka: Just a quick follow-up on Miami. Andaz, looking out a little bit here now, I think the Grand Hyatt Convention Center opens in the fall of '27, I believe. Is there any -- do you guys anticipate any impact, good or bad from having a -- I know it's in a different neighborhood and it's convention oriented, but it's a Hyatt family. Is there anything to think about? Or do you guys expect any, I would think, benefit from having another distribution there?

Bryan Giglia: Yes. I mean, the distribution is absolutely beneficial. I think that it's a very different product. So from a redemption in the Hyatt system from the World of Hyatt, it's a very -- that's a very different stay. So I don't see a lot of impact from there. Look, is there a chance that for a convention that some of the higher-rated guests might want to stay at the beach? Absolutely. So that's -- I think that's a plus and having that in the market is a plus. And then hopefully, while it's not done and we're not at this point yet.

But hopefully, from the cost side, there'll be some complexing and some other things that we can do with Hyatt to help on the cost front. So overall, I think it will be a positive.

Operator: Your next question comes from Michael Hering with Green Street.

Michael Herring: Maybe just sticking on Miami for a second. The market has performed really well this year, and I think you had mentioned this time last year that it had softened a bit. But I'm just curious how you're thinking relative to your original underwriting, where the asset sits and as it ramps up and gets to that original target?

Robert Springer: Yes. No, I'm not sure about the softening comment. But as far as -- I think I know it. So I think we said last year, the market pulled back a little bit, but still well ahead of where our underwriting was. And so when we look at the competitive set and the rate, we're still several hundreds of dollars behind it. And so there's a lot of room for us to run. Our neighborhood in the mid-beach market continues to move upscale with other -- some other -- there's some new supply coming in, but they're very high-rated luxury. And so that's good for the overall market.

I think that our positioning and our expectations of rate in the market are right where they should be. And so going forward, we're very happy with our product relative to the higher price point hotels. We're very happy that we have the full campus functioning now with Bazaar Meat open and the Beach Club open. And so we have all of the amenities that are going to be important to both the transient and the group customer going forward. And having a flagship restaurant in the hotel is already -- and we're not even in high season yet, is already bringing a lot of notoriety to the resort.

So I think all of this, based on where our underwriting was and our expectations for the market, is right where it needs to be. And we look forward to what the resort will do next year.

Michael Herring: All makes sense. And then maybe just one other, maybe asking about how you're thinking about the portfolio generally from a different direction. There's quite a few larger group-oriented hotels and maybe your concentration to that segment of demand is a little bit elevated and caused some lumpiness in results. And just curious how you're thinking about maybe diffusing that relative concentration and diversifying going forward?

Robert Springer: Going forward, and I think I laid it out when I said that we're -- the area of transactions that we'd be looking at were in the $50 million to $200 million range, not the $500 million, $600 million, $700 million, $800 million range. And so I think that if we -- having balance sheet capacity and additional liquidity from the San Francisco sale, acquiring at the point where it makes sense, if we were to add additional assets to the portfolio to add a little bit more balance, knowing that we have some really large hotels that will move a portion of the portfolio at time to time.

But at the same time, those are some really great hotels in some really great markets and some irreplaceable real estate. And so while, yes, there will be ups and downs, I think over time, when looking at value, which is most important, that these are assets that I think we want to be invested in and will return the best over time. And so I think in the short-term, adding a little bit more diversity to the portfolio helps that. But I think next year, especially, we're going to be very happy that we have San Diego and Wailea in the portfolio.

Operator: The last question this afternoon comes from Michael Hirsh with JPMorgan.

Michael Hirsh: Regarding expense growth, are there any specific markets you'd call out as seeing above-average cost pressures? And what is your early view on 2027 wage and expense growth?

Aaron Reyes: On the cost side, your urban markets are going to have higher wage and benefits costs typically. Looking at salaries and wages for next year, it should moderate a bit from where we are this year. I don't think there's going to be as much pressure on it. And so if we're -- labor this year is kind of running at the 4% to 5%, we should -- my expectation is we'd be at the lower end of that. And then I think where we can pick up on that is on the productivity side.

And while we are in the very early stages and our managers have been investing, I do think that there is a chance that we start to see the beginnings of some of their AI investment help and probably the early stages of that will be productivity, scheduling, that is probably one of the first steps. So hopefully, next year, we should be able to start to see some offsetting of some of these costs by making sure that things are scheduled and we get more productivity out of the different departments. Looking at other costs, I mean, probably the biggest cost that has been a bigger expense this year than anticipated is energy.

So energy is something that is a little bit out of our control. We've made improvements where we can with solar in Wailea. But we -- that's something that we'll have to manage going forward, but is somewhat out of our control. Insurance property taxes are all kind of stabilized at this point. So those shouldn't be really an impact on next year.

Bryan Giglia: Yes. What I might just add to that is just to pick up on something. Michael, it's here. I'm going to give you a little more color, particularly on the property tax side. We had a number of favorable outcomes that benefited us in 2025. We'll have property tax appeals in process in pretty much every municipality and jurisdiction that we operate in. It's just hard to pick the timing and the velocity which those will come. And so 2026 was a quieter year for us on the appeal front, but I think that sets us up a little bit better as we move into 2027 that we have an easier comp.

And hopefully, we get a couple of these appeals across the line as well. So I think that should overall be helpful from a flow-through perspective as we move into next year.

Michael Hirsh: Yes, that's helpful context. And just a quick follow-up on Key West. I believe RevPAR was down like 10% in the quarter. So just quickly, your expectations on this asset going forward would be helpful.

Robert Springer: We're rebranding and renovating right now. So there's displacement there. We put the -- we rebranded it to Hilton Key West. Hilton is in as the manager. We have -- the asset is several buildings. So we're working through the renovation right now. So the RevPAR is a reflection of that displacement. Our expectations with the Hilton reservation system and what we've seen on the rate side so far, we think that we'll start to see some of that recover as we get into next year. But the renovation will run -- there'll be some renovation running into next year. But we're -- our expectations is then that will normalize back to where you saw it performing before.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I'll now turn the call back to Bryan Giglia for closing remarks.

Bryan Giglia: Thank you, everyone, for your time and interest, and we look forward to seeing many of you at upcoming conferences and property tours. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3224. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.

A sweeping AI ban is being proposed in the US, with penalties of up to 20 years in prison

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI is advancing at a pace that's making some lawmakers uncomfortable. Now, Senator Bernie Sanders wants to put the brakes on the most powerful AI systems before they become too difficult for humans to control.

Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, a sweeping proposal that would permanently prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States.

But the legislation goes further than banning a hypothetical future technology. It would also temporarily halt development of certain advanced AI models, establish an entirely new federal department to oversee AI and impose serious penalties on those who break the rules.

Those penalties could include up to 20 years in prison for certain individuals responsible for violations.

The bill was introduced in September and remains in committee. It hasn't become law, but it offers a look at how some lawmakers want to change the direction of AI development.

Sanders argues that AI development has reached a point where government oversight is no longer optional.

"When you are racing towards a cliff, you don't just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes," Sanders said in his September 23 announcement.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The concern is that companies developing advanced AI could eventually create systems with capabilities they don't fully understand or control. Supporters point to warnings from AI researchers and industry leaders about the potential dangers of increasingly autonomous systems.

The bill also calls for international agreements designed to prevent artificial superintelligence from being developed outside the United States.

That could be one of its biggest challenges. The Trump administration has emphasized AI development and American competitiveness in the AI arms race.

The biggest part of the proposal is a permanent ban on artificial superintelligence, or ASI.

Unlike today's AI chatbots, artificial superintelligence generally refers to a theoretical system capable of outperforming humans across most intellectual tasks.

Under the proposed legislation, that definition also includes systems powerful enough to plan and carry out actions that could destroy humanity or take away human control.

The legislation would prohibit developing, deploying, acquiring or distributing these systems. It would also restrict certain AI systems that demonstrate dangerous capabilities associated with superintelligence.

One of the more unusual aspects of the legislation is its proposal to create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence. This department would have the authority to monitor advanced AI development, establish safety requirements and inspect powerful models before they're released.

Companies would need government authorization to develop or distribute qualifying advanced AI models, and those models would require approval before deployment.

The department could also order potentially dangerous AI systems to be disconnected from the internet, modified or rendered inoperative.

The bill's enforcement provisions are particularly strict. For example, certain company decisionmakers and unaffiliated individuals who recklessly violate the law could face fines and prison sentences of up to 20 years.

Companies could also lose authorization to operate, while intellectual property and assets associated with violations could be subject to forfeiture.

For anyone using ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini today, there's no immediate reason to worry about losing access.

The legislation has not passed Congress, and there are no new restrictions on consumer AI services resulting from the proposal.

Even if it eventually became law, the bill wouldn't automatically prohibit every existing chatbot. Its restrictions focus on artificial superintelligence, dangerous AI capabilities and advanced systems that meet certain technical requirements.

However, it could affect the next generation of AI models. Companies such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are working to make AI more capable of reasoning, completing complicated tasks and operating with greater autonomy. Under the proposed legislation, qualifying future models would face federal reviews and restrictions before they could be released.

For consumers, that could mean slower releases of more powerful AI tools, although the actual impact would depend on how the law was implemented.

The larger issue is whether the government should restrict the development of AI technology before the potential risks become reality.

For now, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act remains a proposal rather than a law. But it puts a significant question before Congress: How powerful should AI be allowed to become?

#3221. 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

#3220. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3219. Apple will monitor your public iCloud links now, starting with iOS 27.3

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Under Apple's new policy, the company will scan publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content - and possibly ban violators.

Be careful what you share in your iCloud. Apple announced it will start monitoring public iCloud links for harmful content — and potentially disable accounts that violate company policy.

Also: How to free up your iPhone storage almost immediately

The change comes with the impending release of Apple’s 27.3 build across its operating systems. If an iCloud user selects “Anyone with the link” when sharing something in a group chat or Discord server, it’s considered a public link; Apple is within its rights to scan for anything that violates company policy or is potentially illegal.

If you try to upload harmful content, Apple says it reserves the right to “move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” your content at any time. Furthermore, Apple outlines possible actions it may take, including:

Apple’s announcement did not explain what “harmful content” would mean in practice. While there are obvious violations like drug sales and child sex abuse material, the new policy’s vagueness is concerning.

Once an iCloud link is shared under the “Anyone with a link” designation, end-to-end encryption is removed, even if either party has enabled Advanced Data Protection, which allows Apple to view the link’s content.

If you select “People you choose,” which limits access to users who have been invited or approved, the encryption remains in place, and Apple won’t be able to see what you’re sharing.

The new policy does not lay out an appeals process if you think your account or content has been falsely flagged as harmful. However, Apple does have a web page that provides information on how to appeal for other reasons. So there is a framework in place to push back if you think you’ve been caught in the dragnet by accident.
