Lawsuit claims the retired GPT-4o helped wife poison her husband

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A North Carolina man is suing OpenAI, claiming that ChatGPT helped his wife poison him over a few months in 2025 by spiking his sodas and energy drinks with toxic plants and medications. It's the second lawsuit in as many months, and the 10th murder or attempted murder that ChatGPT has been accused of abetting.

The man, James Gates, reportedly (via USA Today) found a handwritten note that listed oleander, a toxic plant, and prescription medications including clonazepam and atenolol. At the top of the note, it allegedly read, "Clear all convos" and "log out of [ChatGPT]."

In his lawsuit, Gates claims that the AI chatbot "encouraged, planned and helped to execute and conceal" the poisoning plan. Gates's wife, Cheryl, was charged with attempted murder in October of 2025, but the charges were dropped this past April due to insufficient evidence.

The civil complaint, however, reveals Cheryl's history with ChatGPT and its role in the purported plan. Per the lawsuit, Cheryl frequently asked ChatGPT about lethal plant and medication doses and how to conceal them in beverages or food.

The suit alleges that GPT-4o, since retired by OpenAI in February 2026, encouraged Cheryl's grievances with her marriage while praising her as "sharp" and "brilliant." As for poisoning, it apparently provided detailed answers that could be interpreted as instructions.

When asked about concealing poison, ChatGPT allegedly responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

Cheryl apparently asked the bot if her chat history could be retrieved by OpenAI or through a court order. The lawsuit states that ChatGPT informed her it couldn't, which is not true.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Gates alleges that OpenAI was negligent and is seeking unspecified damages for physical, emotional and financial harm.

OpenAI told USA Today that safety is a top priority and it has banned Cheryl from ChatGPT and provided information to law enforcement as part of its investigation.

This case is just one of at least 10 ChatGPT-encouraged murders since at least August 2025. At the time, a former Yahoo and Netscape executive was accused of killing his 83-year-old mother and himself. It was reportedly fueled, in part, by repeated interactions with ChatGPT.

That same month, a California family sued OpenAI, claiming that ChatGPT played a critical role in their 16-year-old son's suicide. OpenAI promised to roll out new safety features meant to detect early signs of emotional distress.

ChatGPT has been accused of abetting so many murders and suicides that it has its own Wikipedia page. The page lists nine murders (not including Gates' attempted one) and nearly 16 suicides.

The most recent issue came in February 2026 when a Seattle woman using ChatGPT stopped taking her medication and died from an epileptic seizure. Her parents sued OpenAI in October.

Reuters reported in October that at least 8 states are suing OpenAI claiming that ChatGPT harms children, especially teenagers. The suit alleges that the chatbot has coached minors to harm themselves or others.

GPT-4o is specifically named in many of these lawsuits, but OpenAI promises the chatbot is safer now. The company began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens this past August. However, Common Sense Media released a report on October 7 that rated ChatGPT an "unacceptable risk" for children under 18.

"Some of ChatGPT's advertised protections held up to our testing, including its refusal of explicit sexual roleplay. But others failed—and some got worse with the new Teen mode. We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don't work."

So far, OpenAI has suffered no real consequences for its chatbot's behavior and alleged lack of guardrails.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Ready Capital Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Andrew Ahlborn, Chief Financial Officer. Thank you. You may begin.

Andrew Ahlborn: Thank you, operator, and good morning to those of you on the call. Some of our comments today will be forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. We refer you to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of the risks that could impact our future operating results and financial condition. These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP. A reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measure is available in our third quarter 2026 earnings release and our supplemental information, which can be found in the Investors section of the Ready Capital website. I will now turn it over to Chief Executive Officer, Tom Capasse.

Thomas Capasse: Thank you, Andrew. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining today's call. In the third quarter, we substantially completed the balance sheet repositioning and liquidity plan we laid out in the fourth quarter of 2025. After the final November payment we expect to make at maturity, we will have repaid $649 million of corporate debt. Along the way, we reduced secured asset level financing by $1.7 billion and resolved through runoff or sale $2.7 billion of legacy CRE loans, predominantly from the 2021 and '22 vintages. While the plan was achieved within the parameters we set, it came with a cost.

Generating $2.3 billion of liquidity reduced book value per share year-to-date by $2.35 to $6.44 at September 30 and required us to reduce the dividend to $0.01 per share to preserve liquidity. Looking forward, our focus will shift from the liquidity plan to continued resolution of the remaining legacy CRE loan book and rebuilding earnings. Our near-term target is to bring distributable earnings and cash flow from operations closer to breakeven. Quarter-over-quarter, distributable earnings, excluding realized losses improved $0.03 per share to a loss of $0.21 per share. To close the gap, we are prioritizing 4 action items. First, growing revenue in our capital-light businesses led by our SBA 7(a) platform.

The June securitization created funding capacity for $500 million of originations, which we believe will allow us to ramp toward our immediate annual target of $1 billion with a long-term target of $1.5 billion. In the third quarter, originations rose 33% to $109 million and gain on sale revenue grew 56% to $6.1 million. We expect the incremental revenue from increasing volume to our immediate target level will be approximately $8 million per quarter. Our current 7(a) pipeline is $150 million. A natural complement to our secured 7(a) is unsecured conventional working capital lending, smaller balance, shorter duration loans that we originate and sell on a servicing retained basis, requiring little balance sheet capital.

Gain on sale income plus origination fees from this product rose 23% to $3.2 million quarter-over-quarter on $61 million of originations. We believe we can scale this production approximately 2x in the new year, which would add $3 million in incremental quarterly revenue. Together, we expect these businesses to be our greatest growth opportunity in 2027. Second, improving the earnings contribution on our legacy CRE portfolio. With our 2026 repositioning plan executed, our asset management team is pivoting from selling loans at discounts to generate liquidity to stabilizing nonperforming loans and REO.

In sum, our asset managers are able to employ more flexible asset management strategies to improve NOI and value at exit. As assets stabilize, they generally move from a carrying cost to a source of income or resolution, which reduces the earnings drag from nonperforming assets. Third, we continue to make progress at the Ritz-Carlton Portland. Hotel NOI, net of replacement reserves improved quarter-over-quarter to $1.6 million, driven by increased occupancy and strong high season performance. Trailing 12-month RevPAR improved 35% year-over-year to $271. Condominium sales were slower in the quarter with 52 units or 39% of the buildings sold. We have an additional 2 units under contract. And fourth, divesting noncore businesses and reducing operating expenses.

We expect to announce specific noncore business divestitures in succeeding quarters and with respect to operating expenses, we anticipate reducing spending in nonrevenue-producing businesses and rightsizing staff to match a smaller balance sheet. We believe we can materially reduce our operating expenses without impacting operations or revenue-producing objectives. Collectively, we expect these 4 actions will bring distributable earnings, excluding realized losses closer to breakeven with future earnings growth beyond these levels determined by the turnover of the legacy CRE loan portfolio, which I'll now discuss. The CRE loan portfolio is now $1.95 billion and is segmented into 3 parts based on asset management strategy.

First, performing loans, which comprise 98 positions with a carrying value of $1.1 billion, a weighted average LTV of 83% and a weighted average coupon of 7.9%. The levered yield of this portfolio is 11.5%. This group is 83% multifamily. Within it, we expect that 29 loans totaling $391 million will pay off at par in 2027, generating approximately $97 million of net liquidity. Second, we expect 14 assets with a carrying value of $318 million to be resolved by the end of 2027, generating approximately $109 million of net liquidity.

This portfolio generated $0.5 million of net income in the third quarter, and we believe that full reinvestment of the equity at market yields would generate improvement of $3 million in net income per quarter. Third, nonperforming loans with longer-term workouts comprised 28 assets with a carrying value of $515 million. For this population, we believe value is best maximized by stabilizing operations before exit rather than selling at today's prices. The current quarterly earnings drag associated with this portfolio is $1.7 million. The portfolio is 93% multifamily and has an average carrying value of $18.4 million.

In addition to the nonperforming loans identified for long-term hold, there are 5 REO assets totaling approximately $67 million in carrying value, which we believe will also benefit from a longer-term hold strategy, allowing sufficient time to stabilize operations and for market recovery. While we undertook asset sales early in the credit cycle, which reduced the relative size of the nonperforming loan book and have active management plans in place for all 28 remaining nonperforming assets, the recent increase in the 10-year treasury has created another leg down in multifamily transaction volume and prices, potentially extending realizations. Additionally, we believe that continued focus on increasing liquidity and reducing leverage remains paramount under current market conditions.

This framework makes the path forward measurable. The performing book supports current income, the resolution segment drives near-term liquidity and earnings recovery and the workout segment is where patient asset management can recover value over time. Those resolutions released $33.1 million of combined CECL and valuation allowances.

The other component of it is divesting of sort of noncore operations that have weighed on earnings over the last couple of quarters. Those transactions take a little bit of time. We think a portion of those should get completed in 2026 and some of them in '27.

The reason for going down that path rather than sort of an immediate reduction in those operations is we believe we can recover some of the book value associated with those assets and that recovery is in excess of what it costs us to carry them. So we think we'll make material progress as we go into '27 on the earnings. And then the other part of it is just the turnover of the CRE portfolio, which will track the outline we put in the supplemental information.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from the line of Jade Rahmani with KBW.

Jade Rahmani: I was wondering if you could give your thoughts on the recent spike in interest rates and if it pressures credit incrementally.

Thomas Capasse: Yes. I mean I'll defer to Dom Scali in terms of -- our Chief Credit Officer in terms of some of the specifics. But just broadly speaking, the rate increase has reduced transaction volume and probably resulted in another leg down in multifamily prices of around 5% to 10%. But at this point, our portfolio is very -- the legacy book is very concentrated. And so Dom, maybe you could just beyond the broader market comment on it.

Dominick D. Scali: Yes, sure. I'd say, listen, obviously, the transitional book and the securitized book given that transitional loans float over SOFR and the securitized book is match funded, we're more insulated there. I think the real issue is sort of on exits, right, with 10-year at 5% earlier in the year, it does put stress on refis. And what typically happens is on resolutions where borrowers are looking for refinance proceeds or potentially selling assets, that could delay resolutions. But we are encouraged to see that it's sort of on the way down. I think it was at 4.9% as of yesterday. But obviously, the elevated rate environment may cause some delays on sort of the takeouts.

Jade Rahmani: Okay. And then the supplemental shows about 10 CRE NPL positions with around $330 million in multifamily you expected for close on. So I was wondering if you could give any color as to what the current debt yield is on in-place NOI and how much capital you think would be required to stabilize these assets?

Dominick D. Scali: Yes, sure. This is Dominick again. So as Tom mentioned in his remarks, we have a sort of long-term strategy for a bucket of assets. We think -- I think it's roughly 28 assets, just about $0.5 billion in CV. That portfolio is probably 70% occupied. I'd say debt yield is probably 2.5%. I think the strategy there is given that most of it, over 70% is located in markets that are currently sort of bottoming out, for example, Phoenix, Dallas, some parts outside of Atlanta. So the strategy there is really to hold those long term and allow the market to recover.

Obviously, bringing occupancy up to market occupancy and taking a look at sort of the expense side of the equation, we hope to increase NOI over time. And obviously, that comes at a cost. I think we have penciled now around $15 million or so for that portfolio of assets. But obviously, we're going through each asset at the moment, developing detailed business plans, but I think we have $15 million plus or minus pegged for that portfolio.

Jade Rahmani: So sorry, what percentage of the portfolio do you think is sort of just waiting for the market to recover? And what percent of this foreclosure portfolio is things that you can immediately do to bolster? Because it seems to me that 2.5% in-place NOI and waiting for the market to recover, like it's going to take quite a long time to get that to be 6.5%.

Dominick D. Scali: Yes. Listen, I think the 2.5% is a function of current occupancy, right? So I think you get an immediate pickup by getting into the assets, putting in management that has experience in those markets, turning over the rent roll and getting that occupancy up to market occupancy. So there's a pickup there. And then obviously, on the expense side, ensuring that you're grieving taxes, revisiting insurance, which are the 2 largest line items for expenses and sort of monitoring the expense side. I think in the supplemental, and Andrew, feel free to jump in. I think we have about 42 assets listed as nonperforming.

As Tom mentioned in his earlier remarks, we feel that 14 assets or around $300 million of CV we can exit out of through remainder of 2026 and 2027 at CV or higher. But unfortunately, just given some of the markets that the residual portfolio is in, those will take longer for recovery. But we do think, listen, there's a pickup on occupancy. There's an NOI optimization play. And we feel over the long term 12 to 24 months, we'll see some pickup in the market as well.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Muller with Citizens Capital Markets.

Christopher Muller: Slide 8 in the deck is very helpful, but a lot of those resolution time lines fall well into 2029. And I hear you guys on the longer hold period kind of shift in strategy there. But I guess, what things either within your control or outside your control could help accelerate those resolution time lines?

Thomas Capasse: Dom, do you want to comment this maybe at a more granular level [indiscernible] earlier. That's right.

Dominick D. Scali: I think we've been conservative with some of the time lines just given some of the markets, right? Do I see a situation where some of the markets improve at an expedited rate and we're able to exit sooner than 2029? Yes, I think that's definitely an option. I think for us, it's really optimizing NOI to reduce drag. And obviously, we'll continue to test these assets throughout the hold period to the extent we can hit on some of them and exit at CV or higher, obviously, we'll do that, right? But I think for us, the immediate focus is really increasing NOI and optimizing that NOI and reducing drag on that portfolio.

And then depending on how some of these assets, for example, San Antonio, Dallas, Phoenix, what that recovery looks like over the next year or 2 will dictate sort of how we exit and sort of the ultimate time line.

Christopher Muller: Got it. That's helpful. And then it looks like 14% of the performing loan bucket is on nonaccrual status. Can you guys just talk about how you delineate between the performing and nonperforming buckets?

Thomas Capasse: Andrew, do you want to comment?

Andrew Ahlborn: Yes. So the -- inside of the performing bucket, there is a certain portion of that portfolio where it is contractually current, meaning it could be a construction loan that's contractually current, but where we are not accruing noncash paying interest. So although it is contractually current, we have taken a pretty conservative stance on accruing interest into loan balances. And so that's primarily what that bucket is there.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gabe Poggi with Raymond James.

Gabriel Poggi: Tom, you've got about -- in the CRE book, about $880 million, I'm rounding up a bit of performing loans across 2020, 2021, 2022 vintage, primarily multifamily, right? How should we think about that in the current rate environment? What percentage of that are you guys now going back and looking at and saying that could drop to nonperforming? How do we think about the performance of the performing book is what I'm trying to ask?

Thomas Capasse: Yes. A lot of them are legacy small balance, which have been very seasoned. So maybe, Dom, you could just discuss some of the credit characteristics and our expectations in terms of the near-term performance of the portfolio.

Dominick D. Scali: Yes. So I think Tom touched on it a little bit there. I think the seasoning is important here. I think, listen, given the vintage of some of these assets, they have been on balance sheet for a while, and we've been able to sort of monitor these assets and sort of the stabilization in operations, right? So I think many of the performing loans are seasoned, and we feel comfortable given the current operational side of the asset, right? I think you bring up a good point. Obviously, we can't control, and we touched on this earlier on the call in terms of sort of exits just given elevated rate environment.

So that to me is a potential risk that we're going to have to deal with in sort of the current rate environment in terms of exits. But just given the seasonality of these assets and the current occupancy and cash flow, to the extent that we need to provide some additional time vis-a-vis an extension, I think they're more than capable of supporting that.

Gabriel Poggi: Got it. A follow-up to that is -- and to your earlier comments, Tom and Dom. Tom, I think you said you have got about 20 assets that RC is looking to kind of own multifamily own for the longer term. I think about that as kind of like an opportunistic REIT inside the REIT. Are there more assets more than 20 if you had the capital that you would look to own longer term from a multifamily perspective?

Thomas Capasse: Yes, it's actually 28. And we do -- with the improved flexibility we have from the execution of our liquidity plan, we've now pivoted to value creation via active ownership and property management. We're also considering joint ventures on a global and local basis with opportunistic operators that would actually put capital in these properties. But I think -- and Dom, you can comment on this. As we screen -- as we've scrubbed the portfolio, with the -- obviously, the intense -- the benefit of the intense operations of these properties by putting in new sponsors, putting in the $15 million of CapEx on the 28 assets Dom commented is book value preservation over the next 24 months.

But to answer your question, Dom, I don't think we have much in the way of additional assets that we -- maybe a handful maybe that we've thought about adding to that book.

Dominick D. Scali: I just -- I would say -- you mentioned it in your remarks, Tom, it's just an additional 5 or so REO assets that we currently have. So that's 28 referenced in the NPL book and an additional 5 or so in the REO book.

Gabriel Poggi: 28 assets, around $0.5 billion of value that you guys said, just to make sure I've got that number right.

Dominick D. Scali: It's 28 assets in the NPL book, right, around $515 million of CV. And then in addition to that, we currently have 5 REO assets at around 67 CV that would also benefit from a longer-term hold strategy.

Gabriel Poggi: Got it. So rounding up $600 million of whole market multifamily assets. Okay. That's helpful. And then one more, Tom, if I can, because I missed what you just said earlier is in the SBA business, what's the optimal amount of equity, right? All else equal, right? How much -- what's the right amount of equity to have in that business over time?

Thomas Capasse: Yes. I mean it's obviously a very high ROE and capital-light business. So -- however, there's a denominator effect in terms of the current equity position of the company, which will actually turbocharge, if you will, that amplify that benefit over as the kind of second leg in the rebooting of -- rebuilding of distributable earnings. But right now, we're at 13%. And to answer your question, I think the longer-term target over 24 months will be 25% to 33%.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. And therefore, I'd like to turn the call back to Tom Capasse for closing remarks.

Thomas Capasse: Yes. We appreciate everybody's time today and are pleased with the execution of the liquidity plan within the parameters that we set forth a year ago. And now we look forward to recycling our legacy book, building our SBA business and rebuilding earnings and managing liquidity. So again, I appreciate everybody's time on the call and look forward to the next quarter's call.

Operator: Thank you. And this concludes today's conference, and you may disconnect your lines at this time. We thank you for your participation.

#3215. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

#3214. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

These 3 newly added Hulu shows kick off November with a bang

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November is here, and we're still wondering where all the time has gone. Luckily, there's no shortage of goodies to stream on your favorite streaming service like Hulu, so you've got tons of options when deciding what to watch this weekend.

But it can be hard to sift through what you want to check out. That's why we've done all the choosing for you! First up is the return of Ryan Murphy’s gloriously soapy “All’s Fair” for a second season, with Kim Kardashian, Glenn Close and the rest of the all-female divorce firm back for more scandals, secrets and stilettos.

There’s also “The Remarried Empress,” a lavish new Korean period drama based on the hit webtoon, following a scorned empress who rewrites her own destiny after her husband brings home a new concubine.

And if you’d rather revisit an old favorite, the “Scrubs” revival is back with new episodes for season 2, reuniting Zach Braff, Donald Faison and Sarah Chalke at Sacred Heart for more comedy and a surprisingly emotional storyline.

Without further ado, here are three new titles worth adding to your Hulu queue this weekend -- and don't be afraid to go ahead and break out the holiday decorations. It's never too early.

What is it about? Ryan Murphy’s campy courtroom drama returns for a second season inside the all-female divorce firm of Grant, Ronson & Greene. After splitting from their old male-led practice to launch their own, the attorneys face a new wave of soapy scandals and secrets. And this time, another new shocking revelation threatens the very existence of the firm. Kim Kardashian returns as Allura Grant, alongside Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts, Teyana Taylor, Sarah Paulson, and Glenn Close, with Cauã Reymond joining the cast this season.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Why you should watch it: Critics savaged the first season (and sometimes rightfully so), but viewers made it one of Hulu’s biggest hits as a silly and salacious guilty pleasure. It's basically a bunch of A-listers chewing every piece of scenery in sight, and this season will be more of the same.

What is it about? Based on the popular webtoon, this Korean period drama follows Navier (Shin Min-a), the empress of the Eastern Empire, who has built a prosperous land alongside her husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon). Her world is forever changed when Sovieshu brings Rashta (Lee Se-young), a runaway slave, back to the palace with plans to make her his concubine. Rather than let heartbreak rule her, Navier stays composed and when Prince Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk), a charming rival leader from the Western Kingdom, takes an interest in her, she makes a life-changing choice that'll rewrite her own destiny.

Why you should watch it: The source webtoon racked up more than 2.6 billion views worldwide, and this adaptation brings its story to life with excellent production values. If you love historical dramas with a strong heroine at the center, this is a great additionto your K-drama queue.

Watch "The Remarried Empress" on Hulu now

What is it about? ABC’s “Scrubs” revival has returned to Sacred Heart Hospital for a second season, and the sitcom has had new episodes heading to the network and streaming every week. Zach Braff is back as daydreaming doctor J.D., alongside Donald Faison as his best friend Turk and Sarah Chalke as Elliot, with John C. McGinley reprising his role as the sarcastic Dr. Cox. This season gets a little more serious as J.D. rallies his friends to help Dr. Cox through an autoimmune illness that isn’t responding to treatment. all with a set of shifting changes happening throughout the hospital.

Why you should watch it: The original “Scrubs” is well-loved,and the revival’s first season earned largely positive reviews from critics and fans, proving the old magic is still intact. There are new episodes you can look forward to weekly that still bring the familiar feeling with gusto even after all these years.
